errors.english_quote: For what did Christ not endure on our account, that he should be called Christ?
errors.source_quote: Τί γὰρ δι' ἡμᾶς οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν κληθῆναι Χριστός;
errors.why: Χριστός is the subject; τί is what he submitted to be called (κληθῆναι depends on ὑπέμεινεν). The line introduces the list of names that follows. The English invents a purpose clause about being called 'Christ' and breaks the link to the list.
errors.corrected_english: For what did Christ not submit to be called for our sake?

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the claim. The source is quoted correctly. In section u01-rem-mid of translations/adrb_u01_rem_source.json, the Greek reads "Τί γὰρ δι' ἡμᾶς οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν κληθῆναι Χριστός;". The live English in translations/adrb_u01_rem_english.json reads "For what did Christ not endure on our account, that he should be called Christ?"

The natural parse makes Χριστός the subject of ὑπέμεινεν. κληθῆναι is the infinitive that completes it ("submit to be called"), and τί stands for what he was called. The next sentence confirms this reading: "We cannot count his names..." followed by a list that includes humble ones (sheep, worm, stone). The point is that Christ let himself be called even "worm" for our sake.

The live English takes Χριστός as the name he was called and turns κληθῆναι into a purpose clause ("that he should be called Christ"). The grammar can just about bear that, but it makes no sense here. It says Christ suffered in order to earn the title "Christ," and it cuts the link to the list of names.

This is a real error in meaning, not a matter of style. "High" severity may overstate it, but it is a genuine fix. The proposed correction, "For what did Christ not submit to be called for our sake?", is faithful. A smoother equivalent would be "For what name did Christ not submit to be called for our sake?" Adding "name" makes the implied object explicit and leads into the list.
verdict.better_correction: For what name did Christ not submit to be called for our sake?

errors.english_quote: But since each of us, beloved, receives also the honey-flowing teaching of the fathers, let us seal here the purse of our words with the Holy Spirit, so that when they come from the honey-dripping wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ they may fill the cisterns of our hearts,
errors.source_quote: Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ ἕκαστος ἡμῶν, ἀγαπητοί, ἐκδέχεται καὶ τὴν τῶν πατέρων μελίρρυτον διδασκαλίαν, ἐνταῦθα τὸ βαλάντιον ἡμῶν τῶν λόγων σφραγισώμεθα ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, ἵνα αὐτοὶ ἐλθόντες ἐκ τῆς μελισταγοῦς σοφίας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τὰς δεξαμενὰς τῶν καρδιῶν ἡμῶν πληρώσωσιν
errors.why: ἐκδέχεται means 'is waiting for', not 'receives': the preacher stops because the people expect the other fathers to speak next. αὐτοὶ ἐλθόντες are those fathers coming up to speak; the English makes 'they' read as 'our words'.
errors.corrected_english: But since each of us, beloved, is also waiting for the honey-flowing teaching of the fathers, let us seal here the purse of our words with the Holy Spirit, so that the fathers themselves may come and, from the honey-dripping wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, fill the cisterns of our hearts,

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. I checked translations/adrb_u01_rem_source.json and adrb_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close, and both quotes match the files exactly.

1. ἐκδέχεται here means "waits for / expects", as in its usual Koine sense (1 Cor 11:33, Heb 11:10). The clause gives the reason the preacher stops: the people expect the fathers to speak next, so he "seals the purse" of his own words. "Receives" loses that reason. It reads as a general habit and does not explain why he stops.

2. αὐτοὶ ἐλθόντες ("they themselves, having come") is masculine plural. The emphatic αὐτοί sets them against "us / our words", so it refers to the fathers (τῶν πατέρων). Words just sealed in a purse cannot "come" and fill the cisterns. The current English, "so that when they come... they may fill", leaves "they" nearest to "our words" and hides who is meant.

This is a real change of sense and referent, not a style choice.

The proposed correction is faithful. It renders ἐκδέχεται as "is also waiting for" (keeping καί), names the fathers for αὐτοί, and turns the participle ἐλθόντες into "may come and". Attaching ἐκ τῆς μελισταγοῦς σοφίας to "fill" rather than "come" is a defensible reading, since the Greek allows either. A version that stays closer to the word order would also work: "so that the fathers themselves, coming from the honey-dripping wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, may fill the cisterns of our hearts."

errors.english_quote: “Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:10).
errors.source_quote: Ἵππον καὶ ἀναβάτην ἔρριψεν εἰς θάλασσαν.
errors.why: This line is Exodus 15:1 (repeated at 15:21). Exodus 15:10 is 'You sent your wind, the sea covered them'.
errors.corrected_english: “Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1).

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. In ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/amphilochius-de-recens-baptizatis/translations/adrb_u01_rem_source.json the Greek reads "Τί γὰρ πεποίηκεν; Ἵππον καὶ ἀναβάτην ἔρριψεν εἰς θάλασσαν." adrb_u01_rem_english.json renders this as "“Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:10)." The Greek is word for word Exodus 15:1 in the LXX ("ἵππον καὶ ἀναβάτην ἔρριψεν εἰς θάλασσαν"). Miriam repeats it at 15:21. Exodus 15:10 is a different verse, "You sent your wind, the sea covered them." So the reference is wrong. The neighboring references are correct: 15:1 for "Let us sing to the Lord" and 15:4 for Pharaoh and his army. Changing 15:10 to 15:1 is faithful. "(Exodus 15:1, 21)" would also work, since Amphilochius says he is borrowing Miriam's song, but 15:1 alone is enough.
verdict.better_correction: “Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1).

errors.english_quote: What meadow possesses such fragrance as our meadow, which perfumes the grace of the Spirit?
errors.source_quote: Ποῖος λειμὼν τοιαύτην εὐωδίαν κέκτηται οἵαν ὁ ἡμέτερος λειμὼν τὴν τοῦ πνεύματος ἀρωματίζουσαν χάριν;
errors.why: ἀρωματίζουσαν agrees with χάριν: the Spirit's grace gives off the fragrance, and it is the object of the implied κέκτηται. The English turns it round so the meadow perfumes the grace.
errors.corrected_english: What meadow possesses such a fragrance as our meadow possesses: the fragrant grace of the Spirit?

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in adrb_u01_open_source.json reads exactly as quoted: "Ποῖος λειμὼν τοιαύτην εὐωδίαν κέκτηται οἵαν ὁ ἡμέτερος λειμὼν τὴν τοῦ πνεύματος ἀρωματίζουσαν χάριν;". The participle ἀρωματίζουσαν is accusative feminine singular. It sits inside the article-noun group τὴν ... χάριν, so it is attributive to χάριν: "the grace of the Spirit that gives off fragrance". It cannot modify λειμὼν, which is nominative masculine. With κέκτηται understood a second time after οἵαν, the line says: "What meadow possesses such fragrance as our meadow possesses: the fragrance-giving grace of the Spirit?" The live English, "our meadow, which perfumes the grace of the Spirit", makes the meadow the subject and the grace the thing perfumed. That reverses the roles and so changes the meaning; it is not a matter of style. The next sentence ("you will find in them the immortal fragrance of the Spirit") confirms that the Spirit is the source of the fragrance. The proposed correction keeps the Greek syntax and is faithful. An optional, slightly closer wording: "the grace of the Spirit that breathes out fragrance".
verdict.better_correction: What meadow possesses such a fragrance as our meadow possesses: the fragrant grace of the Spirit?

errors.english_quote: like a pearl in an oyster between two folds, he was born from a virgin without the seed of a man,
errors.source_quote: ὥσπερ μαργαρίτην ἐν μύακι ἀνὰ μέσον δύο πτυχῶν σώματος καὶ ψυχῆς παρθενικῆς ἄνευ σπορᾶς ἀνδρὸς γεγεννῆσθαι
errors.why: The English drops what the two folds are: the virgin's body and soul. That phrase is the point of the image.
errors.corrected_english: like a pearl in an oyster between two folds, the virgin's body and soul, he was born without the seed of a man,

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in adrb_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-close, reads exactly as quoted: "ὥσπερ μαργαρίτην ἐν μύακι ἀνὰ μέσον δύο πτυχῶν σώματος καὶ ψυχῆς παρθενικῆς ἄνευ σπορᾶς ἀνδρὸς γεγεννῆσθαι". The genitives σώματος καὶ ψυχῆς παρθενικῆς name the two folds: the virgin's body and soul. The English in adrb_u01_rem_english.json says "between two folds, he was born from a virgin without the seed of a man". It keeps only "virgin" and drops "body and soul", so the reader cannot tell what the two folds are, and that is the whole point of the oyster image. This is a real omission, not a style choice. The proposed correction is faithful. Putting "the virgin's body and soul" in apposition carries the genitive, and "virgin" is not lost. A slightly closer wording keeps the genitive: "between the two folds of a virgin's body and soul".
verdict.better_correction: like a pearl in an oyster between the two folds of a virgin's body and soul, he was born without the seed of a man,

errors.english_quote: for in Mary her fault has been saved;
errors.source_quote: ἐν γὰρ Μαρίᾳ τὸ ταύτης πταῖσμα ἀνασέσωσται·
errors.why: 'A fault has been saved' is not sense in English. ἀνασέσωσται here means the lapse has been retrieved or made good.
errors.corrected_english: for in Mary her fall has been made good;

verdict.reason: The claim's quotes are exact. In adrb_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-mid reads "Οὐκέτι Εὔα φοβεῖται τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν τοῦ Ἀδάμ, ἐν γὰρ Μαρίᾳ τὸ ταύτης πταῖσμα ἀνασέσωσται". The English in adrb_u01_rem_english.json has "for in Mary her fault has been saved;". Here πταῖσμα means a stumble, lapse or fall. ἀνασώζω means to rescue, recover or restore. The Greek therefore says Eve's fall has been retrieved or set right in Mary: the Eve-Mary pairing, with the second woman undoing the first woman's fall. "Her fault has been saved" makes the sin itself the thing rescued, which is not sense in English and blurs the point. This is a real defect in the English, not a style preference, though the severity is low. The proposed "for in Mary her fall has been made good" is faithful. "Fall" suits πταῖσμα, and "made good" carries the sense of restoring or recovering in ἀνα-σώζω. "Her fall has been repaired" or "her stumble has been set right" would also be acceptable.

errors.english_quote: I mean the myrrh of the heavenly anointing.
errors.source_quote: λέγω δὴ τὸ τοῦ οὐρανίου χρίσματος μύρον.
errors.why: μύρον is perfumed oil or chrism, not myrrh (σμύρνα). Here it is the baptismal chrism.
errors.corrected_english: I mean the ointment of the heavenly anointing.

verdict.reason:
I checked translations/adrb_u01_open_source.json and the matching English file. The quoted Greek and English both match the files exactly: "λέγω δὴ τὸ τοῦ οὐρανίου χρίσματος μύρον" is rendered "I mean the myrrh of the heavenly anointing."

The claim stands. μύρον means perfumed oil or ointment, and here it means the baptismal chrism. It does not mean myrrh, the resin, which is σμύρνα. Some Orthodox English calls chrism "Holy Myrrh," so the choice is not baseless. But this site is for general readers, and to them "myrrh" means the resin, which turns a sacramental oil into a burial spice. The surrounding text stresses fragrance (εὐωδία, ἀρωματίζουσαν), which points to the perfumed oil.

The proposed "ointment" is faithful. "Fragrant ointment" would fit the fragrance imagery slightly better.

The severity is low and correctly rated.
verdict.better_correction: I mean the fragrant ointment of the heavenly anointing.

errors.english_quote: When the season of spring succeeds the gloom of winter,
errors.source_quote: Τοῦ μακαρίου Ἀμφιλοχίου ἐπισκόπου Ἰκονίου περὶ τῶν νεοφωτίστων καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀνάστασιν τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
errors.why: The superscription is in the locked source and left out of the English. It says the homily is also on the Resurrection, which the work title does not say.
errors.corrected_english: Of the blessed Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium: on the newly baptized and on the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ. When the season of spring succeeds the gloom of winter,

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The locked source for u01-open (adrb_u01_open_source.json) begins "De recens baptizatis Τοῦ μακαρίου Ἀμφιλοχίου ἐπισκόπου Ἰκονίου περὶ τῶν νεοφωτίστων καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀνάστασιν τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ." and then "Ὁπόταν τὸ σκυθρωπὸν τοῦ χειμῶνος…". The English (adrb_u01_open_english.json) opens directly with "When the season of spring succeeds the gloom of winter," and nothing renders the superscription. The section title is "The spiritual spring of the newly baptized", the book title is "On the Newly Baptized", and the meta file has no resurrection title either. So the attribution (blessed Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium) and the second subject ("and on the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ") are missing from the English. The repo has no consistent rule here: cyril-alexandria-glaphyra translates its superscription ("Of our father among the saints Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria: ..."), so leaving this one out is not a house convention. It is a low-severity omission of a heading, not of the homily's body. The proposed wording is faithful. Two small notes: render it as its own heading paragraph (english[0]) rather than running it into the first sentence; and leave out the Latin editorial label "De recens baptizatis", which is not part of the Greek.
verdict.better_correction: Separate first paragraph: "Of the blessed Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium: On the newly baptized, and on the resurrection of our Savior Jesus Christ." The body then starts unchanged with "When the season of spring succeeds the gloom of winter, ..."

errors.english_quote: darting past people's heads, and cast their own cry into human ears.
errors.source_quote: τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων κεφαλὰς παρατρέχουσαι δίκην ἄνθους τὴν οἰκείαν κλαγγὴν τοῖς ὠσὶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐμβάλλουσιν
errors.why: δίκην ἄνθους ('like a flower') is left out without comment. The phrase is odd and may be corrupt, but it is in the locked text.
errors.corrected_english: darting past people's heads like a blossom, and cast their own cry into human ears.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim. The locked Greek in adrb_u01_open_source.json (u01-open) reads exactly as quoted: "καὶ τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων κεφαλὰς παρατρέχουσαι δίκην ἄνθους τὴν οἰκείαν κλαγγὴν τοῖς ὠσὶν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐμβάλλουσιν". The live English says "darting past people's heads, and cast their own cry into human ears." It has nothing for δίκην ἄνθους ("like a flower"). The phrase is odd and may be corrupt; ἄνθους may stand for some other word. Even so, the translator dropped it silently. The translator notes say only "Lacunae marked [...]", and nothing marks this spot. So this is a real omission of locked source words, not a choice of wording. The severity is correctly low. The proposed fix, "darting past people's heads like a blossom, and cast their own cry into human ears," is faithful. δίκην + genitive singular means "like a blossom/flower", and it most naturally goes with the participle παρατρέχουσαι that comes just before it. A short translator note would help, saying that δίκην ἄνθους is odd and may be corrupt.
verdict.better_correction: darting past people's heads like a blossom, and cast their own cry into human ears. [Translator note: 'like a blossom' (δίκην ἄνθους) is odd in context and the text may be corrupt; rendered as printed in PG 39.]

works.notes: I checked all 7 sections in 3 files against the locked Greek of Routh's Reliquiae Sacrae (from Eusebius, Church History 5.16-17). Each source section matches an English section, with no missing or extra sections. Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 are clean. Fix 2.1 first: its last sentence reverses the author's disclaimer, and it drops 'they say it happened so.' Section 2.2 has three medium errors: 'against Asterius Urbanus' should be 'by/of Asterius Urbanus'; 'let it be refuted' should be the active 'prove it'; and Zoticus and Julian are the people who were present to test the spirit. Not reported: in 2.1 the English adds 'so-called' to Theodotus, which really belongs to 'prophecy'. Not part of the English text: the 3.3 'orientation' says the author 'is quoting from a Montanist writing against Miltiades', which is wrong. The author is writing against the Montanists and quoting himself, as Eusebius reports. The 3.2 orientation also says the words were 'just quoted'. Grok's red-team report (websites/fathers.saneapps.com/outputs/redteam-20261006) mentions anonymous-antimontanist only for audio, downloads and docx. It has no translation finding for this work, so it adds nothing here. I ran no paid calls or builds and edited no files.

errors.english_quote: But do not think, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them.
errors.source_quote: ἀλλὰ μὴ ἄνευ τοῦ ἰδεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐπίστασθαί τῶν τοιούτων νομίζομεν ὦ μακάριε.
errors.why: In the Greek the author denies that he knows these things, because he did not see them. The English tells the reader not to think he lacks first-hand knowledge, which implies he saw them. That contradicts the next sentence ('perhaps ... perhaps not').
errors.corrected_english: But we do not suppose, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them.

verdict.reason:
The source matches the quote, in antimont_u2_source.json §2.1: "ἀλλὰ μὴ ἄνευ τοῦ ἰδεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐπίστασθαί τῶν τοιούτων νομίζομεν ὦ μακάριε." Eusebius HE 5.16.14 has the same line as the hortatory subjunctive νομίζωμεν. In either reading, the subject of "suppose" is the first person plural ("we"). The author is warning himself and his own side not to claim knowledge of things they did not witness. The next sentence ("ἴσως μὲν γὰρ οὕτως, ἴσως δὲ οὐχ' οὕτως", "perhaps so, perhaps not") confirms this.

The live English, "But do not think, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them", has two problems:
1. It changes the subject to "you" (an order to the reader).
2. It reads naturally as "don't assume our knowledge is second-hand", which suggests the author did see these things. That is the opposite of the author's disclaimer, and it clashes with the "perhaps ... perhaps not" that follows.

So the claim stands: wrong person, with a sense that flips in normal reading.

The proposed fix ("But we do not suppose ...") puts back "we", but the dangling "without having seen them" keeps the same double meaning. It also misses an omission in the same spot: the sentence just before, "φασὶ γοῦν τοῦτο οὕτω γεγονέναι" ("At any rate, they say this is how it happened"), is missing from the English altogether.

Better rendering, from "and having been hurled down, died miserably." onward: "At any rate, they say it happened this way. But let us not suppose, blessed one, that we have knowledge of such things when we did not see them. For perhaps Montanus and Theodotus and the woman mentioned above died in this way, and perhaps not."
verdict.better_correction: At any rate, they say it happened this way. But let us not suppose, blessed one, that we have knowledge of such things when we did not see them.

errors.english_quote: and having been hurled down, died miserably. But do not think, blessed one,
errors.source_quote: καὶ δισκευθέντα, κακῶς τελευτῆσαι. φασὶ γοῦν τοῦτο οὕτω γεγονέναι.
errors.why: The English drops the sentence 'At any rate, they say this happened so.' That sentence is the author's hedge that the story is only hearsay, and it leads into the next sentence.
errors.corrected_english: and having been hurled down, died miserably. At any rate, they say it happened in this way. But we do not suppose, blessed one,

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked antimont_u2_source.json §2.1. The Greek has "καὶ δισκευθέντα, κακῶς τελευτῆσαι. φασὶ γοῦν τοῦτο οὕτω γεγονέναι. ἀλλὰ μὴ ἄνευ τοῦ ἰδεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐπίστασθαί τῶν τοιούτων νομίζομεν ὦ μακάριε." In antimont_u2_english.json §2.1, the English goes straight from "died miserably" to "But do not think, blessed one". The sentence "φασὶ γοῦν τοῦτο οὕτω γεγονέναι" ("at any rate, they say it happened this way") is missing. It is a real omission: it marks the Theodotus story as hearsay, which sets up the disclaimer that follows. The English also has a second, smaller error next to it. "νομίζομεν" is first person plural ("let us not suppose" / "we do not suppose"), but the English turns it into an order to the reader, "do not think". The proposed fix restores the missing sentence and corrects the person, so it is faithful. As written, though, it stops mid-sentence. It needs the rest of the clause, "that we know such things without having seen them", to read correctly.
verdict.better_correction: and having been hurled down, died miserably. At any rate, they say it happened this way. But let us not suppose, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them.

errors.english_quote: in that same work against Asterius Urbanus
errors.source_quote: ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν
errors.why: Here κατά with the accusative names the author or compiler of the work: the book 'of' or 'according to' Asterius Urbanus, the Montanist who collected Maximilla's sayings. It is not a book against him. 'Against' changes which side the work was on.
errors.corrected_english: in that same work by Asterius Urbanus

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source (antimont_u2_source.json §2.2) reads exactly "ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τῷ κατὰ Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανὸν", and the live English has "in that same work against Asterius Urbanus". Here κατά takes the accusative (Ἀστέριον Οὐρβανόν). The "against" sense of κατά needs the genitive, so the case alone rules out "against". The accusative gives "according to / by", the same use as in the Gospel titles. The context agrees. The author is telling the spirit of Maximilla not to say its saying "in that same work", so the work held Maximilla's oracles. That makes it a Montanist collection credited to Asterius Urbanus, not an anti-Montanist book. Standard translations agree: McGiffert (NPNF) has "in the same work according to Asterius Urbanus", and Williamson has "in the book by Asterius Urbanus". Saying "against" puts the book on the wrong side of the dispute, so this is a real error of sense, not a style choice. The proposed "in that same work by Asterius Urbanus" is faithful. "Compiled by" would be a defensible gloss, but it is not needed.
verdict.better_correction: in that same work by Asterius Urbanus

errors.english_quote: But let it clearly show the power in the spirit and let it be refuted.
errors.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ πνεύματι δύναμιν ἐναργῶς δειξάτω καὶ ἐλεγξάτω
errors.why: ἐλεγξάτω is active, and its object is the same power: the spirit is challenged to show and prove its power. The English turns it into a passive 'let it be refuted', which reverses the challenge.
errors.corrected_english: But let it show the power in the spirit clearly, and prove it.

verdict.reason: I checked translations/antimont_u2_source.json and antimont_u2_english.json for §2.2 (Eusebius, Church History 5.16.17), and the claim stands. The Greek reads "ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ πνεύματι δύναμιν ἐναργῶς δειξάτω καὶ ἐλεγξάτω". Both verbs are active third-person imperatives. Their subject is the spirit speaking through Maximilla, and τὴν ἐν τῷ πνεύματι δύναμιν is the object of both, so ἐλεγξάτω means "let it prove (demonstrate) it". The live English says "let it be refuted". That makes the verb passive and turns the author's challenge (prove your power) into the opposite (let it be disproved). The standard English translations of this passage also read it as active: "let him show clearly and prove the power in the spirit". The passive "be refuted" does belong a few lines later, where the Greek has the passive infinitive ἐλεγχθῆναι ("did not allow the false spirit to be refuted by them"). The translator seems to have carried that later sense back into this clause. This is a real reversal of sense, not a matter of style. The proposed fix is faithful. A smoother version that keeps the Greek structure is in better_correction.
verdict.better_correction: But let it clearly show and prove the power in the spirit.

errors.english_quote: And let it compel those who were present then to confess through the spirit, so that men of repute and bishops, Zoticus from the village of Comana and Julian from Apamea, might test and speak with the spirit speaking.
errors.source_quote: καὶ ἐξομολογεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος καταναγκασάτω τοὺς τότε παρόντας· εἰς τὸ δοκιμάσαι καὶ διαλεχθῆναι τῷ πνεύματι λαλοῦντι, ἄνδρας δοκίμους καὶ ἐπισκόπους, Ζωτικὸν ἀπὸ Κομάνης κώμης, καὶ Ἰουλιανὸν ἀπὸ Ἀπαμείας.
errors.why: In the Greek, 'those then present' are Zoticus and Julian, who came in order to test the spirit and question it. The spirit is challenged to make them confess it. The English treats the bishops as a separate group and makes their testing a result of the confession, so it misstates who was present and why.
errors.corrected_english: And let it compel through the spirit, to confess it, those who were then present to test and question the spirit as it spoke: approved men and bishops, Zoticus from the village of Comana and Julian from Apamea.

verdict.reason: I checked the source (antimont_u2_source.json §2.2), and the claim holds. The Greek reads "ἐξομολογεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος καταναγκασάτω τοὺς τότε παρόντας· εἰς τὸ δοκιμάσαι καὶ διαλεχθῆναι τῷ πνεύματι λαλοῦντι, ἄνδρας δοκίμους καὶ ἐπισκόπους, Ζωτικὸν … καὶ Ἰουλιανὸν". The accusative "ἄνδρας δοκίμους καὶ ἐπισκόπους" stands in apposition to "τοὺς τότε παρόντας", and "εἰς τὸ δοκιμάσαι" says why they were present: to test and question the spirit. The next clause confirms this. "ὧν … τὰ στόματα φιμώσαντες" says the Themison party silenced these same men, so that the spirit was not refuted "ὑπ' αὐτῶν", that is, by those who came to test it. This matches the standard reading (McGiffert, NPNF: "those who were then present for the purpose of testing and conversing with the spirit … those eminent men and bishops"). The live English says "compel those who were present then to confess … so that men of repute and bishops … might test". That turns the testing into a result of the forced confession and reads as if the bishops were a group apart from those present. The logic comes out wrong: the bishops testing the spirit is the purpose of their presence, not something the confession leads to. Grammatically, one could take ἄνδρας as the accusative subject of the articular infinitive. But the English that results makes no sense in context and does not fit the follow-up "ὧν … ὑπ' αὐτῶν", so this is a real error of construction, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful. Its "to confess it" supplies an object the Greek leaves implied, which is acceptable. A slightly closer version that keeps the current wording is in better_correction.
verdict.better_correction: And let it compel, through the spirit, those who were then present to confess it, those who were there to test and converse with the spirit as it spoke, men of repute and bishops, Zoticus from the village of Comana and Julian from Apamea.

errors.english_quote: that I might seem to some people to be adding to or taking away from the word of the new covenant of the gospel
errors.source_quote: μή πῃ δόξω τισὶν ἐπισυγγράφειν ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι τῷ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου καινῆς διαθήκης λόγῳ
errors.why: Both verbs mean adding: writing additions and adding new provisions, as with a codicil (compare Gal 3:15). Nothing in the clause means 'taking away'. That idea appears only in the next clause (μήτε προσθεῖναι μήτ’ ἀφελεῖν), so the English moves it forward and loses the author's point.
errors.corrected_english: that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to, or adding new provisions to, the word of the new covenant of the gospel

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against the source and the English in antimont_u1_source.json and antimont_u1_english.json, section 1.1, and it holds. The Greek reads "μή πῃ δόξω τισὶν ἐπισυγγράφειν ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι τῷ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου καινῆς διαθήκης λόγῳ". Both verbs mean adding. ἐπισυγγράφειν means to write something more onto a document. ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι means to add provisions to a will, as with a codicil; Gal 3:15 uses the same verb for adding to a ratified covenant. Nothing in this clause means "take away". The live English, "adding to or taking away from the word of the new covenant", takes the idea of removing from the next clause, "ᾧ μήτε προσθεῖναι μήτ’ ἀφελεῖν δυνατὸν", and puts it here too early. The author's worry is that a new treatise could look like a supplement to the gospel. Standard English versions agree: McGiffert has "add to the writings or injunctions of the word of the new covenant". This is a small error of sense, so severity low is right. The proposed correction is faithful but a little clumsy. A smoother faithful version: "that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to the word of the new covenant of the gospel, or adding new provisions to it".
verdict.better_correction: that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to the word of the new covenant of the gospel, or adding new provisions to it

errors.english_quote: There, they say, one of the newly converted, named Montanus, in the time of Gratus, proconsul of Asia,
errors.source_quote: ἔνθα φασὶ τινὰ τῶν νεοπίστων, πρώτως, Μοντανὸν τοὔνομα, κατὰ Γράτον Ἀσίας ἀνθύπατον
errors.why: The English leaves out πρώτως ('first'). The Greek says Montanus was the first to give the adversary entrance, which marks him as the founder.
errors.corrected_english: There, they say, one of the newly converted, named Montanus, first, in the time of Gratus, proconsul of Asia,

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In antimont_u1_source.json §1.2 the Greek reads "ἔνθα φασὶ τινὰ τῶν νεοπίστων, πρώτως, Μοντανὸν τοὔνομα, κατὰ Γράτον Ἀσίας ἀνθύπατον, ... δόντα πάροδον εἰς ἑαυτὸν τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ". The English in antimont_u1_english.json says "There, they say, one of the newly converted, named Montanus, in the time of Gratus, proconsul of Asia, gave entrance into himself to the adversary". Nothing in that sentence renders πρώτως. The word goes with δόντα πάροδον: Montanus was the first to let the adversary in. That makes him the starting point of the movement, which is the point of the passage, so the gap is a real omission, though a small one. The low severity is right. The proposed fix is faithful in meaning but reads badly. In "named Montanus, first, in the time of Gratus" the bare "first," hangs loose, and a reader could take it as "first in time" or as a list marker. "First" belongs on the verb it modifies.
verdict.better_correction: There, they say, one of the newly converted, named Montanus, in the time of Gratus, proconsul of Asia, first gave entrance into himself to the adversary through an unbounded desire of soul for preeminence.

errors.english_quote: Then again, after saying other things in between to refute the false prophecies of Maximilla,
errors.source_quote: ἐν ταυτῷ δὲ πάλιν ἕτερα μεταξὺ πρὸς ἔλεγχον τῶν τῆς Μαξιμίλλης ψυδοπροφητειῶν εἰπὼν
errors.why: The English leaves out ἐν ταυτῷ ('in the same work'). That phrase is Eusebius telling the reader that the next quotation, the 'thirteen years' passage, comes from the same book.
errors.corrected_english: Then again in the same work, after saying other things in between to refute the false prophecies of Maximilla,

verdict.reason: The source quote matches antimont_u2_source.json §2.2 word for word, typo ψυδοπροφητειῶν included. The English reads "Then again, after saying other things in between...". That covers πάλιν and ἕτερα μεταξὺ ... εἰπὼν but has no word for ἐν ταυτῷ (= ἐν ταὐτῷ, "in the same [work]"). This is Eusebius's own transition. It tells the reader that the "thirteen years" quotation comes from the same book as the Maximilla passage before it. Leaving it out loses a small, real point about where the quotation comes from. It is not a style choice, though the severity is low, as the claim says. The proposed fix, "Then again in the same work, after saying other things in between to refute the false prophecies of Maximilla," is faithful. works.notes: I checked all 8 sections, sentence by sentence, against the locked PG Greek in /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/cyril-jerusalem-homilia-paralyticum/translations/. Nothing was edited.

errors.english_quote: but let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon.
errors.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ προσδράμωμεν
errors.why: ἁρματιῶν is a typo for ἁμαρτιῶν ('of sins'). The translator read it as ἅρμα ('chariot') and wrote 'charioteer'. Cyril closes with 'the one who forgives sins'; no charioteer is in the text.
errors.corrected_english: but let us run to the one who forgives sins.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The last sentence of u01-rem-close in cjhp_u01_rem_source.json reads "Ἀκουέτω τοίνυν ἅπας Ἰησοῦ καὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτανέτω, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ προσδράμωμεν." The word ἁρματιῶν is a letter swap for ἁμαρτιῶν ("of sins"), not a real form. The intended phrase is τῷ ἁμαρτιῶν συγχωρητῇ, "the forgiver of sins", which fits the whole passage on "sin no more". The English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json says "but let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon." That reads the typo as something from ἅρμα ("chariot") and invents a charioteer that is not in the text. The translator likely carried the image over from u01-rem-early, where "charioteer of the sea" and "charioteer and maker of the waters" do come from the source. Here it does not fit: it changes the sense and drops "of sins". The proposed fix, "but let us run to the one who forgives sins.", is faithful, since συγχωρητής means pardoner or forgiver. "The forgiver of sins" would work equally well.

errors.english_quote: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters? Rise, take up your mat and walk."
errors.source_quote: τί περιμένεις τὰ μικρά; τί ζητεῖς ὑδάτων ἰατρείαν; ἔγειραι, ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν.
errors.why: The Greek says only 'Rise,' and adds 'the Resurrection said to you,' a deliberate wordplay naming Christ as the Resurrection (it sets up the list 'resurrection to the dead' that follows). The English drops that title and adds 'take up your mat and walk', which the source does not have here. The full command first appears in the next paragraph (§10).
errors.corrected_english: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this claim. The source matches the quote exactly. cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, §9 of section u01-rem-early, reads: "ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· τί περιμένεις τὰ μικρά; τί ζητεῖς ὑδάτων ἰατρείαν; ἔγειραι, ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν. πανταχοῦ γὰρ ... νεκροῖς ἀνάστασις ...". The live English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, paragraph 5, reads: 'And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters? Rise, take up your mat and walk."'

The English makes two errors:
1. It drops "ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν" ("the Resurrection said to you"). This is the play on ἔγειραι/ἀνάστασις, naming Christ as the Resurrection, and it sets up "resurrection to the dead" in the very next sentence.
2. It adds "take up your mat and walk", which the Greek does not have here. That phrase first appears at the start of §10 ("Ἔγειραι, ἆρόν σου τὸν κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει"), and the English already renders it there as paragraph 6, so it now appears twice.

This is a real omission plus an addition, not a style choice. The proposed correction is faithful. It should keep the lead-in "And he says to him:", giving: And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.
verdict.better_correction: And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.

errors.english_quote: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and he was bound by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.
errors.source_quote: καὶ εἰ ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, ἀλλὰ στέφανος, καὶ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος. βασιλεῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν ἀναγορεύονται.
errors.why: δεδεμένος agrees with στέφανος: the crown was plaited (bound) by soldiers. The point is that soldiers crowned him, as soldiers proclaim kings. The English makes Christ the one 'bound', which breaks the argument.
errors.corrected_english: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and one plaited by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.

verdict.reason: The quote matches the locked source exactly (cjhp_u01_rem_source.json and cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-mid, §12). In Greek "καὶ εἰ ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, ἀλλὰ στέφανος, καὶ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος", the masculine nominative δεδεμένος matches ὁ στέφανος, which is the only nominative subject in that clause. Christ is not named in the nominative anywhere nearby; the last mention is "βασιλεὺς γὰρ ἦν", two sentences earlier. The words read as "a crown, and [a crown] bound by soldiers", which echoes Matthew 27:29, where the soldiers plait the crown of thorns. The next sentence, "βασιλεῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν ἀναγορεύονται", only follows if soldiers crowning him is the royal sign, in line with the purple robe before it. Christ being tied up is not a sign of kingship, so "he was bound by soldiers" gives the wrong referent and breaks the argument. This is a real faithfulness error, not a style preference. The proposed fix "and one plaited by soldiers" is faithful. δέω means bind or tie, and "plaited" or "woven" is a normal English word for making a wreath. A closer literal option would be "and one bound together by soldiers", but the proposed wording is fine.
verdict.better_correction: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and one plaited by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.

errors.english_quote: For the apostle does not want us to take ourselves completely out of the world and do no evil; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh
errors.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀπόστολος τελείως ἑαυτοὺς ἐξαγαγόντας ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι φαῦλον
errors.why: The participle gives the means: the apostle does not want us to avoid evil by leaving the world entirely. As written, the English reads as if the apostle does not want us to 'do no evil'.
errors.corrected_english: For the apostle does not want us to avoid doing evil by taking ourselves completely out of the world; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh

verdict.reason: The quotes match. The Greek in u01-rem-close §18 (cjhp_u01_rem_source.json) reads: "οὐ γὰρ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀπόστολος τελείως ἑαυτοὺς ἐξαγαγόντας ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι φαῦλον, ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντας ἡμᾶς καταδουλῶσαι τὴν σάρκα". The aorist participle ἐξαγαγόντας tells how: the apostle does not want us to keep from doing evil by leaving the world entirely. He wants us to master the flesh while still in it, and the ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντας contrast confirms this. The live English (cjhp_u01_rem_english.json) has "does not want us to take ourselves completely out of the world and do no evil". Joining the two with "and" makes them two separate things the apostle does not want. The plain reading is then that he does not want us to "do no evil", which is close to the reverse of the sense. This is a real error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction, "does not want us to avoid doing evil by taking ourselves completely out of the world; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh", keeps the participle as the means and is faithful. When applied, the edit should keep the existing "and not be ruled by it" (καὶ μὴ ἄρχεσθαι ὑπ' αὐτῆς) that follows.

errors.english_quote: Train the passions away from the passionless text.
errors.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε.
errors.why: Cyril tells the reader to use the passionless (chaste) words to retrain the passions, that is, to read the bridal language chastely. 'Away from the passionless text' suggests turning away from the text, which is the opposite.
errors.corrected_english: Use what is free of passion to retrain the passions.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly: the Greek in cjhp_u01_rem_source.json reads "μηδὲ ἐμπαθῶς ἄκουε ταῦτα, ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε". μεταγυμνάζω means "train differently, retrain". ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν means "out of / by means of the passionless things", meaning the chaste bridal words Cyril has just described as "nuptial, sober, chaste". The Greek has no idea of moving "away from" the text. The live English, "Train the passions away from the passionless text", invents that direction. A reader can take it to mean "train your passions to leave the text", which turns Cyril's point upside down: he wants the reader to stay with the chaste words and let them reshape the passions. This is garbled, not a matter of style, so the claim stands. The proposed fix, "Use what is free of passion to retrain the passions", is faithful, but it drops the word for "words/text". It also hides a likely pun: the section opens with "τοῦ πάθους ... τὰ σύμβολα" (the symbols of the Passion), and the next sentence speaks of the songs "τοῦ πάθους Χριστοῦ μηνυτικά" (revealing Christ's Passion). So τὰ πάθη may also hint at reading Christ's sufferings out of passionless words. A closer rendering keeps the "from ... words" frame and leaves that double sense open.
verdict.better_correction: From the passionless words, retrain the passions.

errors.english_quote: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions were at work in our members."
errors.source_quote: ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν
errors.why: The English drops τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ('aroused through the law') from Romans 7:5. There is also no citation for this quotation, though others in the text have one.
errors.corrected_english: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members" (Romans 7:5).

verdict.reason: Confirmed. In u01-rem-close the locked Greek reads "ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν" (Rom 7:5). The English, "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions were at work in our members.", leaves out τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου. That phrase carries meaning: it is Paul's point that the law aroused the passions. Dropping it is a real omission, not a style choice. The proposed fix, "the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members", is faithful ("aroused by the law" or "that came through the law" would also do). The missing citation is a minor consistency point, not a faithfulness error. The book does cite references inline elsewhere (John 5:6, John 7:38 and others), but this same paragraph also leaves James 1:13 and Gen 6:3 uncited. Adding "(Romans 7:5)" is optional. The required fix is restoring the law phrase.
verdict.better_correction: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members." (A "(Romans 7:5)" tag is optional and only for consistency.)

errors.english_quote: Let our soul follow the great physician who gives knowledge.
errors.source_quote: τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν·
errors.why: τὴν ψυχήν is the accusative of respect that ends the clause 'εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν τὴν ψυχήν' ('if we are in pain in soul'). The section split cut off 'εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν', and the English made 'soul' the subject of 'follow'. 'Great' is not in the source; it is simply 'the physician of knowledge'. This section repeats the source of u02-open, which renders the same words correctly (except for 'great').
errors.corrected_english: [If we are in pain] in soul, let us follow the physician of knowledge.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked both files in cjhp_u02_rem_*.json. The source for u02-rem-early starts mid-clause with "τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν·". In u02-open, the words before it are "εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν", so "τὴν ψυχήν" is an accusative of respect: "if we are in pain in soul". "Who gives knowledge" reads more into the genitive than it says but is a minor point. The same section text is already covered, nearly correctly, in u02-open ("If our soul is in pain, let us follow the great physician of knowledge"). So u02-rem-early is a duplicate, and its split broke the sense. The fix is faithful. A cleaner option is to repair the split, or drop the duplicate if it is published alongside u02-open. Note that "great" also appears in u02-open and should be cut there too.

(Better still: restore 'εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν' to the start of this section's source, or drop the duplicate u02-rem-early section if u02-open already carries this text. errors.english_quote: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one my Father has revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters"
errors.source_quote: εἰ σὺ εἶ ὃν ἐγὼ οἶδα, μᾶλλον δὲ ὃν ὁ πατήρ μοι ἐμήνυσεν
errors.why: μοι is the dative 'to me' and is already rendered by 'revealed to me'. ὁ πατήρ is 'the Father' (echoing Matthew 16:17), not 'my Father'. As written, Peter calls God 'my Father'.
errors.corrected_english: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters"

verdict.reason:
The source quote is accurate. cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, §8 reads "ὁ δὲ Πέτρος πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει· εἰ σὺ εἶ ὃν ἐγὼ οἶδα, μᾶλλον δὲ ὃν ὁ πατήρ μοι ἐμήνυσεν, κέλευσόν μοι ἐλθεῖν πρὸς σὲ ἐπὶ τὰ ὕδατα." The English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, paragraph 4, has "the one my Father has revealed to me".

Nothing in the Greek supplies "my". The only first-person word in that clause is μοι, and the English already uses it for "to me". A Greek article can sometimes stand in for a possessive with kinship nouns. But when ὁ πατήρ names the divine Father in a Christological passage, the standard reading is "the Father". Cyril is pointing to Matthew 16:17, where Christ says the Father revealed this to Peter. In the current English, Peter instead calls God "my Father", a phrase the Gospels give to Christ.

This is a small addition, not a reversal of sense, so "low" severity is right. Still, it is a real addition that a careful translator would remove, not a style preference.

The proposed fix is faithful: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters". The simple past "revealed" matches the aorist ἐμήνυσεν better than "has revealed", though both are acceptable.

errors.english_quote: The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste.
errors.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα.
errors.why: σοφά means 'wise', which completes the contrast with κατὰ σοφίαν. 'Chaste' (σώφρονα) is a different word and loses the wordplay.
errors.corrected_english: For the passions are not in keeping with wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The locked source in translations/cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-mid, reads exactly "οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα." The live English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json renders it as "The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste."

σοφά means "wise", not "chaste". The chastity words in this passage are σωφρονικοῖς and σωφροσύνης, and σοφά is not one of them. The sentence sets κατὰ σοφίαν ("in keeping with wisdom") against σοφά ("wise"), and "chaste" breaks that contrast. The English also drops γάρ ("for"), so the sentence no longer reads as the reason for the line before it.

The error is minor, since the general sense is still close, but it is a real wrong word. The proposed correction is faithful to the Greek: "For the passions are not in keeping with wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise." It restores both "for" and "wise".

The object of λέγει is the articular τὸ ποθούμενον, "the thing longed for". The anarthrous ἐρώτημά πως is predicative and means "in a way, as a question". So Cyril says Jesus voices the man's desire, health, in question form. The live English reads "he speaks a question that was longed for". That makes the question the thing desired and drops πως. The sense shifts, though only slightly. The next lines support the claim's reading: Cyril stresses "θέλεις" and says "ἐπὶ τῷ θέλειν τὴν βοήθειαν τιθεμένου", which ties the question to the man's own wish.
