errors.english_quote: Didymus comments: This Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the work of the Master in the same way as I do.
errors.source_quote: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ Τιμόθεος οὗτος περὶ οὗ γράφω τὰ προκείμενα, τῶν γνησίων τοῦ θεοῦ δοῦλος, τὸ ἔργον τοῦ δεσπότου παραπλησίως ἐμοὶ ἐργαζόμενος.
errors.why: This is Didymus paraphrasing Paul in Paul's own voice (1 Cor 16:10 'he does the work of the Lord, as I do'). The added 'Didymus comments:' makes Didymus the 'I' who writes about Timothy and works like him. Nothing in the Greek says 'Didymus comments'.
errors.corrected_english: For this Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the Master's work just as I do.

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source (translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-close) reads: "Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ Τιμόθεος οὗτος περὶ οὗ γράφω τὰ προκείμενα, τῶν γνησίων τοῦ θεοῦ δοῦλος, τὸ ἔργον τοῦ δεσπότου παραπλησίως ἐμοὶ ἐργαζόμενος." Nothing in it corresponds to "Didymus comments:". The "γράφω" (I write) and "ἐμοί" (as I do) are Paul's voice. Didymus is paraphrasing 1 Cor 16:10-11 as Paul, and the next clause, "περιμένω γὰρ ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ ἕως ἐπανέλθῃ πρός με", is still Paul in the first person. The English adds a label that makes Didymus the "I" who writes about Timothy and works the way Timothy does, so the speaker is wrong. The proposed correction is faithful: "γάρ" becomes "For", and "παραπλησίως ἐμοί" becomes "just as I do". In the same paragraph, the English "For Paul says: I am waiting in Asia..." also inserts "Paul says"; the Greek is just "περιμένω γάρ". With the bad label removed, that clause should stay in Paul's voice too. A side note outside this claim: in paragraph 9, "Didymus's teacher Origen" adds "Didymus's teacher"; the Greek has only "ὁ Ὠριγένης".
verdict.better_correction: For this Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the Master's work just as I do. So let him not be despised among you, but let him be received genuinely with love, and also sent on his way; for I am waiting in Asia until he returns to me with the brothers.

errors.english_quote: So also Didymus's teacher Origen holds
errors.source_quote: οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει
errors.why: The Greek says only 'Origen'. 'Didymus's teacher' is invented, and it is false: Origen died c. 254 and Didymus was born c. 313.
errors.corrected_english: So also Origen holds

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/didymus-fragmenta-1cor/translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json and df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close, and it holds. The Greek reads only "οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει τὸ πνεῦμα πλείω τι ἔχειν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν ἀρετῇ". It names "Origen" with no word for teacher or for Didymus, yet the English says "So also Didymus's teacher Origen holds". The added phrase is commentary the translator made up, and it is false. Origen died around 254, and Didymus was born around 313, so Origen could not have taught him. Didymus followed Origen's ideas but was never his pupil. A reader of the live text would take this as a fact from the source. The proposed fix, "So also Origen holds ...", matches the Greek. The rest of the sentence can stay as it is. A side note outside this claim: "even though both spirit and soul exist" is a loose reading of the elliptical "εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή". It can be defended and should be looked at separately.
verdict.better_correction: So also Origen holds that the spirit has something more than the soul in virtue, even though both spirit and soul exist.

errors.english_quote: even though both spirit and soul exist.
errors.source_quote: εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή.
errors.why: The Greek means 'even though the soul too is spirit', i.e. the spirit outranks the soul in virtue although the soul is also spirit. 'Both spirit and soul exist' says something else and makes the concession pointless.
errors.corrected_english: even though the soul too is spirit.

verdict.reason: The claim stands. The source in translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json for u01-rem-close reads "οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει τὸ πνεῦμα πλείω τι ἔχειν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν ἀρετῇ, εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή." This is an elliptical clause with ἐστί understood. Only ψυχή takes the article, so ἡ ψυχή is the subject and πνεῦμα the predicate, with the second καί meaning "also": "even if/though the soul too is spirit." The context backs this. The sentence before it says the same inner principle is called soul in the wicked and spirit in the holy (ἐπὶ μὲν φαύλων ψυχήν, ἐπὶ δὲ ἁγίων πνεῦμα λέγεσθαι). So the concession is that spirit outranks soul in virtue even though the soul is also spirit. The live English, "even though both spirit and soul exist," adds "exist," which is not in the Greek, and it loses the predication, which leaves the concession empty. The proposed fix, "even though the soul too is spirit," is faithful. "Even if the soul also is spirit" would work equally well. A separate point outside this claim: the same sentence says "Didymus's teacher Origen," but the Greek has only ὁ Ὠριγένης. "Didymus's teacher" is an addition. It should be cut, leaving "So also Origen holds...".

errors.kind: omission that breaks the comment / wrong sense
errors.english_quote: a great and effectual opportunity has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the open opportunity for the word of godliness a door.
errors.source_quote: θύρα γὰρ ὑπερέχουσα καὶ πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα εἰς τοὺς ἀκροατὰς ἀνέῳκται αὐτῷ ... ἔθος δὲ αὐτῷ τὴν παρρησίαν τοῦ τῆς εὐσεβείας λόγου θύραν καλεῖν.
errors.why: The English removes the word 'door' (θύρα) from the verse, so Didymus's closing remark about why Paul says 'door' explains a word the reader never saw. It also turns παρρησία (boldness, freedom of speech) into 'open opportunity', losing Didymus's actual gloss.
errors.corrected_english: a great and very effective door has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the bold, free preaching of the word of godliness a door.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked df1c_u01_rem_source.json and df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close. The Greek gives the verse as "θύρα γὰρ ὑπερέχουσα καὶ πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα εἰς τοὺς ἀκροατὰς ἀνέῳκται αὐτῷ". The English renders it "a great and effectual opportunity has opened for him among his hearers", so the word "door" never appears in the verse. Didymus then explains Paul's metaphor: "ἔθος δὲ αὐτῷ τὴν παρρησίαν τοῦ τῆς εὐσεβείας λόγου θύραν καλεῖν". That remark only makes sense if the reader has just seen "door". The current English puts Didymus's explanation into the verse itself, which makes the closing remark circular ("he calls the opportunity a door" after already saying "opportunity"). This is a real fault a careful translator would fix, not a matter of style. "Open opportunity" for παρρησία is also loose: the word means openness or freedom of speech, not opportunity. Still, the larger problem is the missing "door". The proposed correction is faithful. "Very effective" matches πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα. "Bold, free preaching" adds the idea of "preaching", which is acceptable but slightly expanded. A closer version is offered below.
verdict.better_correction: a great and very effective door has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the freedom to speak the word of godliness openly a door.

errors.kind: wrong sense (scripture word treated as commentary)
errors.english_quote: And "sober up" is well said—rightly so—since not all do this. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up for wicked ends
errors.source_quote: καλῶς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐκνήψατε δικαίως ὡς μὴ πάντων τοῦτο ποιούντων· οἱ γὰρ σοφοὶ τοῦ κακοποιῆσαι ἀγρυπνοῦντες περὶ τὰ βλαβερὰ ἀδίκως ἐκνήφουσιν
errors.why: 'ἐκνήψατε δικαίως' is the lemma of 1 Cor 15:34 ('sober up righteously'). Didymus's point is that 'righteously' is well added, because the clever at evil sober up 'unrighteously' (ἀδίκως). Rendering δικαίως as the aside 'rightly so' loses the verse word and the contrast the comment rests on.
errors.corrected_english: And "sober up righteously" is well said, since not all do this righteously. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up unrighteously

verdict.reason: The source (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-early, under the heading 1 Kor 15,34) matches the quote exactly: "καλῶς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐκνήψατε δικαίως ὡς μὴ πάντων τοῦτο ποιούντων· οἱ γὰρ σοφοὶ τοῦ κακοποιῆσαι ἀγρυπνοῦντες περὶ τὰ βλαβερὰ ἀδίκως ἐκνήφουσιν". The verse 1 Cor 15:34 reads ἐκνήψατε δικαίως, so the lemma is "ἐκνήψατε δικαίως" and δικαίως is the Bible's word. Didymus is not adding his own "rightly so". His whole point depends on the contrast δικαίως / ἀδίκως: Paul is right to add "righteously" because people who are clever at doing evil also "sober up", but unrighteously. The live English, "'sober up' is well said—rightly so", takes the verse word out of the quotation and turns it into the commentator's aside. It also renders ἀδίκως as "for wicked ends", which hides the contrast the comment rests on. This is a real wrong-sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful in substance. It has two small flaws: it drops καί ("also": "is also well said"), and it adds a second "righteously" after "not all do this", which is not in the Greek. Leaving that word out still keeps the sense, because the quoted lemma now carries it.
verdict.better_correction: And "sober up righteously" is also well said, since not everyone does this. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up unrighteously, supposedly casting off the sleep of ignorance.

errors.english_quote: since it is a natural body, being a body of a soul, the prior quality of which was corrupted in it. It is raised by the power of God
errors.source_quote: τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος, ἀνίσταται θεοῦ δυνάμει
errors.why: The genitive absolute 'φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος' goes with 'ἀνίσταται': when the body's former quality (dishonor, weakness) has been destroyed in it, it is raised. The English attaches it to the soul and says the soul's quality 'was corrupted', which reverses the point (the old quality is abolished at resurrection; it is not the soul that was corrupted).
errors.corrected_english: being a body of the soul. When the former quality in it has been destroyed, it is raised by the power of God

verdict.reason:
The claim holds; I could not refute it. The Greek in df1c_u01_rem_source.json (u01-rem-mid) reads: "εὐλόγως καὶ ἀτιμία καὶ ἀσθένεια περὶ αὐτὸ ἔσται, τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος, ἀνίσταται θεοῦ δυνάμει, ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ τιμὴν ἔχον". The phrase "φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος" is a genitive absolute: it has its own subject, ποιότητος, and an aorist participle. It describes what happens before the main verb ἀνίσταται: once the former quality in the body (the dishonor and weakness just named) has been destroyed, the body is raised with incorruptibility, power and honor. Nothing in the Greek makes it a relative clause on ψυχῆς. That reading would need ἧς or αὐτῆς, and ἐν αὐτῷ is neuter, so "in it" means the body (σῶμα), not the soul.

The English says "being a body of a soul, the prior quality of which was corrupted in it. It is raised by the power of God". That ties the corruption to the soul's quality and cuts it off from the raising, so the point is lost: the old quality is removed at the resurrection, not corrupted in the soul. This is a real error of sense, not a style choice. One smaller point: "since it is a natural body" is a gloss. The Greek has only "τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα" ("being a soul's body"). The gloss is harmless here because the passage is about the ψυχικὸν σῶμα.

The proposed correction is faithful. "Destroyed" is fine; "has perished" would keep the play on φθαρτός/ἄφθαρτος.
verdict.better_correction: since it is the body of a soul. But once the former quality in it has perished, it is raised by the power of God

errors.kind: unmarked lacuna filled with invented text
errors.english_quote: it is unchangeable and unalterable not in the sense of undergoing change—for it became incorruptible through change—but in the sense of enduring into long-lasting life
errors.source_quote: οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν
errors.why: The Greek has a lacuna (**). The English fills it with 'for it became incorruptible through change' without marking the gap, although the work's notes say lacunae are marked [...]. 'Became incorruptible' is not in the source.
errors.corrected_english: it is unchangeable and unalterable not by way of change [...] for such a thing did undergo [change], but by enduring into long-lasting life

verdict.reason: The quotes match the files. Greek (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-mid): "οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν ἤτοι κολαζόμενον ἢ τιμώμενον". The ** marks a gap in the printed text. The likely reading is "[οὐ] κατὰ μεταβολήν· [μεταβολὴν] γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον", meaning "not by way of change, for such a thing underwent change". The English gets this general sense right, and "became incorruptible" fits the previous sentence ("τὸ ἐκ φθαρτοῦ γεγονὸς ἄφθαρτον"). So the meaning is not reversed. Still, the claim holds on two points: (1) the gap is filled silently, including the supplied "not", even though the work's own translator note says "Lacunae marked [...]"; (2) "it became incorruptible through change" is an editorial gloss. The surviving Greek says only "γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον" ("for such a thing underwent [it]"). A careful translator would mark the gap and translate what survives. This is a real but low-severity faithfulness problem, not just style. The proposed fix is faithful but drops "whether being punished or being honored", which belongs in the same sentence, and it reads awkwardly. A cleaner version is suggested below.
verdict.better_correction: In the same way, it is unchangeable and unalterable not by way of change [...]—for such a thing did undergo [change]—but by enduring into long-lasting life, whether being punished or being honored.

errors.english_quote: Paul reasonably says: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun."
errors.source_quote: εἰκότως φησίν· ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος·
errors.why: Only 'Behold, I tell you a mystery' is Paul's text. 'Only the righteous', 'die and', and 'shining like the sun' (Matt 13:43) are Didymus's gloss, but the quotation marks put them in Paul's mouth as if they were 1 Cor 15:51.
errors.corrected_english: Paul reasonably says, "Behold, I tell you a mystery." That is: we will all die and sleep, but only we the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.

verdict.reason: I checked both files: translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json and translations/df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-mid. The claim holds. The Greek reads "εἰκότως φησίν· ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος". Only "ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω" is the wording of 1 Cor 15:51. The rest is Didymus's paraphrase, spoken in Paul's "we". "τεθνηξόμενοι", "μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι" and "ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος" (from Matt 13:43) do not appear in any text of 1 Cor 15:51. The paraphrase explains the reading Didymus prefers ("we will all sleep, but not all be changed"). The next sentences, which reject the other reading, confirm this. The English puts the whole sentence in one set of quotation marks after "Paul reasonably says". A reader would therefore take "only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun" as Paul's own words, which misattributes the gloss to Scripture. The source has no quotation marks, so this is a fault in how the English presents the words, not a defensible word choice. It also drops the first person of "ἀλλαγησόμεθα" ("we will be changed"). The proposed correction is faithful. Its "That is:" is an added signpost, but harmless. The better correction below avoids even that addition and keeps the future participle.
verdict.better_correction: Paul fittingly says, "Behold, I tell you a mystery": all of us, being about to die, will sleep, but only we the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.

errors.english_quote: Nevertheless, even if the dead rise, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone
errors.source_quote: ὅμως, εἰ καὶ τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα ἀνίσταται, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτον καὶ πνευματικόν· διὸ οὐδὲ πᾶσιν ἐφαίνετο
errors.why: The Greek speaks of 'the body that died' (Christ's body, which is why he did not appear to all). The English drops 'body', switches to 'the dead' in general, and leaves 'it' with no antecedent.
errors.corrected_english: Nevertheless, even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked the Greek in df1c_u01_open_source.json, section u01-open. It reads "ὅμως, εἰ καὶ τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα ἀνίσταται, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτον καὶ πνευματικόν· διὸ οὐδὲ πᾶσιν ἐφαίνετο ἀλλ' οἷς ἤθελεν", exactly as the claim quotes it. "τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα" is a singular neuter noun phrase meaning "the body that died". In context it is Christ's body, and that is why the next clause says "he did not appear to everyone". The English in df1c_u01_open_english.json reads "Nevertheless, even if the dead rise, it rises incorruptible and spiritual." That drops σῶμα and turns the phrase into a plural, general "the dead". "It" is then left with nothing to refer to, and the "For this reason" link to Christ's appearances is lost. This is a real omission with garbled grammar, not a style choice. The proposed fix is faithful: "even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual". Here εἰ καί is concessive, so "even though" is right, and "it rises" fills in the verb implied after ἀλλ'.
verdict.better_correction: Nevertheless, even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone, but to those he willed.

errors.english_quote: since every soul united to it undergoes death, which is united to wickedness.
errors.source_quote: ἐπείπερ πᾶσα ἑνουμένη αὐτῷ ψυχὴ ὑφισταμένη θάνατον τὸν ἑνούμενον τῇ κακίᾳ.
errors.why: αὐτῷ most naturally picks up αὐτοῦ (Christ) from 'πόδας αὐτοῦ' and 'καταλύοντος αὐτοῦ'. The English 'it' makes it death, which gives no reason for death being destroyed. The souls are united to Christ and undergo the death that is joined to wickedness.
errors.corrected_english: since every soul united to him undergoes the death that is joined to wickedness.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote: "μεθ' ἣν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ ἀρχίκακος καταλύεται θάνατος, ἐπείπερ πᾶσα ἑνουμένη αὐτῷ ψυχὴ ὑφισταμένη θάνατον τὸν ἑνούμενον τῇ κακίᾳ." The nearest masculine noun before αὐτῷ is θάνατος, which closes the main clause directly before it. That makes "united to it" (death) the most natural grammatical reading, not a wrong referent. The Christ references ("πόδας αὐτοῦ", "καταλύοντος αὐτοῦ") come one clause earlier, and the subject has since switched to death. The English reading also makes sense. Death, the "arch-evil one", is the spiritual death of sin, and any soul joined to it undergoes the death that is bound up with wickedness. The clause explains which death is destroyed. The claim's reading does worse: souls united to Christ undergoing "the death that is joined to wickedness" is theologically odd. Making it work would need an unstated idea like "dying to sin", which the Greek does not say (that would be a dative of reference, not ἑνούμενον τῇ κακίᾳ). The clause is elliptical and may be corrupt. Still, the current English follows it closely and can be defended, so this is at most an ambiguity, not a real error. The proposed correction is not more faithful because it puts a doubtful referent into the text. The only change worth considering is a small clarity edit that keeps "it": make "the death" definite and drop the loose "which" clause.
verdict.better_correction: since every soul united to it undergoes the death that is joined to wickedness.

errors.english_quote: Some commentators say these words were spoken against Greek mythology and deception
errors.source_quote: Πρός τε τὴν Ἑλλήνων μυθολογίαν τε καὶ ἀπάτην εἰρῆσθαι ταῦτα εἰπόντες
errors.why: The Greek has only a participle with no stated subject ('having said'). 'Some commentators' is added and hands the view to unnamed third parties instead of leaving it as the catena's (Didymus's) own explanation.
errors.corrected_english: These words were said against the mythology and deception of the Greeks

verdict.reason: Source checked in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/didymus-fragmenta-1cor/translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, at the 1 Kor 15,27-28 lemma. The Greek reads: "Πρός τε τὴν Ἑλλήνων μυθολογίαν τε καὶ ἀπάτην εἰρῆσθαι ταῦτα εἰπόντες τῶν φασκόντων πατραλοίας εἶναι θεούς, καὶ ὅτι ... αὐτὸς λέγεται ὑποτάττεσθαι". The quote in the claim is accurate. The claim's reasoning is not. εἰπόντες is a masculine plural nominative aorist participle ("having said / those who said"), and the sentence has no finite verb. A catena often keeps a fragment like this cut short. The plural participle points to a group of people stating this view. It is not a bare statement in the author's own voice. So supplying a plural subject such as "Some ... say" is a defensible way to make the truncated Greek into an English sentence, and it matches what the Greek grammar suggests. The proposed correction, "These words were said against the mythology and deception of the Greeks", drops εἰπόντες entirely and turns a reported view into Didymus's own direct claim. That is less faithful than the current English. The only real excess is the word "commentators", which is more specific than the Greek. It is a small explanatory supplement, not invented commentary, and it does not change the meaning. This is at most a style point, not a real faithfulness error.
verdict.better_correction: If any change is wanted, drop only the over-specific noun and keep the plural reported speech: "Some say these words were spoken against the mythology and deception of the Greeks, against those who claim the gods are father-killers, and that when the church is subjected, he himself is said to be subjected..."

errors.english_quote: For those who deceive you corrupt others along with themselves, thinking that it is destroyed.
errors.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἀπατῶντες ὑμᾶς συμφθείρονται αὐτὴν φθείρεσθαι οἰόμενοι.
errors.why: συμφθείρονται is middle/passive ('perish together'); there is no object 'others'. The passage is about the deceivers thinking the soul perishes together with the body. 'Corrupt others along with themselves' is not in the text.
errors.corrected_english: For those who deceive you think that it perishes, and perishes together [with the body].

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, at the 1 Cor 15:33 lemma): "οἱ γὰρ ἀπατῶντες ὑμᾶς συμφθείρονται αὐτὴν φθείρεσθαι οἰόμενοι." συμφθείρονται is middle/passive and takes no object. It means "are corrupted/destroyed together with," not "corrupt others." The English "corrupt others along with themselves" turns it into an active verb and adds the object "others," which the Greek does not have. The claim holds as a real low-severity sense error. The proposed correction is wrong, though. συμφθείρονται is plural, so its subject is οἱ ἀπατῶντες (the deceivers), not αὐτήν (the soul). αὐτήν is only the subject of the infinitive φθείρεσθαι. The correction "think that it perishes, and perishes together [with the body]" makes the soul the one perishing together, misreads the grammar, and adds "[with the body]" on a guess. The Greek leaves the partner of συμ- unstated. Context suggests "with you" (the deceived) or a wordplay: they think the soul perishes, and they perish along with it.
verdict.better_correction: For those who deceive you, thinking that it [the soul] is destroyed, are themselves destroyed along with [you].

errors.english_quote: means that we are some others besides the dead, who, they say, are raised with incorruptible bodies, while their souls are changed
errors.source_quote: ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς, οἵτινες, φησίν, ἄφθαρτοι ἐγειρόμεθα τὰ σώματα, ἀλλασσομενῶν τῶν ψυχῶν
errors.why: ἐγειρόμεθα is first person plural: 'we', not the dead, are raised incorruptible in body with souls changed. The English 'who ... are raised ... their souls' reads as a description of the dead.
errors.corrected_english: means that we, being other than the dead, are, he says, raised with incorruptible bodies, while our souls are changed

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source in df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-mid, reads: "τὸ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς, οἵτινες, φησίν, ἄφθαρτοι ἐγειρόμεθα τὰ σώματα, ἀλλασσομενῶν τῶν ψυχῶν κατὰ κρείττονα καὶ θειοτέραν ποιότητα ἀλλοιουμενῶν."

1. **Wrong referent.** The relative pronoun οἵτινες goes with the first-person plural verb ἐγειρόμεθα. So the people raised incorruptible in body are "we", the ones "other than the dead". The live English reads "besides the dead, who, they say, are raised with incorruptible bodies, while their souls are changed". Here "who" sits next to "the dead", and "their souls" ties the soul-change to the dead too. That turns the view around: Paul's "we shall be changed" becomes a description of the dead.
2. **Wrong number and wrong possessive.** φησίν is singular ("he says"), not "they say". τῶν ψυχῶν has no "their"; with the first-person verb it should read "our souls" or "the souls".

These are errors of person and referent, not style. The proposed correction is faithful: "means that we, being other than the dead, are, he says, raised with incorruptible bodies, while our souls are changed". Keep the rest of the sentence as it is: "and altered for a better and more divine quality."

errors.english_quote: as Wisdom says in Proverbs 8:17: I love those who love me.
errors.source_quote: ὃς κρίνει τὰ ἔργα τῶν ἀνθρώπων, λέγων· ἐγὼ τοὺς φιλοῦντάς με ἀγαπῶ.
errors.why: The Greek has λέγων: the Lord who judges is the one saying it. 'As Wisdom says' changes the speaker. The reference (Prov 8:17) is correct, so it can stay as a citation.
errors.corrected_english: who says: I love those who love me (Proverbs 8:17).

verdict.reason: I checked the source myself (translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-close). It reads: "εἰδὼς ὅτι ὁ κύριος ἦλθεν ὃς κρίνει τὰ ἔργα τῶν ἀνθρώπων, λέγων· ἐγὼ τοὺς φιλοῦντάς με ἀγαπῶ." The participle λέγων goes with ὁ κύριος ... ὃς κρίνει, so the Lord who judges is the one speaking. The English (translations/df1c_u01_rem_english.json) instead says "as Wisdom says in Proverbs 8:17: I love those who love me." That adds a speaker the Greek does not name, adds an inline citation as if it were Didymus's own words, and breaks the link the argument depends on. The next sentence, "εἰ δὲ ἀγαπᾷ τοὺς φιλοῦντας" (But if he loves those who love him), only works if "he" is the judging Lord who has just spoken. Under "as Wisdom says", "he" becomes unclear. The meaning is not reversed, because for Didymus the Wisdom of Proverbs 8 is Christ. So the claim stands, but low severity is right. The reference is correct: LXX Proverbs 8:17 reads ἐγὼ τοὺς ἐμὲ φιλοῦντας ἀγαπῶ. The proposed fix is faithful, but as written it is only a fragment. The better_correction field gives the full clause.
verdict.better_correction: Therefore this one is anathema, knowing that the Lord has come who judges the works of human beings, saying: I love those who love me (Proverbs 8:17).

errors.english_quote: and all the holy ones and brothers staying there
errors.source_quote: καὶ πάντες οἱ ἐν αὐτῇ διατρίβοντες ἅγιοι καὶ εὐλαβεῖς ἄνδρες
errors.why: εὐλαβεῖς ἄνδρες means 'devout men', not 'brothers'.
errors.corrected_english: and all the holy and devout men staying there

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against df1c_u01_rem_source.json and df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close, and it holds. The Greek reads 'ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς αἱ ἐκκλησίαι τῆς Ἀσίας καὶ πάντες οἱ ἐν αὐτῇ διατρίβοντες ἅγιοι καὶ εὐλαβεῖς ἄνδρες', which means 'all the holy and devout men staying in it' (in Asia). The English has 'and all the holy ones and brothers staying there'. 'εὐλαβεῖς ἄνδρες' means 'devout men' (as in Acts 2:5). No word for 'brothers' (ἀδελφοί) appears in the source. The translator seems to have taken 'brothers' from the wording of 1 Cor 16:20, but this is Didymus's own paraphrase. So the English replaces the source's 'devout' with a different word: a small wrong-word error, not a style choice. The proposed fix, 'and all the holy and devout men staying there', is faithful. It reads ἅγιοι and εὐλαβεῖς together as describing ἄνδρες, which suits the grammar, and 'there' rightly stands for ἐν αὐτῇ (Asia). The severity is correctly marked low.

works.notes: I checked all 4 sections (didymus-fragmenta-romanos, translations/dfr_u01_open_* and dfr_u01_rem_*) sentence by sentence. Source and English section ids match. The two most important problems: (1) u01-rem-close turns 'then not everyone will say good does not dwell in us' into a question that reverses it; (2) u01-rem-mid renders ἄναρχος as 'without a ruler' when it means 'without beginning'. There is also a visible 'then then' typo on the live page. Grok's REPORT.md (websites/fathers.saneapps.com/outputs/redteam-20261006/REPORT.md) does not check this work's translation. It only says the paid Didymus Romans Word file still sells the old wording ('unquenchable image' against 'unspotted image' on the live page), and that 3 Didymus audiobooks are built but not uploaded. So it confirms a download mismatch, not a translation error. Any fix here will need a fresh upload of the paid files too, or they will drift again.

errors.english_quote: But if there are those who enact the good, even if only a few do it, will not all of them say, "We know that good does not dwell in us"? For the good they willed, this they practice.
errors.source_quote: εἰ δέ εἰσιν ἐνεργοῦντες τὸ καλόν, κἂν ὀλίγοι εἶεν οἱ τοῦτο δρῶντες, ἄρ' οὐχ οἱ πάντες φήσουσιν· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγαθόν· ὃ γὰρ ἠθέλησαν ἀγαθόν, τοῦτο πράττουσιν.
errors.why: ἄρ' (elided ἄρα, 'then') + οὐχ states a conclusion: then NOT everyone will say good does not dwell in them, because some do the good they willed. The English reads it as a question expecting yes ('will not all of them say...?'), which reverses the point and contradicts the next sentence. The same ἄρ' οὐ form is rendered correctly two sentences later ('then the cause ... must not be attached to the flesh').
errors.corrected_english: But if there are those who do the good, even if only a few do it, then not everyone will say, "We know that good does not dwell in us"; for the good they willed, this they do.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in dfr_u01_rem_source.json matches the quote exactly: "εἰ δέ εἰσιν ἐνεργοῦντες τὸ καλόν, κἂν ὀλίγοι εἶεν οἱ τοῦτο δρῶντες, ἄρ' οὐχ οἱ πάντες φήσουσιν· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγαθόν· ὃ γὰρ ἠθέλησαν ἀγαθόν, τοῦτο πράττουσιν." The elided ἄρ' could be read as ἆρα (a question) or ἄρα (a conclusion), so the context has to decide. Three things point to the conclusion reading. (1) The γάρ clause, "for the good they willed, this they do", explains why these people would NOT say that good does not dwell in them. With the question reading ("will not all of them say...?", which expects a yes), it supports the opposite of what it follows, and the English becomes self-contradictory. (2) Didymus's argument here is that some people do the good, so Paul's "the good I will I do not do" cannot cancel the good for every human being. A yes-question would concede the impious man's point. (3) The same ἄρ' οὐ pattern appears twice more in this section, and both times it is a negated conclusion: "ἄρ' οὐ τῇ σαρκὶ τὸ αἴτιον ... περιαπτέον, ἀλλὰ τῇ τούτων μαλακοψυχίᾳ", where the ἀλλά shows that οὐ negates τῇ σαρκί, and "ἄρ' οὐ φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ τὰ σώματα ἡμῶν ἐστι φαῦλα". The live English renders both of those as conclusions, so this sentence is inconsistent with them. This is a real reversal of sense, not a style point. The proposed correction is faithful. "then not everyone will say" correctly renders οὐχ οἱ πάντες φήσουσιν, the quotation is kept, and the γάρ clause is kept as its support. Changing "enact" to "do" and "practice" to "do" is optional and does no harm.
verdict.better_correction: But if there are those who do the good, even if only a few do it, then not everyone will say, "We know that good does not dwell in us"; for the good they willed, this they do.

errors.english_quote: But the kingdom of death is not without a ruler or unbegotten; for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey.
errors.source_quote: ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄναρχος ἢ ἀγέννητος ἡ τοῦ θανάτου βασιλεία· ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει
errors.why: Paired with ἀγέννητος and justified by 'dying comes from the living', ἄναρχος here means 'without beginning', not 'without a ruler'. Didymus argues death's reign had a start. 'Without a ruler' breaks the argument.
errors.corrected_english: But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote. In dfr_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-mid reads: "ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄναρχος ἢ ἀγέννητος ἡ τοῦ θανάτου βασιλεία· ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα." Here ἄναρχος is paired with ἀγέννητος ("unbegotten"), so it means "without beginning", the usual sense in patristic Greek. The γάρ clauses back that reading. Death comes out of a prior state, the living, and disobedience comes out of a prior obedience. So death's reign had an origin. "Without a ruler" breaks this argument. It also clashes with the sentence just before, where death "reigned" holding a scepter. The current English is a real mistranslation, not a choice of style. The proposed fix ("not without beginning or unbegotten") is faithful. One optional touch: ὑπηκόων could read "of subjects", which fits the kingdom image, but "of those who obey" is defensible.

errors.english_quote: For this reason the apostle also declared that sin must not reign in your mortal body (Romans 6:12).
errors.source_quote: ὅτου χάριν καὶ βασιλεύειν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων αὐτὸν ὁ ἀπόστολος ἀπεφήνατο· μὴ οὖν βασιλευέτω ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐν τῷ θνητῷ ὑμῶν σώματι.
errors.why: Drops Didymus's claim that the apostle declared HIM (the devil) to reign over sins, with Rom 6:12 cited as proof. The English collapses his point into a bare paraphrase of the verse, so the identification of 'sin' as a ruling person is lost.
errors.corrected_english: For this reason the apostle also declared that he reigns over sins: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body" (Romans 6:12).

verdict.reason:
I checked the claim against the source and it holds. In dfr_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, the Greek reads "ὅτου χάριν καὶ βασιλεύειν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων αὐτὸν ὁ ἀπόστολος ἀπεφήνατο· μὴ οὖν βασιλευέτω ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐν τῷ θνητῷ ὑμῶν σώματι." That means "for this reason the apostle also declared him [the devil] to reign over sins: 'Let not sin reign...'" The grammar is an accusative subject with an infinitive after ἀπεφήνατο. βασιλεύειν takes a genitive, so βασιλεύειν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων means "reign over sins." αὐτόν points back to the devil, named in the sentence before.

The live English says "the apostle also declared that sin must not reign in your mortal body (Romans 6:12)." That drops αὐτόν and τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων. It folds Didymus's own claim, that the devil reigns over sins, into a paraphrase of the verse, and it turns the quoted proof-text into indirect speech. The claim is the link in his argument that "sin" names a ruling person, which the next sentence builds on ("so also he calls the devil himself 'sin'"). Losing it is an omission of meaning, not a style choice.

The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly closer version that keeps οὖν: For this reason the apostle also declared that he reigns over sins: "Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body" (Romans 6:12).

errors.english_quote: But if this is true, I will now speak in the voice of the impious. From the impious person's perspective, the good never was and never will be in life,
errors.source_quote: εἰ δὲ τοῦτο ἀληθές ἐστιν, κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἐρῶ· ἄρα οὐκ ἦν οὐδ' ἔσται ἐν βίῳ τὸ καλόν,
errors.why: κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς means 'according to the impious' (or 'against the impious'). Didymus draws an absurd conclusion from their premise in his own voice; he does not adopt their voice. The English makes the whole following refutation sound like the impious speaking, and adds a whole sentence ('From the impious person's perspective') not in the Greek.
errors.corrected_english: But if this is true, as the impious hold, I will say: then the good never was and never will be in life,

verdict.reason:
The source matches the quote exactly (dfr_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-close). The claim is half right.

The "wrong speaker" charge is overstated. In κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἐρῶ, κατά takes the accusative, so it means "I will say, following the impious," not "against" them. Didymus is pushing their premise to its absurd end. The previous section already does this: "souls of the same substance as himself" (ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχάς) is the heretics' premise. So "I will now speak in the voice of the impious" is a loose but defensible paraphrase. The real problem is the second sentence opener, "From the impious person's perspective." It renders the same three Greek words a second time. That is a genuine addition: a careful translator would cut it, and it makes the passage sound more like the impious speaking than the Greek does. It does not reverse the sense, so severity should drop from medium to low.

The proposed fix, "as the impious hold, I will say," moves the phrase onto "if this is true." In the Greek, κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς goes with ἐρῶ (the way Didymus will speak), not with the truth of the premise.
verdict.better_correction: But if this is true, I will reason as the impious do: then the good never was and never will be in life,

errors.english_quote: then our bodies are not weak by nature or substance.
errors.source_quote: ἄρ' οὐ φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ τὰ σώματα ἡμῶν ἐστι φαῦλα
errors.why: φαῦλα means bad or evil, not weak. The whole argument is whether flesh is evil by nature; the very next sentence renders the same word as 'evil' (οὐ φαύλη κατὰ φύσιν ἡ σάρξ -> 'the flesh is not evil by nature'). 'Weak' changes the claim.
errors.corrected_english: then our bodies are not evil by nature or substance.

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against dfr_u01_rem_source.json and dfr_u01_rem_english.json in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/didymus-fragmenta-romanos/translations/, and it holds. The source is quoted exactly: "ἄρ' οὐ φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ τὰ σώματα ἡμῶν ἐστι φαῦλα". In this moral argument φαῦλος means bad, base or worthless. It never means weak in the sense of lacking strength. Its milder senses ("slight", "trivial") describe things of little worth, not physical frailty. The paragraph argues that good or evil comes from the free will of the soul, not from the nature of the flesh. The verse that follows sums up the same point with the same word: "οὐ φαύλη κατὰ φύσιν ἡ σάρξ", rendered "the flesh is not evil by nature". So "weak" turns a claim about the moral nature of bodies into a claim about their strength, and it breaks the link between the two sentences. "Weak" was probably carried over from the line just before, where μαλακοψυχίᾳ is correctly rendered "weakness of ... souls"; φαῦλα is a different word. Reading ἄρα οὐ as "then ... not" (a conclusion) is correct, so the error is in that one word only. The proposed fix, "then our bodies are not evil by nature or substance", is faithful and matches how the next verse is rendered. "Bad" would also be correct, but "evil" keeps the passage consistent.

errors.english_quote: then then one might say the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.
errors.source_quote: εἰς μάτην ὁ ἀγαθὸς θεὸς τὰς ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὰς ἐν τοῖς σώμασι κατέπεμψεν
errors.why: Doubled 'then then' is a visible typo on the live page, and 'one might say' is added; the Greek states the consequence directly.
errors.corrected_english: then the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The live English in dfr_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-mid, reads: "If only the willing is in us, and the accomplishment of the willed good is not in us, then then one might say the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain."

errors.english_quote: The first dispute about this appears to have arisen in Antioch, because the apostles wrote that they should not be subject to the law
errors.source_quote: καὶ πρώτη περὶ τούτου φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν μὴ ὑποκεῖσθαι νόμῳ
errors.why: The apostolic letter (Acts 15) was the outcome of the Antioch dispute, not its cause. 'Because' makes the decree the cause of the quarrel. Here ὅτι states the dispute's result or content.
errors.corrected_english: The first dispute about this appears to have arisen in Antioch, and the apostles wrote that they should not be subject to the law

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote: "καὶ πρώτη περὶ τούτου φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν μὴ ὑποκεῖσθαι νόμῳ..." (eemgal_u01_open_source.json, u01-open). The ὅτι clause most naturally explains φαίνεται, and the reading is evidential: the dispute *appears* to have started in Antioch, and we can tell because the apostles wrote their ruling there (Acts 15:23 is addressed to the brethren in Antioch). The English "appears to have arisen in Antioch, because the apostles wrote..." keeps that structure and the same ambiguity. "Because" can attach to "appears" (how we know), not just to "arisen" (what caused it). So it does not have to mean the letter caused the quarrel. The claim's other reading, that ὅτι gives the content of the dispute ("a dispute that the apostles wrote..."), makes no sense. The proposed fix "and the apostles wrote" drops the subordinating ὅτι and turns a stated reason into a bare sequence. That is less faithful than the current text, so it is no improvement. At most, the evidential sense could be made clearer (see better_correction). This is clarity, not a faithfulness error.
verdict.better_correction: The first dispute about this appears to have arisen in Antioch, as the apostles' letter shows: they wrote that they should not be subject to the law, but should abstain from idol-sacrifice, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality; for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit.

errors.english_quote: so that they will not think he is currying favor because he is being manipulated

errors.why: The middle ὑπαγόμενος means Paul winning them over or coaxing them. It does not mean someone else manipulating him. The worry is that his reminder might look like flattery meant to win them over, which is why the next clause says that he rebukes.

The source in eemgal_u01_open_source.json, section u01-open, reads exactly as quoted: "προλαβὼν ἀσφαλίζεται ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν ὅτι θεραπεύει ὑπαγόμενος· ἐπιπλήττει γὰρ νουθετῶν." The live English, "so that they will not think he is currying favor because he is being manipulated", has two faults. First, it reads ὑπαγόμενος as a passive ("being manipulated") when the middle is the natural reading: ὑπάγεσθαι means to win someone over, to coax or bring them to one's side. Second, "because" makes up a cause that the Greek does not state; the participle goes with θεραπεύει ("courts/flatters while winning over"). The context supports the middle. Gal 1:10 is about Paul seeming to please people, and the next clause, "for he rebukes while admonishing", answers the charge that he is flattering the Galatians. Nobody in the passage is manipulating Paul, so the passive gives an odd and unsupported sense. errors.english_quote: For this reason a law able to give life—meaning that if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God, but neither could it have power forever.
errors.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο.
errors.why: 'For this reason a law able to give life—' has no verb and makes no sense. The phrase διὰ τοῦτο ends the preceding 'since' argument ('for this reason [the law was added]'). ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι is the Gal 3:21 lemma, and ἀντὶ τοῦ glosses it as standing for 'if a law had been given'.
errors.corrected_english: For this reason [the law was added]. "A law was given that could give life" stands for "if a law had been given." It was not given, he says, against the promises of God; but neither could it prevail for all time.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the claim. The source and English in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json and eemgal_u01_rem_english.json match the quotes. The Greek reads "διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο."

The English "For this reason a law able to give life—meaning that..." drops the finite verb ἐδόθη ("was given") and leaves a sentence fragment. It also blurs ἀντὶ τοῦ, which marks a gloss on the Gal 3:21 lemma. This is garbled English, not a style choice.

The proposed correction has two faults:
1. It brackets in "[the law was added]", but ἐδόθη is already in the source. It then reuses ἐδόθη for the lemma, so the source's own verb is never cleanly placed.
2. It ends the gloss at "stands for 'if a law had been given.'" and starts a new sentence. In the Greek, the gloss after ἀντὶ τοῦ is the whole conditional: "if a law was given, it was not given against the promises." Splitting it cuts the "if" clause off from its main clause. The past counterfactual "had been given" also misreads Eusebius's concessive "if (granted) a law was given".
verdict.better_correction: This is why the law was given. "A law able to give life" stands for this: if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God; but neither could it prevail for all time.

errors.source_quote: οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ παρέμιξε τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν–ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον–, ἀλλ' εἰ

The source is difficult, so the exact rendering is uncertain, but the current English is meaningless.
errors.corrected_english: He did not add female and male idly—for the point at hand needed only the word "one"—but if baptism brings male and female

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source quote matches the locked Greek in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json word for word: "οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ παρέμιξε τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν–ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον–, ἀλλ' εἰ τὸ ἄρρεν καὶ τὸ θῆλυ διαφέρον εἰς μίαν χάριν συνάγει τὸ βάπτισμα, πόσῳ μᾶλλον Ἕλληνα καὶ Ἰουδαῖον." The live English, "as far as one sought in one phrase for the matter at hand", has no clear meaning. It also says "one" twice where the Greek has εἷς once and τῷ ῥήματι ("in the statement"), and it leaves out γάρ, so the aside no longer explains anything. The sense is clear from context. Paul's point at hand (Gal 3:28) was about Jew and Greek, so adding male and female looks unneeded. Eusebius says Paul did not add it idly (οὐχ ἁπλῶς): it sets up a stronger-case argument (if baptism unites even male and female, how much more Greek and Jew). That makes this a real faithfulness and readability error, not a style point. The proposed fix is better than the current text, and "idly" for οὐχ ἁπλῶς is right. But "needed only the word 'one'" picks one guess about εἷς and fits the argument poorly. Paul's statement does not need just the word "one". The aside means only one pair (Jew/Greek) mattered for the point, which is why the male/female pair needs explaining. Either εἷς refers loosely to one pair, or the text is corrupt. I suggest the correction below and a translator note that the clause is textually uncertain.
verdict.better_correction: He did not add female and male idly (for the point at hand called for only one pair in the statement, Greek and Jew), but to argue that if baptism brings male and female, though different, into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew. [Translator note: ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει is textually uncertain; rendered by sense.]

errors.source_quote: Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελευομένοις
errors.why: ἀνήλισκον means 'were spending' (money or resources), not 'acting'. Gal 6:6-8 is about material support: sowing means giving, which is what the next sentence ('the one who gives ... sows only into the flesh') relies on. 'Eusebius explains that' is framing the translator added; it is not in the source.
errors.corrected_english: He made clear from this that many were spending unwisely, giving to those who urged them to keep the law

verdict.reason:
The claim is correct. I checked the passage in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json and eemgal_u01_rem_english.json in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/eusebius-emesa-fragmenta-galatas/translations/, section u01-rem-close. The Greek is quoted correctly: "Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελευομένοις, τοῖς δὲ τὴν Παύλου διδασκαλίαν κηρύττουσιν οὐδὲν παρεῖχον."

1. ἀνήλισκον means "were spending" or "were using up" money or resources. It does not mean "were acting". Translating it as "acting" hides the money point that the rest of the paragraph depends on. The next clause says they gave nothing (οὐδὲν παρεῖχον) to Paul's preachers. The closing sentence says that whoever gives (παρέχων) to such a teacher "sows only into the flesh". So the error changes the meaning.
2. "Eusebius explains that" is not in the Greek. The subject of Ἐδήλωσεν is Paul, the author of the verse under comment. The added phrase is the translator's own commentary. It also makes Eusebius sound like a third party describing himself, which is odd inside his own commentary.
3. "At the wrong time" is a defensible literal reading of ἀκαίρως. "Unwisely" or "to no good purpose" fits the context better, but this part is a matter of word choice.

The proposed correction is faithful. Naming Paul as the subject would make it slightly clearer.
verdict.better_correction: Paul made clear from this that many were spending unwisely, supplying those who urged them to keep the law, but giving nothing to those who preached Paul's teaching.

errors.english_quote: What then is the blessedness? It belongs to no one.
errors.source_quote: Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς.
errors.why: ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς is a commentator's gloss meaning that the question stands for 'none': your blessedness has come to nothing. 'It belongs to no one' changes the point.
errors.corrected_english: What then is the blessedness? That is, there is none.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (eemgal_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-mid): "Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς. ἢ οὕτως· τὸ τηρεῖν νόμον ἢ τὸ πίστει ζῆν;" "ἀντὶ τοῦ" is the usual scholiast's formula for "this stands for" or "that is." The masculine "οὐδείς" agrees with "μακαρισμός," so it means "no blessedness" or "none," and the question is rhetorical (compare Gal 4:15, "where then is your blessedness?"). The live English reads "It belongs to no one," which treats οὐδείς as a person who might own the blessedness. Nothing in the Greek supports that, and it changes Eusebius's point from "your boasted blessedness has come to nothing" to a claim about who owns it. This is a real, minor wrong-sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed fix, "What then is the blessedness? That is, there is none.", is faithful and fits what follows, where "ἢ οὕτως" ("or [read it] this way") brings in a second reading: is it keeping the law or living by faith? It would also be acceptable to make "Or rather:" into "Or else, read it this way:", but that is optional.

errors.english_quote: For in allegorical interpretation of the Song, it is not literally a kiss, nor hair
errors.source_quote: ἐκεῖ γὰρ οὔτε φίλημα οὔτε θρὶξ οὔτε κοιλία οὐδὲ μηροὶ οὐδὲ ἕτερόν τι
errors.why: 'in allegorical interpretation of the Song' and 'literally' are not in the source. The source says only 'for there it is neither kiss nor hair...'. The added words build a theory of reading into the text.
errors.corrected_english: For there it is neither a kiss, nor hair

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Greek reads "ἐκεῖ γὰρ οὔτε φίλημα οὔτε θρὶξ οὔτε κοιλία οὐδὲ μηροὶ οὐδὲ ἕτερόν τι, ἀλλ' ἄλλα δι' ἄλλων εἰσάγεται", which means "for there [in the Song] is neither kiss nor hair nor belly nor thighs nor anything else; rather, other things are introduced through other things." "ἐκεῖ" points back to "τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων" (the Song of Songs). The words "in allegorical interpretation of" and "literally" have no basis in the Greek. They also shift the claim slightly. Eusebius says the Song itself contains no real kiss or hair, because its words point to other things; the English makes this a statement about how interpreters read the Song. Severity is low, since the overall sense survives, but it is a real addition a careful translator would remove. The proposed correction is faithful, though "it is neither a kiss" reads oddly. The Greek is existential ("there is no kiss"), and "there" needs its referent, the Song, made clear.
verdict.better_correction: For there, in the Song, there is no kiss, no hair, no belly, no thighs, nor anything else; rather, other things are introduced through other things

errors.english_quote: The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin.
errors.source_quote: Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
errors.why: ἀποσπῶν is an active participle with Paul as subject: Paul draws them away from the law. It does not say the law 'is removed'. 'Still' is added and suggests a contrast the source does not make. The answer that follows ('whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin') assumes the plain sense.
errors.corrected_english: The question is raised why, in drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source quote matches eemgal_u01_rem_source.json section u01-rem-close exactly: "Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας." ἀποσπῶν is a present active masculine nominative participle that agrees with the subject of μέμνηται, which is Paul. So the Greek says "while drawing [them] away from the law, he mentions sin." The live English reads "why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin." That turns Paul's own action into an impersonal passive ("the law is removed"), as if the law were already gone. It also adds "still", which sets up a contrast the Greek does not make. The answer that follows ("ὅτε νόμου ἦν μνήμη, μέμνηται καὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας", "whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin") supports the plain sense. Severity is low but the error is real, not a style choice.

The proposed fix, "The question is raised why, in drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin", is faithful. "Them" stands in for the object the Greek leaves unstated, which is acceptable. "While drawing his readers away from the law" would work equally well.

Other likely problems in the same section, outside this claim:
- "the lawgiver foresaw that Christ was going to come" adds "Christ"; the source has only "ὁ τὸ λεῖπον τῷ νόμῳ προστιθείς".
- "Eusebius explains that" in the Gal 6:7–8 paragraph is added; the source just says "Ἐδήλωσεν".
- "acting at the wrong time" for "ἀκαίρως ἀνήλισκον" should be "spending unwisely / at the wrong time".
- "the law commanded eating" for "τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν" weakens the sense, which is "feasting / living in luxury".
verdict.better_correction: The question is raised why, while drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin.

errors.english_quote: It is because the law commanded eating, and through this desire is provoked
errors.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν ὁ νόμος, διὰ δὲ τούτου διερεθίζεται ἡ ἐπιθυμία
errors.why: τρυφᾶν means to feast or live in plenty, not simply to eat. The argument depends on indulgence stirring up desire, and the translation itself later renders τρυφᾶν as 'feasting'.
errors.corrected_english: It is because the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I could not refute it. The source in translations/eemgal_u01_rem_source.json reads exactly as quoted: "ἐπειδὴ τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν ὁ νόμος, διὰ δὲ τούτου διερεθίζεται ἡ ἐπιθυμία". τρυφᾶν means to live in plenty or to feast. It does not mean plain eating. The passage itself keeps the two words apart. A few lines later it asks "διὰ τί δὲ συνεχωρήθη τὸ τρυφᾶν καὶ ἐσθίειν;", which the English renders as "why was feasting and eating permitted?". It also says "ἀδύνατον τρυφῶντας κρατεῖν ἡδονῶν", rendered "those who feast". So the English gives τρυφᾶν as "feasting" everywhere except here, where it becomes "eating". That breaks the argument, because indulgence is what "provokes desire" and makes it "uncontrollable". Plain eating does not carry that sense, so this is a small but real weakening of the meaning and not a choice of style. The proposed fix, "It is because the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked", is faithful. It also matches how the rest of the passage renders τρυφᾶν. Severity "low" is fair.

works.notes:
I compared all four sections (u01-open, u01-rem-early, u01-rem-mid, u01-rem-close), 137 sayings in all, sentence by sentence against the locked PG/Khazarzar Greek in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/evagrius-sententiae-monachos/translations/. On the whole the English is faithful. It invents no commentary. It drops no whole sayings, and section ids match. The Scripture tags check out: Mt 19:24,26 / Mk 10:25,27 for saying 17, and Ps 68:29 LXX / 69:28 for saying 90. Saying 19's tag (Prov 3:33) is a loose allusion but defensible.

Not reported because they are defensible choices: saying 39 ('Monks have no feast that consists in filling a man's belly' collapses 'there is no feast among monks, nor is filling one's belly [one]', a defensible reading given sayings 40-43). Saying 88 glosses 'his children' as 'his spiritual father's other disciples'. Saying 95 uses 'brings stillness' for ἡσυχίαν ἄγει. Saying 110 adds 'Holy' before Trinity.

The source numbers saying 13 as '3', which is only an OCR artifact. The Grok red-team REPORT.md has no Evagrius entries, so there was nothing to cross-check.

errors.english_quote: Do not be afraid to kill the offspring of snakes, and do not torment the thoughts of their hearts.
errors.source_quote: 59 Κτείνειν γεννήματα ὀφέων μὴ φείσῃ, καὶ μὴ ὠδίνῃς λογισμοὺς καρδίας αὐτῶν.
errors.why: ὠδίνω means to be in labor with or give birth to. Evagrius warns the monk not to conceive and bring forth the snakes' heart-thoughts. 'Torment' turns this into hurting the thoughts, which is the wrong sense. Also μὴ φείσῃ means 'do not spare / do not hold back', not 'do not be afraid'.
errors.corrected_english: Do not spare the offspring of snakes; kill them, and do not go into labor with the thoughts of their hearts.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in esm_u01_rem_source.json (u01-rem-early) reads "59 Κτείνειν γεννήματα ὀφέων μὴ φείσῃ, 59 καὶ μὴ ὠδίνῃς λογισμοὺς καρδίας αὐτῶν." The second "59" is a stray extraction mark. The live English says "Do not be afraid to kill the offspring of snakes, and do not torment the thoughts of their hearts." Two problems: (1) With an accusative object, ὠδίνω means "to be in labor with" or "to bring forth with pain" (compare Ps 7:15 LXX ὠδίνησεν ἀδικίαν and Isa 59:5). Evagrius means "do not conceive and nurse their thoughts." "Torment the thoughts" makes the monk hurt the thoughts, which is the opposite of the warning, so this is a real wrong sense. (2) μὴ φείσῃ + infinitive means "do not refrain or hold back from killing." "Do not be afraid" brings in fear, which the source does not have. That is a smaller drift, but it is still not in the Greek. The proposed fix is faithful in meaning. Its "Do not spare the offspring...; kill them" reorders the clause but loses nothing. A closer version follows the Greek order.
verdict.better_correction: Do not hold back from killing the offspring of snakes, and do not go into labor with the thoughts of their hearts.

errors.english_quote: Whenever he sends you, lead him and accompany him in your mind.
errors.source_quote: Ἡνίκα ἂν ἀποστείλῃ σε, ἐπάγου αὐτὸν καὶ κατὰ διάνοιαν συνόδευε αὐτῷ.
errors.why: ἐπάγου (middle) means 'bring him along with you'. 'Lead him' makes the disciple lead his spiritual father. That reverses the relation. Evagrius means the monk carries the father with him in thought when sent out.
errors.corrected_english: Whenever he sends you out, take him along with you and keep company with him in your mind.

verdict.reason: The source in /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/evagrius-sententiae-monachos/translations/esm_u01_rem_source.json (saying 73) matches the quoted Greek exactly: "Ἡνίκα ἂν ἀποστείλῃ σε, ἐπάγου αὐτὸν καὶ κατὰ διάνοιαν συνόδευε αὐτῷ." The live English in esm_u01_rem_english.json reads "Whenever he sends you, lead him and accompany him in your mind." ἐπάγου is the middle imperative of ἐπάγω. In the middle it means "bring along with yourself" or "take with you", not "lead". The father sends the monk out, and the monk takes the father with him in thought; συνόδευε ("travel with him") says the same thing. "Lead him" turns the monk into the one guiding the father. That reverses the relation, so this is a real wrong-sense error, not a style choice. "Sends you" also drops the "out/away" in ἀποστείλῃ, though that is minor. The proposed fix is faithful. An optional, slightly closer version: "Whenever he sends you out, take him along with you and travel with him in your thought."
verdict.better_correction: Whenever he sends you out, take him along with you and travel with him in your thought.

errors.english_quote: and if he grows negligent he will add even his monastic habit to those losses.
errors.source_quote: 93 Ὀκνηρὸς μοναχὸς πολλὰ ζημιωθήσεται, ἐὰν δὲ θαρσύνηται καὶ τὸ σχῆμα αὐτοῦ προσθήσει.
errors.why: θαρσύνηται means 'grows bold / becomes confident', not 'grows negligent'. The English invents the condition. The point is that if the lazy monk grows bold in his laziness, he will lose even his habit.
errors.corrected_english: and if he grows bold in it, he will add even his monastic habit to those losses.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute it. The source in esm_u01_rem_source.json (section u01-rem-mid, saying 93) matches the quote exactly: "Ὀκνηρὸς μοναχὸς πολλὰ ζημιωθήσεται, ἐὰν δὲ θαρσύνηται καὶ τὸ σχῆμα αὐτοῦ προσθήσει." The live English is "A listless monk will suffer many losses, and if he grows negligent he will add even his monastic habit to those losses." θαρσύνομαι means to grow bold or confident, and in a bad sense to grow reckless or brazen. It never means negligent. "Grows negligent" also just repeats ὀκνηρός and loses the step from laziness to brazenness. Driscoll's published translation agrees: "if he becomes reckless." This is a real wrong-sense error, not a style choice. The proposed fix is faithful. Its only flaw is "in it", which the Greek does not have, so it should be dropped.
verdict.better_correction: A listless monk will suffer many losses, and if he grows bold, he will add even his monastic habit to those losses.

errors.english_quote: contemplation of the Holy Trinity is better than the words of all the ages. / you will know the words of bodiless beings; serve Him and He will show you the words of the ages. / The words of providence are dark / a gentle monk will recognize the words of bodiless beings. / words of providence and judgment lift it up.
errors.source_quote: 110 θεωρία αὐτῆς ὑπὲρ λόγους πάντων τῶν αἰώνων; 116 γνώσῃ λόγους ἀσωμάτων ... δείξει σοι λόγους αἰώνων; 132 Λόγοι προνοίας σκοτεινοὶ; 133 λόγους δὲ ἀσωμάτων ἐπιγνώσεται; 135 λόγοι δὲ προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως
errors.why: In these sayings λόγοι is Evagrius's technical term for the inner reasons or principles of created things, providence and judgment. It does not mean spoken words. 'The words of bodiless beings' tells the reader that angels speak, and 'words of providence' tells the reader that providence makes statements. Both readings are false. A careful translator would use 'principles' or 'reasons' throughout this cluster. Elsewhere, 'words of God' and 'words of the father' are correct.
errors.corrected_english: ...than the principles of all the ages / you will know the principles of bodiless beings ... He will show you the principles of the ages / The principles of providence are dark / will recognize the principles of bodiless beings / the principles of providence and judgment lift it up.

verdict.reason:
The source matches the quotes. ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/evagrius-sententiae-monachos/translations/esm_u01_rem_source.json reads: 110 "θεωρία αὐτῆς ὑπὲρ λόγους πάντων τῶν αἰώνων"; 116 "γνώσῃ λόγους ἀσωμάτων ... δείξει σοι λόγους αἰώνων"; 132 "Λόγοι προνοίας σκοτεινοὶ"; 133 "λόγους δὲ ἀσωμάτων ἐπιγνώσεται μοναχὸς πραΰς"; 135 "λόγοι δὲ προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως ὑψοῦσιν αὐτήν". The live English in esm_u01_rem_english.json gives "words" each time.

In these sayings λόγοι is Evagrius's technical term for the inner reasons or principles. The surrounding words show it. The λόγοι stand next to θεωρία (110) and κρίσεως θεωρίαι (132). Saying 135 pairs them with κόσμων θεωρίαι. They are objects of contemplative knowledge, things the monk "knows" or "recognizes" (γνώσῃ, ἐπιγνώσεται). They are not speech. The standard English translations agree: Driscoll uses "reasons" ("reasons of providence," "reasons of the incorporeals," "reasons of the aeons") and Sinkewicz uses "principles." I cite both from memory and did not check them here. "Words of providence" and "words of bodiless beings" mislead the reader into thinking providence or angels speak. That is a wrong sense, not a style choice.

The proposed fix is faithful. "Principles" (or "reasons") throughout 110, 116, 132, 133 and 135 is right. It reads naturally in 110: "contemplation of it is better than the principles of all the ages." Keep "words" in 108 (λόγους θεοῦ, which a wise man searches out and a fool mocks), in 125 (λόγοι αἱρετικῶν) and in 126 (σκοτεινοὺς λόγους αὐτῶν, the heretics' speech). In those places λόγοι means real speech or doctrine.

errors.english_quote: If someone entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, give it back.
errors.source_quote: ἐὰν πιστεύσῃ σοι ἀργύριον, οὐ διασκορπιεῖς αὐτό, καὶ κἂν ἐπεργάσῃ, ἀποδώσεις αὐτό.
errors.why: This is the end of saying 73. The unstated subject of πιστεύσῃ is the spiritual father from the previous sentence ('Listen, monk, to the words of your father... Whenever he sends you'). Because the section split cuts the saying, 'someone' loses that link. As a result, the duty reads as a general one rather than a duty to one's father.
errors.corrected_english: If he entrusts silver to you, you will not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, you will give it back.

verdict.reason: The claim holds; it is a minor error. In esm_u01_rem_source.json, saying 73 runs across two sections. u01-rem-early ends with "73 Ἄκουε, μοναχέ, λόγους πατρός σου ... Ἡνίκα ἂν ἀποστείλῃ σε ... οὐκ ἰσχύσουσι κατά σου." u01-rem-mid then opens with "ἐὰν πιστεύσῃ σοι ἀργύριον, οὐ διασκορπιεῖς αὐτό, καὶ κἂν ἐπεργάσῃ, ἀποδώσεις αὐτό." No verse number comes before "ἐὰν", so this is the end of 73. The third-person singular πιστεύσῃ has no stated subject, so it carries over from the 'he' of the sentence before (ἀποστείλῃ, the father). The English "If someone entrusts silver to you" turns a duty owed to one's spiritual father into a general rule about deposits. The section split makes this worse: the line now opens a new section with no father in sight. The rest of the English holds up. ἐπεργάσῃ is the second-person aorist subjunctive of the deponent verb ἐπεργάζομαι, so "even if you put it to work" is right. The future indicatives οὐ διασκορπιεῖς and ἀποδώσεις can stand as commands ("do not scatter", "give it back"), so the future-tense wording in the proposed fix is fine but not required. The fix is faithful. Because the line stands alone at the head of the section, naming the father may read more clearly than a bare "he".
verdict.better_correction: If he (your father) entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it; and even if you put it to work, give it back. (Or, without the parenthesis: "If your father entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, give it back.")

errors.english_quote: A prudent monk will have freedom from passions, but a foolish one will pour out evils.
errors.source_quote: 105 Μοναχὸς φρόνιμος ἀπαθὴς ἔσται, ὁ δὲ ἄφρων ἐξαντλήσει κακά.
errors.why: ἐξαντλέω means to drain to the dregs, or to endure to the end. The foolish monk will drain a cup of evils, which means he will suffer them. 'Pour out evils' turns the fool into someone who spreads evil.
errors.corrected_english: A prudent monk will be free from passions, but a foolish one will drain evils to the dregs.

verdict.reason:
I checked both quotes in the files and they match exactly. The Greek is in esm_u01_rem_source.json: "105 Μοναχὸς φρόνιμος ἀπαθὴς ἔσται, ὁ δὲ ἄφρων ἐξαντλήσει κακά." The English is in esm_u01_rem_english.json: "...but a foolish one will pour out evils."

ἐξαντλέω does not mean "pour out" in the sense of giving off or spreading. Its literal meaning is to draw out or bail out completely, so to drain. Its figurative meaning is to exhaust, or to endure to the end, as with toils or a life. The line also seems to echo Proverbs 9:12 LXX: "ἐὰν δὲ κακὸς ἀποβῇς, μόνος ἀντλήσεις κακά", which Brenton gives as "thou alone shalt bear evil." There, drawing evils means suffering them.

The pairing in the sentence points the same way. The prudent monk ends up free of passions, and the fool ends up draining his own evils. "Pour out evils" makes the fool someone who does or spreads evil, which is the wrong sense. The error is real but low severity.

The proposed correction is faithful. "To the dregs" is a fair rendering of the ἐκ- prefix ("completely"). A plainer option is "will drain the cup of evils."
verdict.better_correction: A prudent monk will be free from passions, but a foolish one will drain evils to the dregs. (Alternative: "...but the fool will drain the cup of evils.")

errors.english_quote: do not leave your house and do not turn aside at a time when it is again profitable.
errors.source_quote: οἶκόν σου μὴ ἀφῇς καὶ μὴ ἐκκλίνῃς ἐν καιρῷ πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ.
errors.why: The English does not make sense. The locked Greek is corrupt at this point: 'πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ' is very likely a scribal error for 'πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς', meaning 'the profitable struggle'. That reading fits the image of whitening silver that follows. The English renders the corrupt words literally and produces nonsense. It should translate the evident sense, or mark a lacuna or emendation.
errors.corrected_english: do not leave your house, and do not turn aside at that time from the profitable struggle [text uncertain].

verdict.reason: The quotes are exact. The locked source (esm_u01_rem_source.json, and sources/sententiae_ad_monachos_pg.txt line 96) reads "μὴ ἐκκλίνῃς ἐν καιρῷ πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ". As written, that Greek does not parse cleanly: it has no relative pronoun, and "πάλιν" ("again") has nothing to refer back to. The English "do not turn aside at a time when it is again profitable" follows the corrupt words literally. It also misses the point of sentence 55, which is to stay put and endure listlessness the way silver is polished bright. The obvious repair is πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς, "of the profitable struggle". It changes only a few letters, and it is the sense modern English versions of Ad Monachos give ("do not turn aside in the time of profitable struggle", my recollection of Driscoll's version, which follows Gressmann's edition). So this is a real sense error, not a style preference. One caveat: I could not confirm Gressmann's reading online today; one web search for the phrase found nothing. Treat the emendation as highly probable, not proven. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly better one names the change rather than only flagging uncertainty.
verdict.better_correction: If a spirit of listlessness comes upon you, do not leave your house, and do not turn aside from the profitable struggle at that time. For as one whitens silver, so your heart will be made bright. [Translator note: the PG/Khazarzar text reads πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ, which does not make sense here; translated as πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς, "the profitable struggle", the reading of Gressmann's critical edition.]

errors.english_quote: Do not let wine gladden you, and do not let meat delight you, so that you do not nourish the flesh of your body, and shameful thoughts will not cease from you.
errors.source_quote: 38 Μὴ εὐφραινέτω σε οἶνος καὶ μὴ τερπέτω σε κρέας, ἵνα μὴ διαθρέψῃς σάρκας σώματός σου, καὶ λογισμοὶ αἰσχροὶ οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν ἀπό σου.
errors.why: The final clause belongs inside the 'lest' clause: lest you fatten the flesh and then shameful thoughts never leave you. The English reads as though abstaining causes shameful thoughts not to cease, which is the opposite of the meaning.
errors.corrected_english: Do not let wine gladden you or meat delight you, lest you fatten the flesh of your body and shameful thoughts never leave you.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (esm_u01_open_source.json lines 72-73: "ἵνα μὴ διαθρέψῃς σάρκας σώματός σου, καὶ λογισμοὶ αἰσχροὶ οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν ἀπό σου"). The καί clause goes with the negative purpose clause ἵνα μή. The future indicative is normal in Koine ἵνα clauses. The sense is "lest you fatten your flesh and shameful thoughts never leave you." The live English (esm_u01_open_english.json line 45) reads "so that you do not nourish the flesh of your body, and shameful thoughts will not cease from you." Read as a free-standing clause, it says shameful thoughts will stay. Read as part of the "so that" clause, it says the purpose of abstaining is that shameful thoughts will not cease. Both readings miss or reverse the point, which is that indulging keeps the thoughts with you. This is a real meaning problem, not a style preference, and low severity fits. The proposed fix keeps the clause under "lest" and keeps the Greek's sense. "Fatten" is a fair rendering of διαθρέψῃς, though "nourish" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: Do not let wine gladden you, and do not let meat delight you, lest you fatten the flesh of your body and shameful thoughts never leave you.

errors.english_quote: but the one who keeps it glorifies the one who made it.
errors.source_quote: 20 ... ὁ δὲ φυλάσσων αὐτὸν δοξάζει τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτόν.
errors.why: The final αὐτόν most naturally points to the man who keeps the law: he glorifies his own Maker. It is less likely to point to the law's author. 'Made it' narrows God to lawgiver and loses the creation sense that standard translations keep.
errors.corrected_english: but the one who keeps it glorifies the one who made him.

verdict.reason:
The quote is accurate. Line 20 of esm_u01_open_source.json reads: "Ἀτιμάζει θεὸν ὁ παραβαίνων νόμον αὐτοῦ, ὁ δὲ φυλάσσων αὐτὸν δοξάζει τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτόν." The English has "but the one who keeps it glorifies the one who made it."

The final αὐτόν is masculine, and so is νόμον. Inside that same clause, the first αὐτόν ("φυλάσσων αὐτὸν", "keeps it") clearly means the law. Reading the second αὐτόν as the law too ("made it") is therefore grammatically sound. It is not a wrong referent.

The claim's own wording admits this is about which reading is likelier ("most naturally", "less likely"). The meaning also stays the same either way: the one glorified is God, whether called the law's maker or the man's Maker. No person is swapped, nothing is reversed or left out, and nothing is added.

There is a fair case for "him": τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτόν echoes LXX Proverbs 14:31, where ὁ ποιήσας means the Creator, and Evagrius models these sayings on Proverbs. That makes "made him" a slightly better choice, not a needed fix. Treat it as an optional polish. "But the one who keeps it glorifies the one who made him" is faithful and fine to use if the editor wants the Creator sense.
verdict.better_correction: Optional polish, not an error: "but the one who keeps it glorifies his Maker." This keeps the creation sense and removes the ambiguous "him".

errors.english_quote: Heirs of God, listen to the words of God.
errors.source_quote: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ συνοδίαις μοναχούς.
errors.why: The source's own heading, 'To the monks in coenobia or communities', is left out of the English. The English title is a generic summary. The heading defines the audience the sayings address, which is not hermits.
errors.corrected_english: To the monks who live in monasteries or communities. Heirs of God, listen to the words of God.

verdict.better_correction: Insert the superscription as its own first paragraph, separate from saying 1: "To the monks who live in monasteries or in communities." Then leave saying 1 unchanged as the next paragraph: "Heirs of God, listen to the words of God. Co-heirs of Christ, receive the sayings of Christ, ..."
verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source for u01-open (translations/esm_u01_open_source.json) has, after the edition label "Sententiae ad monachos", the transmitted superscription "Πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ συνοδίαις μοναχούς." The English (esm_u01_open_english.json) starts straight at saying 1, "Heirs of God, listen to the words of God." Nothing in the English carries that line. The section title ("Opening exhortation and first sayings...") is editorial, and the book title "Sentences to Monks" drops the audience: monks in coenobia or communities, not hermits. Every numbered saying is rendered, so the superscription is the only gap. Severity low is right. It is real source text that names the intended readers, not just a style choice. The proposed wording is faithful (κοινόβια = monasteries, συνοδίαι = communities or brotherhoods of monks). But merging it into the same sentence as saying 1 turns a heading into part of the exhortation. It should stand as its own heading line before saying 1. The edition label "Sententiae ad monachos" is not text that needs translating.
