works.notes: I checked all 15 sections of justin-second-apology against the locked Greek of the Rauschen 1911 edition (First1KGreek). The work is short (about 25k characters), so I checked the whole of it, not just 8 sections. I found 11 errors in 8 sections; the other 7 sections are clean. The worst error is in §10: the objects are swapped, so Socrates expels the demons and rejects Homer. Two notes on readings I did not count as errors. In §2 the English 'whom Urbicus had summoned' follows the source as transmitted (ἐκαλέσατο); ANF reads 'punished'. In §7 'as I mentioned in my earlier defense' glosses προέφημεν, but the gloss is probably correct. Grok's REPORT.md (/Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/websites/fathers.saneapps.com/outputs/redteam-20261006/REPORT.md) has no faithfulness findings for this work. Its only Justin item is the duplicate First Apology 65 excerpts. Files: /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/justin-second-apology/translations/jsa_english.json and jsa_source.json. Read-only; nothing was edited.

errors.english_quote: But he cast out of the commonwealth the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets said, he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets,
errors.source_quote: Ὁ δὲ δαίμονας μὲν τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας ὰ ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταί, ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς, παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε
errors.why: Socrates expelled Homer and the poets from the state (Plato's Republic) and taught men to reject the wicked demons. The English swaps the objects: it has him expel the demons from the commonwealth and teach people to reject Homer.
errors.corrected_english: But he expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, and taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of,

verdict.reason: I checked translations/jsa_source.json, section 10. The Greek matches the quote: "Ὁ δὲ δαίμονας μὲν τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας ὰ ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταί, ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς, παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε". The participle phrase "ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς" means "having cast out of the state both Homer and the other poets"; the "καὶ ... καὶ" pair makes Homer and the poets its object. The accusatives "δαίμονας ... τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας" belong with "παραιτεῖσθαι ... ἐδίδαξε" ("he taught men to reject"). The μὲν goes with the "δὲ" in the next clause ("πρὸς θεοῦ δὲ ... προὐτρέπετο"): reject the demons, but seek God. This matches Plato's Republic, where the poets are expelled, and the standard ANF reading: "he cast out from the state both Homer and the rest of the poets, and taught men to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things which the poets related." The live English ("he cast out of the commonwealth the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets said, he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets") swaps the two objects. That is a real error of sense, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly closer version that keeps the participle and the μὲν/δὲ contrast: "But he, having expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of, and urged them..."
verdict.better_correction: But he, having expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of, and he urged them to gain knowledge of the God who was unknown to them through the search of the Word,

errors.english_quote: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself and to his sons, to the brothers of those sons, and to their children, such as the gods Poseidon and Pluto.
errors.source_quote: εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ γενομένους υἱοὺς καὶ τῶν λεχθέντων ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν καὶ τέκνων ὁμοίως τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων, Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος, ἀνήνεγκαν
errors.why: Poseidon and Pluto are the ones 'called HIS brothers' (ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν), and the children are theirs. The English makes them brothers of the sons or their children, and adds 'such as the gods'.
errors.corrected_english: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds, and the source in jsa_source.json §4 matches the quote exactly. The Greek reads: εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ γενομένους υἱοὺς καὶ τῶν λεχθέντων ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν καὶ τέκνων ὁμοίως τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων, Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος. In ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν, the pronoun ἐκείνου is singular and refers back to θεόν: these are the brothers of God himself, meaning Zeus in the poets' story. Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος stands in apposition to those brothers. The τέκνων τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων are the brothers' children. Myth confirms this reading: Poseidon and Pluto are the brothers of Zeus, not his sons' brothers or anyone's children.

The live English, "to the brothers of those sons, and to their children, such as the gods Poseidon and Pluto", has three errors:
1. It makes the brothers belong to the sons.
2. It makes Poseidon and Pluto examples of the children.
3. It adds "such as the gods", which is not in the Greek.

It also drops two hedges. ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ means "reputed to be born from his seed", and λεχθέντων means "so-called". Both show Justin is reporting the poets' claims, not making them himself. This is a real error in who is identified, not a style preference.

The proposed correction is faithful. It would be better still if it kept the ὡς hedge, for example: "attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those supposedly born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children."
verdict.better_correction: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those supposedly born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children.

errors.english_quote: This is also why God continues to delay the destruction and dissolution of the whole world, so that the wicked angels, demons, and human beings may no longer exist.
errors.source_quote: ἐπιμένει ὁ θεὸς τὴν σύγχυσιν καὶ κατάλυσιν τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου μὴ ποιῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ οἱ φαῦλοι ἄγγελοι καὶ δαίμονες καὶ ἄνθρωποι μηκέτι ὦσι
errors.why: The ἵνα clause describes what the destruction would do (end the wicked); the English makes it the purpose of God's delay, which reverses the logic: the delay keeps the wicked in being.
errors.corrected_english: This is also why God delays bringing about the confusion and dissolution of the whole world, by which the wicked angels, demons, and human beings would cease to exist.

verdict.reason: I checked jsa_source.json and jsa_english.json for section 6, and both quotes match the files exactly. In the Greek, ἐπιμένει ὁ θεὸς ... μὴ ποιῆσαι means "God holds back from bringing about the confusion and dissolution." The ἵνα clause (ἵνα ... μηκέτι ὦσι) belongs to that dissolution: it is what the world's end would do, which is make the wicked cease to exist. It is not God's purpose in waiting. The next clause, διὰ τὸ σπέρμα τῶν Χριστιανῶν, gives the actual reason for the delay. The ANF reads the passage the same way: "delays causing the confusion and destruction of the whole world, by which the wicked angels and demons and men shall cease to exist, because of the seed of the Christians." The current English says God delays "so that the wicked angels, demons, and human beings may no longer exist." Any reader takes that as the purpose of the delay, which reverses Justin's logic. The rest of the paragraph shows the delay is what lets the wicked go on acting ("it would no longer be possible for you to do these things"). This is a real sense error, not a style choice. The proposed fix ("delays bringing about the confusion and dissolution of the whole world, by which the wicked angels, demons, and human beings would cease to exist") is faithful and matches the ANF. The following sentence, "He delays because of the seed of the Christians...", can stay as it is.

errors.english_quote: or if he does know, but does not dare to speak because of his hearers, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher
errors.source_quote: ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος
errors.why: Drops 'like Socrates' (ὁμοίως Σωκράτει), the point of the comparison that sets up the Socratic saying in the next clause.
errors.corrected_english: or if he does know, but does not dare, because of his hearers, to speak as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher

verdict.reason: I checked section 8 of jsa_source.json, and the claim holds. The source reads "ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος ἀλλὰ φιλόδοξος ἀνὴρ δείκνυται". The source spells it "Σωρκάτει", a typo for Σωκράτει. The live English says "or if he does know, but does not dare to speak because of his hearers, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher". It leaves out ὁμοίως Σωκράτει ("like Socrates") completely. That phrase is not filler. Socrates spoke the truth whatever his audience thought, and this is the contrast that sets up the "Socratic saying" quoted in the next clause. Without it, the later reference to Socrates has nothing to point back to. Standard translations keep the phrase; Dods has "does not dare to speak out, like Socrates". So this is a real omission, not a matter of style. The proposed fix is faithful. It reads "or if he does know, but does not dare, because of his hearers, to speak as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher". It is a little clumsy, so the alternative in better_correction may read more smoothly. Separately, the typo "Σωρκάτει" in the locked source text could be fixed as well.
verdict.better_correction: or if he does know, but because of his hearers does not dare to speak out as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher

errors.english_quote: he confessed that he was a Christian.
errors.source_quote: τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν
errors.why: The Greek says he confessed 'the school of divine virtue'; the English replaces Justin's phrase with a flat repeat of the earlier question.
errors.corrected_english: he confessed the school of divine virtue.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute it. The locked Greek source (jsa_source.json, section 2) reads: "Καὶ πάλιν, τὰ καλὰ ἑαυτῷ συνεπιστάμενος διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδαχήν, τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν." The object of ὡμολόγησεν is "τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς", meaning "the school (or teaching) of divine virtue". The certified English (jsa_english.json, section 2, paragraph 5) instead says "he confessed that he was a Christian." That repeats the wording of the question two sentences earlier ("εἰ εἴη Χριστιανός") and drops Justin's own description of the Christian faith. The overall sense survives, since he still confesses his faith, so the severity is low. But a careful translator would put back Justin's phrase, which is the point of "καὶ πάλιν". Standard translations keep it; ANF/Dods has "he confessed his discipleship in divine virtue". The proposed "he confessed the school of divine virtue" follows the Greek closely and is acceptable. "He confessed himself of the school of divine virtue" would read more naturally.
verdict.better_correction: he confessed himself of the school of divine virtue.

errors.english_quote: We have also learned that he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him,
errors.source_quote: χαίρειν τε τοῖς τὰ προσόντα αὐτῷ μιμουμένοις προέφημεν
errors.why: προέφημεν means 'we said before', a cross-reference to Justin's earlier statement, not 'we have learned'.
errors.corrected_english: And, as we said before, he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him,

verdict.reason: Checked jsa_source.json §3. The locked source has the misspelling 'φροέφημεν' for προέφημεν, which is the standard reading of 2 Apol. 4 (Otto/Migne; ANF has 'And we have before stated that He takes pleasure in those who imitate His properties'). προέφημεν is aorist of πρόφημι, 'we said before'. It is not 'we have learned'. It points back to Justin's earlier statement (1 Apol. 10). It also governs both infinitives, χαίρειν and ἀπαρέσκεσθαι, so the whole sentence is reported earlier speech. The live English, 'We have also learned that he rejoices...', turns Justin's back-reference into a second taught doctrine that copies the δεδιδάγμεθα of the sentence before. That is a real wrong-sense error, though a minor one. The proposed fix, 'And, as we said before, he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him, and is displeased with those who embrace what is base, whether in word or in deed', is faithful. One detail: the source's spelling differs slightly from the quote in the claim (φροέφημεν against προέφημεν). This is an OCR typo in the source file and does not change the meaning.
verdict.better_correction: And we said before that he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him, and is displeased with those who embrace what is base, whether in word or in deed.

errors.english_quote: and that they were spreading lies about these teachings. So I laughed at that covering and at the opinion held by the many.
errors.source_quote: καὶ ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ περιβλήματος κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης
errors.why: ψευδολογουμένων is the first of three genitive objects of κατεγέλασα: Justin laughed at the liars, the disguise, and popular opinion. The English moves it into what he 'learned' and drops the liars as something he laughed at.
errors.corrected_english: So I laughed at those who told these lies, at the covering itself, and at the opinion held by the many.

verdict.reason:
I checked jsa_source.json and jsa_english.json for section 13. The source quote is exact: "μαθὼν περίβλημα πονηρὸν ... περιτεθειμένον ... τοῖς Χριστιανῶν θείοις διδάγμασι, καὶ ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ περιβλήματος κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης."

The claim stands. The repeated καὶ ... καὶ ... καὶ links three genitives that all depend on κατεγέλασα: ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα ("those telling lies about these things"), τοῦ περιβλήματος and τῆς ... δόξης. The participle cannot hang on μαθὼν, because μαθὼν takes the accusative περίβλημα ... περιτεθειμένον. So "and that they were spreading lies about these teachings", which makes the lying part of what Justin learned, misreads the syntax and drops the liars as a target of his laughter. The standard translations agree. Dods has "laughed both at those who framed these falsehoods, and at the disguise itself, and at popular opinion", and Falls and Barnard read it the same way.

It is a minor error: the lying is still mentioned, just in the wrong role. But a careful translator would fix it.

The proposed fix only rewrites the second sentence. It leaves the clause "and that they were spreading lies about these teachings" in the first sentence, so the lying would appear twice. "Those who told these lies" also has nothing to refer back to once that clause is gone.
verdict.better_correction: I too once learned that wicked demons had wrapped an evil covering around the divine teachings of Christians to turn other people away. So I laughed at those who spread lies about these teachings, at the covering itself, and at the opinion held by the many.

errors.english_quote: since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human reason.
errors.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη
errors.why: Drops τὰ σκεύη ('the vessels/instruments'): Christ is not the instrument of human reason. The English blurs it into 'power ... of human reason'.
errors.corrected_english: since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not the instrument of human reason.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source quote is exact. Section 10 of jsa_source.json ends with "ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη." The English in jsa_english.json ends with "since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human reason." That leaves τὰ σκεύη untranslated.

The English keeps the contrast between divine origin and human reason, so the sense is not reversed and the error is low severity. It is still a real omission. Justin is not saying Christ's power is "not of human reason" in a loose sense. He says Christ is not the vessel or instrument (σκεύη) of human reason. That ties back to the Socrates contrast: what philosophers worked out with human tools is set against the power of the Father.

The passage is a known textual crux, and some editors emend the text to κατασκευή ("a construct of human reason"). Rauschen's text, which is the copy text here, reads τὰ σκεύη. The standard English rendering (ANF/Dods) is "not the mere instrument of human reason."

The proposed correction, "and not the instrument of human reason," is faithful. The singular "instrument" for the plural σκεύη is fine, since the subject is Christ ("he is"). An optional, slightly more literal version would be "and not a vessel of human reason."

errors.english_quote: These people become liable to punishment through their own fault, so that these things may be known to all people, because the ability to know good and shameful is part of human nature,
errors.source_quote: οἳ παρὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν αἰτίαν ὑπεύθυνοι ταῖς τιμωρίαις γίνονται [εἰς τὸ γνωσθῆναι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ταῦτα], διὰ τὸ ἐν τῇ φύσει τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἶναι τὸ γνωριστικὸν
errors.why: The bracketed phrase is an editor-marked intrusion. Rendering it as the purpose of their liability ('liable to punishment ... so that these things may be known') makes no sense.
errors.corrected_english: These people become liable to punishment through their own fault, because the ability to know good and shameful is part of human nature,

verdict.reason: I checked §14 in jsa_source.json and jsa_english.json. The Greek quote is accurate: the copy-text (Rauschen 1911) does carry "[εἰς τὸ γνωσθῆναι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ταῦτα]" right after "ὑπεύθυνοι ταῖς τιμωρίαις γίνονται". The English renders those words where they stand, so it follows the transmitted Greek. The odd sense is in the Greek itself, and that is why the editor bracketed the phrase. Translating it is defensible: ANF also renders this phrase as a purpose clause at the same point. It also matches this book's own rule. book.yml says the scope is "Complete as transmitted in the copy-text edition", and the book's other bracketed passage (§15, "Καὶ τοῦ ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ἔθνει ἀσεβοῦς ... κατεφρόνησα") is translated: "I also despised the impious and deceitful teaching of the Simonians in my own nation." Silently dropping the §14 phrase, as the claim proposes, would be an omission against the locked source and would break that rule, so the correction is not faithful. One real but small flaw: "to all people" adds "all", which is not in "τοῖς ἀνθρώποις" ("to people"). That is a nit, not the garbling the claim describes. If a fix is wanted, keep the words, mark them as the editor's suspect phrase, and drop "all".
verdict.better_correction: These people become liable to punishment through their own fault [so that these things may be made known to people], because the ability to know good and shameful is part of human nature,

errors.english_quote: These were things the demons themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.
errors.source_quote: ὧν ἐνδεεῖς γεγόνασι μετὰ τὸ πάθεσιν ἐπιθυμιῶν δουλωθῆναι
errors.why: The subject running through the sentence is the fallen angels (οἱ δ᾿ ἄγγελοι ... ἐδούλωσαν), the ones who were enslaved to lust. Naming 'the demons' as the subject is an addition that shifts the referent.
errors.corrected_english: These were things they themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute the claim. I read section 4 of jsa_source.json against jsa_english.json. In the Greek, the subject running through the sentence is "Οἱ δ᾿ ἄγγελοι" (the angels). The main verb "ἐδούλωσαν" (they enslaved) continues that subject, and so does the relative clause "ὧν ἐνδεεῖς γεγόνασι μετὰ τὸ πάθεσιν ἐπιθυμιῶν δουλωθῆναι". The word "demons" appears only in the earlier side clause "οἵ εἰσιν οἱ λεγόμενοι δαίμονες". The text supports the angels as the ones "enslaved to the passions of their desires": they are the ones just described as "γυναικῶν μίξεσιν ἡττήθησαν" (overcome by intercourse with women). The English "These were things the demons themselves came to need" adds a noun that isn't in the Greek and switches the subject from the angels to their offspring. The Greek has no word for "themselves" either. A reader could argue that Justin elsewhere treats angels and demons together, and the next sentence says "τοὺς ἀγγέλους καὶ τοὺς ἐξ αὐτῶν γεννηθέντας δαίμονας". That makes the Greek's "they" open to reading as both, but it doesn't justify narrowing it to "the demons" alone. Severity low is right. The proposed fix, "These were things they themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires", is faithful because it restores the unnamed "they". Its "themselves" is a harmless addition; the better_correction field drops it to match the Greek more closely.
verdict.better_correction: These were things they had come to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.

errors.english_quote: When her own people entreated her to remain still,
errors.source_quote: ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων
errors.why: 'remain still' reads as 'keep quiet'. ἔτι προσμένειν means 'stay on a while longer' in the marriage.
errors.corrected_english: When her own people urged her to stay with him a while longer,

verdict.reason:
The claim holds; I read both files. The source in jsa_source.json §2 matches the quote: "Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων, ὡς εἰς ἐλπίδα μεταβολῆς ἥξοντός ποτε τοῦ ἀνδρός, βιαζομένη ἑαυτὴν ἐπέμενεν." In jsa_english.json §2, paragraph 2, ἔτι προσμένειν is rendered "to remain still". In this Greek, ἔτι means "still / yet longer" and goes with προσμένειν, "stay on" (in the marriage). Here, though, "still" falls after "remain", so most readers will take it as "keep still / stay quiet". That is a different sense, and it hides the point that she stayed in the marriage. The ANF has "advised her still to continue with him". This is a real if minor wording fault, not a style preference: the English invites the wrong meaning. Severity: low.

The proposed correction is faithful. "Urged" fits ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο, which means she was moved by their pleas. "With him" is implied by the context. It also fits the rest of the sentence: "...stay with him a while longer, advising her in the hope that her husband would one day come to a change, she forced herself and remained." The participle "advising" repeats "urged" slightly but stays faithful. A tighter option: "When her own people prevailed on her, advising her to stay on with him still, in the hope that her husband would one day change, she forced herself and remained."
verdict.better_correction: When her own people prevailed on her, advising her to stay on with him still, in the hope that her husband would one day come to a change, she forced herself and remained.

works.notes: I checked 8 of the 17 sections against the Latin (CSEL 20, Reifferscheid-Wissowa), spread across the work: 1, 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 16 and 17. Every section had at least one real error. The worst are four reversals: §6 'omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat' (discipline made the subject), §9 food and drink swapped, §16 'purpuras ponunt' rendered as 'put on', and §10 Peter going up to eat before praying. There are also two inventions: §16 'comendis' read as 'eating', and §6's added gloss 'as far as fasting makes them so'. One Scripture reference is wrong: §2 cites Acts 10:9 where it should be Acts 3:1. The Grok red-team REPORT.md (~/SaneApps/websites/fathers.saneapps.com/outputs/redteam-20261006/REPORT.md) does not mention this work, so it neither confirms nor contradicts these findings. Minor points I left out: 'botuli' rendered as 'gluttons', 'fastos' (calendars) rendered as 'fasts', and 'forte' rendered as 'perhaps' in the Jonathan passage. Read-only: no files changed. The files are in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-fasting/translations/ (tof_source.json, tof_english.json).

errors.english_quote: Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds.
errors.source_quote: omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat.
errors.why: 'omnem disciplinam' is the object. Feeding (the full belly) kills or wounds all discipline. The English makes discipline the subject that kills, which reverses Tertullian's argument for fasting.
errors.corrected_english: Feeding either kills or wounds every discipline.

verdict.reason: I could not refute it; the claim holds. The Latin in tof_source.json §6 is exactly "omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat." "omnem disciplinam" is accusative, so it can only be the object. The subject has to be "uictus" (nominative: food/diet). The English "Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds" reads "uictus" as a genitive and makes "discipline" the subject. The accusative case rules that out. It also breaks the logic of the passage. The sentence before it says nobody remembers God when the man "slips away from himself" through fullness. The sentence after it says the Lord blames forgetting him on "plenitudini" (fullness). So food is what kills or wounds discipline. Thelwall's ANF rendering agrees: "Every discipline food either slays or else wounds." The proposed fix "Feeding either kills or wounds every discipline" is faithful. "Food" is a slightly closer match for "uictus" than "Feeding". Files: /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-fasting/translations/tof_source.json and tof_english.json, section 6.
verdict.better_correction: Food either kills or wounds every discipline.

errors.english_quote: there the pressure on drink should also be understood as establishing the pattern for food.
errors.source_quote: illic intellegatur etiam pabuli pressura formam praestruens potui.
errors.why: 'pabuli pressura' (restriction of food) sets the pattern 'potui' (for drink). The English swaps food and drink.
errors.corrected_english: there a restriction of food should also be understood, setting the pattern for the drink.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. tof_source.json §9 reads: "quamquam ubi abstinentia uini aut a deo exigitur aut ab homine uouetur, illic intellegatur etiam pabuli pressura formam praestruens potui. qualis enim esus, talis et potus."

The grammar settles it:
- "pabuli pressura" (restriction of food, literally fodder) is the nominative subject of "intellegatur".
- "praestruens" agrees with "pressura".
- "potui" is a dative: for the drink.

So the Latin says that where wine is given up, a restriction of food is also implied, and it sets the pattern for the drink. The next sentence ("as the eating is, so is the drinking") backs this up: the argument goes from drink to food. The live English reads "there the pressure on drink should also be understood as establishing the pattern for food." That swaps food and drink and breaks the argument. It is a reversed sense, not a style choice. ANF (Thelwall) also renders it as a restriction of food that gives the pattern for drink.

The proposed correction is faithful. A small option: "praestruens" can also be read as "laying the groundwork for" the drink, but "setting the pattern for" is fine.
verdict.better_correction: there a restriction of food should also be understood, setting the pattern for the drink.

errors.english_quote: magistrates put on their purple
errors.source_quote: magistratus purpuras ponunt
errors.why: 'ponunt' here means 'lay aside', a sign of mourning, which fits the next clause about turning the fasces backward. 'Put on' says the opposite.
errors.corrected_english: magistrates lay aside their purple

verdict.reason: I checked the source and it matches the quote: tof_source.json §16 has "nudipedalia denuntiantur, magistratus purpuras ponunt, fasces retro auertunt, precem indigitant, hostiam instaurant." The certified English renders "ponunt" as "magistrates put on their purple", and that gets the sense backwards. With clothing or insignia, "ponere" means "lay down, take off", the same as "deponere" ("ponere arma", "ponere vestem"). The whole sentence lists acts of public humbling: the sentence before reads "omnem ταπεινοφρόνησιν ethnici agnoscunt". It also lists barefoot processions and fasces turned backward, which was a Roman sign of mourning (Tacitus, Annals 3.4). Putting on the purple would be a show of rank, which runs against the point Tertullian is making. The standard ANF translation (Thelwall) also reads "the magistrates lay aside their purple." The proposed fix, "magistrates lay aside their purple", is faithful and fits the existing sentence without other changes.

errors.english_quote: Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to eat, before praying
errors.source_quote: Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi causa prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse
errors.why: Peter went up to pray first, before eating (Acts 10:9-10). The English says he went up to eat before praying, which reverses the order the argument depends on: prayer completes the station before food.
errors.corrected_english: Peter, before taking food, first went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to pray

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked tof_source.json §10, which reads "atqui facilius inuenias Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi causa prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse, quo magis sexta diei finiri officio huic possit, quae illud absolutura post orationem uidebatur." In this sentence "ad orandum" gives the purpose of going up: to pray. "Prius" means he did this first, and "capiendi cibi causa" ties it to the meal that would follow. That matches Acts 10:9-10, where Peter goes up to pray, grows hungry and wants to eat. The tradition agrees: ANF renders it "for the sake of taking food, gone up first to the higher place for prayer." The argument needs prayer first and food second. The sixth hour can only end the station because the duty is "completed after prayer," with the meal coming after the prayer. The live English ("Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to eat, before praying") makes eating the purpose of going up and puts it before prayer. That reverses the order, and the next clause in the same English ("completed after prayer") then contradicts it. This is not a style point. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly closer version that keeps "capiendi cibi causa" would be: "Peter, with a view to taking food at the sixth hour, first went up to the upper room to pray."
verdict.better_correction: Yet you could more easily find that Peter, with a view to taking food at the sixth hour, first went up to the upper room to pray

errors.english_quote: since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 10:9).
errors.source_quote: quando et orationes fere hora nona concludat de Petri exemplo, quod Actis refertur.
errors.why: Acts 10:9 is Peter praying at the sixth hour. The ninth-hour example is Acts 3:1, where Peter and John go up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. Section 10 cites that verse for this same point.
errors.corrected_english: since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 3:1).

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in tof_source.json §2 reads "quando et orationes fere hora nona concludat de Petri exemplo, quod Actis refertur", and the English in tof_english.json §2 matches the quote, ending "(Acts 10:9)". The Latin gives no verse number, so the translator added this reference, and it is wrong. Acts 10:9 is Peter praying on the housetop at the sixth hour. The ninth-hour example is Acts 3:1, where Peter and John go up to the temple "at the ninth hour of prayer". Tertullian's own §10 shows he means that verse: "Petrus et qui cum eo ad horam nonam orationis templum introgressi leguntur" ("Peter and those with him are recorded as entering the temple at the ninth hour of prayer"). In the same chapter he treats the sixth-hour housetop scene (Acts 10:9) as a separate event ("Petrum hora sexta ... in superiora ad orandum"). One detail in the claim is off but does not change the verdict: §10's English has no inline "Acts 3:1" citation. It only describes the scene. Changing the reference to (Acts 3:1) is faithful. Deleting the added parenthesis would also be acceptable.

errors.english_quote: those who fawn over idols by eating and adorning them
errors.source_quote: qui in idolis comendis et in hac re ornandis
errors.why: 'comendis' comes from como (to dress or deck out), not comedo (to eat). Nobody eats the idols. The English adds a meaning that is not in the source.
errors.corrected_english: those who fawn over idols by dressing them and adorning them

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim. In tof_source.json §16 the Latin reads "qui in idolis comendis et in hac re ornandis et ad singulas horas salutandis diis adulantur, curationem facere dicuntur." "comendis" is the gerundive of como, comere, meaning to dress, deck or arrange, as with the hair of cult statues. If the word came from comedo (to eat), the form would be "comedendis". Nothing in the clause means eating. So "by eating and adorning them" in tof_english.json §16 brings in a sense the Latin does not have, and it makes the image odd, since nobody eats idols. The point is the daily care of cult statues (dressing, adorning, greeting at set hours), which pagans called curatio, "service". The proposed fix ("dressing them and adorning them") is faithful. One small point the fix keeps from the current English: the dative "diis adulantur" says the people fawn on the gods, and the gerundives describe what they do to the idols.
verdict.better_correction: This is why those who fawn on their gods by dressing and adorning the idols and greeting them at every hour are said to offer service.

errors.english_quote: and the little water is the altar
errors.source_quote: et aqualiculus altare
errors.why: 'aqualiculus' means paunch or stomach (the belly-god image). 'The little water' is nonsense in context.
errors.corrected_english: and your paunch is the altar

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source, tof_source.json §16, reads exactly "deus enim tibi uenter est et pulmo templum et aqualiculus altare et sacerdos cocus...". In Lewis & Short, "aqualiculus" means the stomach, paunch or belly. Its root sense of a small water vessel is not what the word means here. The context is a list of digestive organs set against worship: belly as god, lung as temple. That list needs "paunch/stomach" to make sense, and Thelwall's ANF version gives "thy paunch an altar". The live English, "and the little water is the altar", takes the word apart by its roots and makes nonsense of the sentence, so a careful translator would fix it. The proposed "and your paunch is the altar" is faithful. "The paunch is the altar" would match the list's other items, which carry no "your", but either wording is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: and the paunch is the altar

errors.english_quote: Certainly the God who was not pleased by a people lacking self-control in gluttony was not pleased by priest or prophet either.
errors.source_quote: ille certe deus, cui nec populus incontinens gulae placuit, nec sacerdos nec prophetes.
errors.why: 'incontinens gulae' covers all three. God was pleased by no people, priest or prophet who lacked self-control in gluttony. The English says God was not pleased by priests or prophets at all.
errors.corrected_english: He is surely the God whom neither a people, nor a priest, nor a prophet lacking self-control in gluttony ever pleased.

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source in tof_source.json matches the quote exactly: "ille certe deus, cui nec populus incontinens gulae placuit, nec sacerdos nec prophetes." The three subjects share one verb, "placuit", in a nec...nec...nec series. "incontinens gulae" sits next to "populus", but the passage reads it with all three. The examples that follow prove this. The people are the quail-gluttons. The priest is Eli, whose house "cheated the fleshly sacrifices", a matter of greed for meat. The prophet is Shemaiah, who broke his fast by eating. The paragraph then sums up: "examples both to the people and to bishops ... if they admit any lack of self-control in gluttony." The current English attaches the qualifier only to the people. "was not pleased by priest or prophet either" then reads as God disliking priests and prophets as such. That is a real change of sense, not a style point, though "low-medium" fits it better than "medium". The proposed fix gets the sense right but has two flaws. It adds "ever", which is not in the Latin. And with "lacking self-control in gluttony" placed after "prophet", it can read as qualifying only the prophet, which is the same kind of ambiguity in reverse. The smallest faithful fix keeps the current sentence and adds "such", so the qualifier covers all three.
verdict.better_correction: Certainly the God who was not pleased by a people lacking self-control in gluttony was not pleased by such a priest or prophet either.  (A closer alternative: "Surely this is the God whom no people, no priest and no prophet lacking self-control in gluttony pleased.")

errors.english_quote: I do not mean from the business of collecting contributions, as you are quick to point out
errors.source_quote: non dico de industria stipium conferendarum, ut uestrae capturae est
errors.why: 'ut uestrae capturae est' is Tertullian's jab: 'as is your way of making gain', meaning the psychic bishops call fasts to raise money. The English turns his charge into an objection from the opponents.
errors.corrected_english: I do not mean for the business of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In tof_source.json §13 the Latin reads exactly: "bene autem, quod et episcopi uniuersae plebi mandare ieiunia adsolent, non dico de industria stipium conferendarum, ut uestrae capturae est, sed interdum et ex aliqua sollicitudinis ecclesiasticae causa." "captura" means gain, a catch, or profit, and "ut uestrae capturae est" means "as is your way of making gain". It is Tertullian's own jab: the psychic bishops call fasts to raise collections. Thelwall reads it the same way ("as your capturing policy has it"). The live English, "as you are quick to point out", makes it a remark by the opponents. That reverses whose charge it is and drops the accusation of profiteering. Nothing in "capturae" means pointing anything out, so this is a wrong sense, not a matter of word choice. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly smoother version that keeps the idiom "de industria" ("on purpose, for the purpose of") would be: "I do not mean for the purpose of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain, but sometimes also from some cause of concern for the church."
verdict.better_correction: I do not mean for the purpose of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain, but sometimes also from some cause of concern for the church

errors.english_quote: if you conduct a gathering of everyone together even at a human edict
errors.source_quote: si et ex hominis edicto et in unum omnes ταπεινοφρόνησιν agitatis
errors.why: The Greek word (garbled in the source, = tapeinophronesis, 'humiliation') is the object. They practise a common self-humbling or fast, not just 'a gathering'. Losing it drops the parallel to 'unitatem ieiunationum' in the next clause.
errors.corrected_english: if you all practise a common humiliation (fasting) together, and at a human edict

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in tof_source.json §13 reads "itaque si et ex hominis edicto et in unum omnes 'tCl'itEtVoą'póV'tjatv agitatis". The garbled OCR token stands for ταπεινοφρόνησιν (humiliation, self-abasement), and it is the object of "agitatis". "In unum omnes" means "all together as one"; it does not mean "a gathering". The live English reads "if you conduct a gathering of everyone together even at a human edict". That turns the adverbial phrase into an invented object and drops ταπεινοφρόνησιν altogether. As a result the reader loses the point: the bishops' commanded common fast is the parallel to the "unitatem ieiunationum et xerophagiarum et stationum" that Tertullian is defending. Thelwall also renders this as "all unanimously practise humiliation". The proposed correction is close but not fully faithful. It adds "(fasting)" as a gloss that is not in the source. It also turns "et ... et" (even/both) into "and at a human edict", which weakens the concession that this happens even at a mere man's edict.
verdict.better_correction: Therefore, if even at a human edict you all practise humiliation together as one, how do you censure in us that very unity of fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts?

errors.english_quote: equal in truth to his equal, as far as fasting makes them so.
errors.source_quote: parem reuera pari.
errors.why: 'as far as fasting makes them so' has no counterpart in the Latin. It is an added gloss.
errors.corrected_english: equal in truth to his equal.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin at the end of section 6 (tof_source.json) reads exactly: "tanta est circumscripti uictus praerogatiua, ut deum praestet homini contubernalem, parem reuera pari." Nothing in it limits the equality, so "as far as fasting makes them so" is the translator's own hedge. The next sentence already says how man becomes equal to God ("hoc erit tempus, quo homo deo adaequetur, cum sine pabulo uiuit"), so the hedge is not needed and blunts Tertullian's deliberately bold claim. It is a real addition, though small. I would rate it low to medium rather than medium, because it softens the meaning without reversing it. The proposed fix, "equal in truth to his equal.", is faithful: reuera means "in truth" or "in fact", and parem ... pari means "equal to equal". The full corrected sentence would read: "So great is the prerogative of a restricted diet, that it makes God a tent-companion to man, equal in truth to his equal."

errors.english_quote: fed by God and fattened in name by his fasting
errors.source_quote: Moysen deo pastum inediamque eius nomine saginatam
errors.why: The Latin says Moses was fed by God and his fasting was fattened (enriched) by God's name. 'Fattened in name by his fasting' makes no sense and loses the paradox.
errors.corrected_english: Moses, fed by God, his fasting fattened by God's name

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source (tof_source.json, §6) reads: "cum quidem nec ipsum Moysen deo pastum inediamque eius nomine saginatam constanter contemplari ualeret pinguior populus." Grammatically, "pastum" goes with Moses, and "saginatam" goes with "inediam" (his fasting). So "deo pastum" means "fed by God", and the second phrase means "his fasting, fattened by [God's] name". It is the fasting that is fattened, by the name. The English "fed by God and fattened in name by his fasting" makes Moses the one fattened, and it turns "fasting" into the cause instead of the thing fattened. That reverses the structure and loses Tertullian's deliberate paradox: the fatter people cannot look at a man whose very fasting is "fattened". It is a real sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful. "eius" most naturally points to God (deo), but "His name" would keep the slight ambiguity of the Latin. The suggested phrasing also drops the "-que" link, which is minor.
verdict.better_correction: although indeed the fatter people could not steadily look upon even Moses himself, fed by God, and his fasting fattened by God's name.

errors.english_quote: does not reckon the cause to fullness
errors.source_quote: causam plenitudini reputat
errors.why: Not English. The meaning is that the Lord attributes Israel's forgetting to fullness (satiety).
errors.corrected_english: does not attribute the cause to fullness

verdict.reason: The source (tof_source.json §6) reads "mentior, si non dominus ipse obliuionem sui exprobrans Israeli causam plenitudini reputat", and the English gives "I lie, if the Lord himself, reproaching Israel with forgetfulness of him, does not reckon the cause to fullness." The sense is right: same speaker, same negation, and fullness is the cause. Nothing is left out or added. "Reckon X to Y" is a real English construction meaning "impute X to Y", as in RSV Romans 4:9, "faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness". It is stiff but it is English, not garbled, so this is a style preference, not a faithfulness error. If the line is smoothed anyway, "does not attribute the cause to fullness" (or "ascribe") is faithful to "causam plenitudini reputat".
verdict.better_correction: does not ascribe the cause to fullness

errors.english_quote: equate them with those of chaste Isis and Cybele
errors.source_quote: casto Isidis et Cybeles eas adaequas
errors.why: 'castus' is a noun here: the ritual abstinence of Isis and Cybele. The goddesses are not called chaste. The point is that the rites are compared.
errors.corrected_english: equate them with the abstinence rites of Isis and Cybele

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in tof_source.json, section 16, reads "sed bene quod tu nostris xerophagiis blasphemias ingerens casto Isidis et Cybeles eas adaequas." "casto" is masculine or neuter singular. It cannot agree as an adjective with "Isidis" and "Cybeles", which are feminine genitives. It is the cult noun castum/castus (dative after adaequas): the set period of ritual abstinence, as in Festus and Arnobius's "castum Cereris". So the Latin says "you equate them [our dry-food fasts] with the abstinence-rite of Isis and Cybele". The English, "equate them with those of chaste Isis and Cybele", misreads "casto" as an epithet of the goddesses and drops the noun that names the rite. This is a grammar error, not a style choice, though it is minor because the point that fasts are being compared survives. The proposed correction, "equate them with the abstinence rites of Isis and Cybele", is faithful. The singular, "the sacred abstinence of Isis and Cybele", would also work.

errors.english_quote: "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a healing" (Joel 2:15, LXX)
errors.source_quote: sancite ieiunium et praedicate curationem
errors.why: 'curatio' renders LXX therapeia, meaning service or worship. The next sentences use the same word for 'services that care for God' and the pagans' 'curationem facere' (rendered 'offer service'). 'Healing' breaks that link.
errors.corrected_english: "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a service" (Joel 2:15, LXX)

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. tof_source.json §16 reads: "nam et Iohel exclamauit: sancite ieiunium et praedicate curationem, prospiciens ... praedicaturos officia curantia deum. unde et qui in idolis comendis ... diis adulantur, curationem facere dicuntur." The LXX of Joel 2:15 (and 1:14) has κηρύξατε θεραπείαν, where θεραπεία means service or worship, not medical healing. Tertullian's whole point depends on that sense. The prophets will proclaim "officia curantia deum", and "unde" ("this is why") pagans who attend to idols are said to "curationem facere". The English already gives those two later uses as "services that care for God" and "offer service". Rendering the quotation itself as "proclaim a healing" therefore breaks the chain of reasoning, so the "This is why..." sentence no longer follows. That is a real sense error inside the argument, not a style choice. Low severity is right. The citation (Joel 2:15, LXX) is valid. The proposed fix, "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a service", is faithful and restores the link. "Proclaim a service of worship" would be an acceptable alternative.

I also noticed two other errors in the same section while checking. They are outside this claim but worth logging. (1) "magistratus purpuras ponunt" is rendered "magistrates put on their purple". "Ponunt" here means "lay aside", which is the mourning gesture, so the English reverses the sense. It should read "magistrates lay aside their purple". (2) "aqualiculus altare" is rendered "the little water is the altar". "Aqualiculus" means paunch or belly, so it should read "the paunch is the altar".

errors.english_quote: For he had been guilty of gluttony, even if innocent.
errors.source_quote: gulae enim licet simplicis reus fuerat.
errors.why: 'simplicis' describes the gluttony as simple or unwitting. Jonathan is not called innocent. 'Guilty ... even if innocent' contradicts itself.
errors.corrected_english: For he had been guilty of gluttony, though an unwitting one.

verdict.reason: The claim stands, as a low-severity error. The source quote is exact. The Latin in tof_source.json, §10 reads: "gulae enim licet simplicis reus fuerat." Here "simplicis" is genitive and agrees with "gulae", so it describes the gluttony, not Jonathan. The meaning is "guilty of a gluttony, albeit a simple/guileless one." The live English, "For he had been guilty of gluttony, even if innocent," moves the innocence onto Jonathan, so the sentence says he was both guilty and innocent. A careful translator would fix that. The intended sense (no guilty intent) can still be recovered, which is why the severity is low. This is not a style preference: the English changes what the adjective describes and produces a contradiction the Latin does not have. The proposed fix, "For he had been guilty of gluttony, though an unwitting one," is faithful. "Unwitting" fits the context ("quamquam ignarus ieiunationis"), and it keeps simplicis attached to the gluttony. A slightly more literal option: "For he had been guilty of gluttony, though of an innocent sort." The ANF translation is similar: "although of a simple kind."
verdict.better_correction: For he had been guilty of gluttony, though of an innocent (unwitting) sort.

errors.english_quote: For they say that where they wish, they recognize what the law and the prophets mean, up to John
errors.source_quote: ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem.
errors.why: This is Tertullian's own sarcastic aside that they invoke 'until John' only when it suits them. 'They say' turns it into the opponents' own claim.
errors.corrected_english: For where it suits them, they recognize what 'the law and the prophets until John' means

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I could not refute it. The Latin in tof_source.json §2 reads exactly as quoted: "ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem." The verb is a plain indicative (adgnoscunt), and the sentence has no verb of saying. The opponents' views around it are given in reported speech: "illos dies ... determinatos putant", "hos esse ... solos legitimos", then "itaque ... ieiunandum" and "sic et apostolos obseruasse". This one sentence breaks out of that pattern, so it is Tertullian's own jab: they invoke "until John" (Matthew 11:13) only when it suits them. The English adds "they say that", which turns the jab into the opponents' own statement. That also makes no sense, because no one would boast that they read the law selectively. The error is real but minor, so "low" severity fits. The proposed fix is faithful: it drops the invented "they say", keeps "ubi uolunt" as "where it suits them", and quotes "the law and the prophets until John" as the phrase they appeal to. Keep the (Matthew 11:13) reference after it.
verdict.better_correction: For where it suits them, they recognize what "the law and the prophets until John" means (Matthew 11:13).

errors.english_quote: your young men recline with the sisters
errors.source_quote: adulescentes tui cum sororibus dormiunt
errors.why: 'dormiunt' (sleep with) is a sexual charge, and the next sentence ties it to wantonness (lasciuia). 'Recline' turns it into table posture and drops the charge.
errors.corrected_english: your young men sleep with the sisters

verdict.reason: I read the Latin source at §17 of ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-fasting/translations/tof_source.json. It says "sed maioris est agape, quia per hanc adulescentes tui cum sororibus dormiunt. appendices scilicet gulae lasciuia atque luxuriae", which matches the claim's quote. The live English in tof_english.json says "because through it your young men recline with the sisters". "Dormiunt" means "sleep", not "recline". Latin's word for reclining at table would be "accumbunt" or "discumbunt". The next sentence makes the sexual meaning plain: lust and luxury follow gluttony, and Paul's "nec in cubilibus et libidinibus" (not in beds and lusts, Romans 13:13) is cited as the proof. "Recline" drops Tertullian's charge of sexual misconduct at the love-feast and makes the "beds and lusts" citation pointless. Thelwall's ANF translation also reads "sleep with". The claim stands. The fix, "your young men sleep with the sisters", is faithful and keeps "tui" (your). "The sisters" means the women of the congregation and is a fair choice for "sororibus".

errors.english_quote: without assessing my opponents
errors.source_quote: sine taxatione aduersariorum
errors.why: Here 'taxatio' means censure or reproach. Tertullian cannot defend chastity without attacking his opponents. 'Assessing' misses that.
errors.corrected_english: without censuring my opponents

verdict.reason: The source quote is exact. In tof_source.json §1 the Latin reads: "piget iam cum talibus congredi, pudet etiam de eis altercari quorum nec defensio uerecunda est. quomodo enim protegam castitatem et sobrietatem sine taxatione aduersariorum?" In classical Latin, "taxatio" means a valuation or appraisal. Tertullian, though, regularly uses taxare/taxatio to mean "censure, reproach". From memory, Lewis & Short gives that late sense for "taxatio" and may cite this very passage (Tert. Jejun. 1); I could not check that here. The context requires the reproach sense. He has just said it is shameful even to argue with these people, and he is explaining why he must attack them anyway. "Assessing my opponents" uses the classical sense. It reads as a neutral evaluation and loses the point that defending chastity forces him to rebuke them. The error is minor, but it is a real wrong sense, not a style preference, so low severity is right. "Without censuring my opponents" is faithful. "Without rebuking my opponents" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: How am I to protect chastity and sobriety without censuring my opponents?

works.notes:
I compared 8 of 14 sections with the Latin, sentence by sentence: 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 13 and 14 (Oehler 1853 Latin, file tofip_source.json). This was read-only on the Mini. Only section 14 had no errors.

The most important finding is in section 12. A prior AI review (reviews/justifications/12.json, lines ~238-260) wrongly ruled that 'traduci' means 'handed over'. The certified English was changed from 'exposed' to 'handed over' to match, and that broke the tradi/traduci wordplay. Reverting to 'exposed/paraded' fixes it.

Other notes:
- Section 13: the source has a gap, '(??)ianeos'. The English fills it with 'doorkeepers', a guess. Critical editions read 'lanios' (butchers) or 'ganeones'. It needs a source check, not a translation fix.
- Section 2: 'Phygellum et Hermogenem tradidit satanae' follows Tertullian's own slip (1 Tim 1:20 has Hymenaeus and Alexander). The English matches the source, so it is not an error.
- The Grok REPORT.md in outputs/redteam-20261006 says nothing about this work.

errors.english_quote: But if you were not handed over, were you going to be handed over? Therefore, by not wanting to be handed over, you did not want to be exposed; by not wanting it, you denied what you did not want to be handed over as. But, you say, by not wanting to be handed over as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be handed over as—that is, a Christian.
errors.source_quote: Non traditus autem traduci habebas? Ergo dum nolendo tradi non vis traduci, nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti. Immo, inquis, dum nolo traduci quod sum, sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci, id est Christianum.
errors.why: Tertullian contrasts tradi (be handed over) with traduci (be paraded, publicly exposed). The English renders traduci as 'handed over' too, so the argument collapses and the first question becomes nonsense. A prior review (reviews/justifications/12.json) wrongly ruled that 'traduci means to be handed over'. Lewis & Short give traduco as 'to expose, parade, disgrace publicly'.
errors.corrected_english: But if you were not handed over, would you have been publicly exposed? So while, by refusing to be handed over, you refuse to be exposed, by that refusal you have denied what you refused to be exposed as. 'No,' you say, 'by refusing to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I refuse to be exposed as, that is, a Christian.'

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked the Latin in tofip_source.json §12 and it matches the quote word for word: "Non traditus autem traduci habebas? Ergo dum nolendo tradi non vis traduci, nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti. Immo, inquis, dum nolo traduci quod sum, sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci, id est Christianum." Tertullian sets two verbs against each other here: tradi (to be handed over to the authorities) and traduci (to be publicly exposed or paraded as something). Lewis & Short gives traduco as "to expose, parade, disgrace publicly", and Thelwall's ANF translation also uses "publicly exhibited/exposed" for this passage. The live English uses "handed over" for traduci three out of four times and "exposed" once. That turns the first question into nonsense ("if you were not handed over, were you going to be handed over?") and breaks the argument: refusing to be handed over means refusing to be exposed as a Christian, and that refusal is a denial. The English also contradicts itself, using "exposed" in one clause and "handed over" for the same verb in the next. This is a real error of sense and garbled English, not a matter of style. The earlier review in reviews/justifications/12.json, which treated traduci as meaning "handed over", was wrong. The proposed correction gives tradi and traduci each the right meaning and follows the Latin. One small improvement is optional: "habebas" with an infinitive reads more exactly as "would you have had to be publicly exposed?"
verdict.better_correction: But if you had not been handed over, would you have had to be publicly exposed? So while, by refusing to be handed over, you refuse to be exposed, by that refusal you have denied what you refused to be exposed as. 'No,' you say, 'by refusing to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I refuse to be exposed as, that is, a Christian.'

errors.english_quote: we confess that it comes from him from whom we beg its pardon
errors.source_quote: ab eo illam profitemur accidere a quo veniam eius deprecamur
errors.why: Here 'venia eius' means being spared or let off from the temptation. 'Beg its pardon' is meaningless English and loses the logic: we ask God to spare us, so the temptation must come from him.
errors.corrected_english: we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin is quoted correctly. In section 2 of tofip_source.json it reads: "Sed in legitima oratione, cum dicimus ad patrem, Ne nos inducas in temptationem (quae autem maior temptatio, quam persecutio?), ab eo illam profitemur accidere a quo veniam eius deprecamur." The pronoun "eius" refers to the temptation (persecution). "Veniam ... deprecamur" means we beg to be let off or spared it, not forgiveness for it. The argument depends on this: we ask the Father not to lead us into temptation, so we admit that temptation comes from him. The certified English is in tofip_english.json, section 2, paragraph 6: "we confess that it comes from him from whom we beg its pardon". In English, "beg its pardon" is the idiom for apologizing to something. It makes no sense here and hides the point that we ask God to spare us. A reader would not follow the logic. ANF's "whose forgiveness we implore" is also loose, but at least it reads as English; the current wording does not. The proposed fix, "we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it", is faithful. It keeps "profitemur" as "confess", "accidere" as "comes", and gives "veniam eius deprecamur" as "pray to be spared it". "Beg to be excused from it" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it

errors.english_quote: the man whom Christ bought for the whole world, and indeed set free
errors.source_quote: ut furtivo, quem ceram [= coram] toto mundo Christus emit, immo et manumisit
errors.why: 'ceram' is an OCR slip for 'coram' (openly, before). The point is that you buy him back secretly, as if he were stolen goods, though Christ bought him openly before the whole world. 'For the whole world' loses that contrast.
errors.corrected_english: as if he were stolen goods, the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free

verdict.reason: The locked source in tofip_source.json §12 reads "sub tunica et sinu, quod aiunt, ut furtivo, quem ceram toto mundo Christus emit, immo et manumisit". "ceram" is not a word that fits here. It is plainly a copy-text slip for "coram" ("openly, in the presence of"), and the standard text of De fuga 12 reads "coram toto mundo". The contrast is the point of the sentence. You haggle for him secretly, under your tunic, as if he were stolen goods ("ut furtivo"), when Christ bought him openly before the whole world. The live English reads "as if by stealth—the man whom Christ bought for the whole world, and indeed set free". That turns "in the presence of the world" into "for the benefit of the world", so the sense is wrong and the contrast Tertullian builds is lost. This is a real but low-severity sense error, not a style preference. The proposed fix is faithful. To fit the existing sentence, splice it in as: "...under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if he were stolen goods—the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free." "as if by stealth" for "ut furtivo" could stand, but "as if he were stolen goods" is more exact and keeps the contrast with "openly".
verdict.better_correction: But you bargain for him with an informer or a soldier or some petty thief of a governor, under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if he were stolen goods—the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free.

errors.english_quote: never up to now has anything of this kind been devised against Christians, to reduce them under some buying one's way out for their lives and their sect
errors.source_quote: nec umquam usque adhuc ex Christianis tale aliquid prospectum est sub aliqua redemptione capitis et sectae redigendis
errors.why: Here 'redigendis' means revenue to be collected, as in 'ex Christianis ... redigendis' (to be raised from Christians). It does not mean 'to reduce them'. The English is garbled, and the point (the state never planned to raise revenue from Christians as a head-ransom) is lost.
errors.corrected_english: never yet has any such revenue been planned, to be raised from Christians by some ransom of their persons and their sect

verdict.reason: The Latin is quoted correctly: "nec umquam usque adhuc ex Christianis tale aliquid prospectum est sub aliqua redemptione capitis et sectae redigendis". The claim misreads the grammar. "redigendis" is a gerundive that agrees with "Christianis" ("ex Christianis ... redigendis"), and it pairs with "sub aliqua redemptione". "redigere sub" is the standard idiom for "bring under" something, so the clause means "from Christians brought under some ransom of head and sect". "redigere" can also mean "to collect money", and that sense colours the passage, since the context is revenue for the treasury: "aerario augendo", "fructus ingens meti posset". But the word does not mean "revenue to be collected" on its own, as the claim says. The English "to reduce them under some buying one's way out for their lives and their sect" follows the Latin closely. "Reduce under" is old English for "bring under". The meaning is not lost, because the sentence starts with the treasury remedies and goes on to the "enormous profit" that could be reaped. Two small slips: "against Christians" for "ex Christianis" (from Christians) is loose, and the English is clumsy. That is a style problem, not a reversed or wrong sense, so I refute the claim as a faithfulness error. The proposed correction does give the right sense (a head-and-sect ransom as a revenue source) and is faithful enough. It drops the "brought under" idea, and "of their persons" weakens "capitis", which means poll-tax, a tax per head. If anyone smooths the line, the better version is below.
verdict.better_correction: and never up to now has anything of this kind been devised to raise revenue from Christians by bringing them under some ransom for their heads and their sect

errors.english_quote: since he is selling nothing other than what he will provide for your reward
errors.source_quote: siquidem non aliud venditat, quam quod praestaturus est praemio tuo
errors.why: Here 'praemio tuo' means 'for your payment' (the bribe you give him), not a reward to you.
errors.corrected_english: since he is selling nothing other than what he will deliver in return for your payment

verdict.reason: I checked the source and English for section 12 in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-flight-in-persecution/translations/tofip_source.json and tofip_english.json. Both quotes match exactly. The Latin reads: "Da mihi pecuniam. Certe ne eum tradat, siquidem non aliud venditat, quam quod praestaturus est praemio tuo." The extortionist sells only what he will hand over, which is his silence, and he hands it over in return for the payment you give him. Here "praemio tuo" means your payment to him. The ablative marks the price he gets. Thelwall's ANF translation reads it the same way ("for the reward you give"). The live English, "what he will provide for your reward", most naturally means something given to you as your reward. That reverses who pays whom, so it is a real wrong-sense error, though a minor one. It is not a style preference. The proposed fix, "since he is selling nothing other than what he will deliver in return for your payment", is faithful. A slightly closer option that keeps the original verb is: "since he is selling nothing other than what he will provide in return for your payment".

errors.english_quote: Why then do you buy Christ back at the cost of a man, in the man in whom Christ is?
errors.source_quote: Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est?
errors.why: Here 'de homine' means 'from a man' (the extortioner you pay), not 'at the cost of a man'.
errors.corrected_english: Why then do you ransom Christ from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?

verdict.reason: The source is quoted correctly: tofip_source.json §12 reads "Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est?". The surrounding lines use redimere/mercari with de or ab for the party something is bought away from: "hominem de terris, immo ab inferis mercatus" and "illum redemit ab angelis munditenentibus potestatibus...". Tertullian's point is a contrast. Christ bought man back from the cosmic powers, and now you buy Christ back from a mere man: the informer, soldier or governor named just before ("pacisceris cum delatore vel milite vel furunculo aliquo praeside"). "At the cost of a man" would need a price ablative or "pretio hominis", not "de homine", and it loses the contrast with the next line about Simon and the bribe. This is a real error of sense, not a style choice, though a minor one. The proposed fix "Why then do you ransom Christ from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?" is faithful. "Buy Christ back from a man" would match the section's existing buy-back wording equally well.
verdict.better_correction: Why then do you buy Christ back from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?

errors.english_quote: so that its outcome can be established more easily
errors.source_quote: quo facilius de obitu eius constare possit
errors.why: Here 'obitus' (from obire, to go to meet) means how we should meet or face persecution, which is the question of the whole treatise. It does not mean its outcome.
errors.corrected_english: so that it may more easily be settled how we ought to meet it

verdict.reason: The quote checks out. The source (tofip_source.json §1) reads "utrum a deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu eius constare possit", and the English gives "so that its outcome can be established more easily". Here obitus is the noun from obire, "to go to meet" or "to face". The question is how the Christian should meet persecution, which is the subject of the whole treatise: "quomodo eas excipere fides debeat", flee or not. Thelwall's ANF translation reads it the same way: "as to our duty in respect of meeting it." "Outcome" would be exitus, and Tertullian uses that word a few lines later ("what is the outcome of persecution"). So the current English blurs two separate points: how to face persecution, and what persecution produces. That is wrong sense, not a style choice, though it is minor. The proposed fix keeps the right sense and the meaning of constare: "so that it may more easily be settled how we ought to meet it". "How we ought to face it" would also work.

errors.english_quote: I answered on the spot, as the place and time allowed and as the insistence of certain people demanded, and I carried away with me the subject only half treated.
errors.source_quote: Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore et quarundam personarum importunitate semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum
errors.why: The intrusiveness of certain people is why the subject was left half-treated. It is not something that 'demanded' his answer.
errors.corrected_english: I said something on the spot to suit the place and time, and, because of the intrusiveness of certain people, I carried the subject away with me only half treated.

verdict.reason: The Latin in tofip_source.json section 1 matches the quoted text: "Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore et quarundam personarum importunitate semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum". The phrase can be parsed two ways. Most naturally, "pro" governs all three ablatives (loco, tempore and importunitate): "in keeping with the place, the time and the pressing of certain people". On that reading, the importunity limited the reply he gave on the spot. Thelwall's ANF reads it this way: "having made some reply, suitable to the place and time, and to the pressing urgency of certain persons, took away the subject with me only partially treated". The live English, "as the place and time allowed and as the insistence of certain people demanded", follows the same grammar, so it is a defensible rendering, not a wrong sense. The proposed correction takes "importunitate" as a causal ablative tied only to "semitractatam". That parse is possible but not required, and it drops the link to "pro". The proposed text also renders "oblocutus aliquid" as "said something", which is fine, but it is no more faithful overall. At most this is a style choice: "demanded" could be softened to "allowed" or "permitted". It is not a faithfulness error.
verdict.better_correction: No change needed. For a tighter version: "I said something on the spot, as the place and time and the pressing of certain people allowed, and carried the subject away with me only half treated."

errors.english_quote: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:31)
errors.source_quote: Et vidit deus quia bonum est
errors.why: Genesis 1:31 reads 'very good' (valde bona). The refrain quoted is Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25.
errors.corrected_english: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:10)

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in tofip_source.json §4 reads only "Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est, Et vidit deus quia bonum est". It gives no verse number, so "(Genesis 1:31)" was added by the translator. That added reference points to the wrong verse. Genesis 1:31 says "very good" ("valde bona"), about everything God made. Tertullian quotes the shorter refrain "it was good" ("bonum est"), which appears at Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21 and 25. A careful editor would fix this, though it changes no meaning, so "low" severity is right. The fix "(Genesis 1:10)" is accurate. Writing "(Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25)" would show that Tertullian is quoting a repeated phrase rather than one verse, and dropping the reference would also be faithful, since the Latin names no verse.
verdict.better_correction: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25)

errors.english_quote: This was not to evade danger under the name of persecution.
errors.source_quote: non propter eludendum periculum proprio nomine persecutionis
errors.why: Here 'proprio nomine' means 'for its own sake / on its own account'. The sense is that flight was not commanded to dodge the danger of persecution for its own sake. 'Under the name of' misreads the idiom.
errors.corrected_english: This was not to escape the danger of persecution for its own sake.

verdict.reason: The quotes match. Source §6: "ideo illis fugere tunc ad tempus praecepti, non propter eludendum periculum proprio nomine persecutionis (atquin persecutiones eos passuros praedicabat...), sed propter profectum annuntiationis". English: "This was not to evade danger under the name of persecution." Here "proprio nomine" means "on its own account" or "as such", the sense it has in legal Latin. It sets up a contrast with "sed propter profectum annuntiationis": flight was not commanded so they could escape persecution's danger for its own sake. It was commanded so the preaching could advance. "Under the name of persecution" is a word-for-word rendering that does not give that sense. A reader will most likely take it as "using persecution as a pretext", which is wrong and also unclear. So the claim stands as a low-severity wrong-sense error. The proposed fix, "to escape the danger of persecution for its own sake", has the right idea but is ambiguous. "For its own sake" can be read as attaching to "persecution" ("persecution's own sake") instead of to the act of escaping. Placing the phrase so it modifies the purpose makes the contrast with "the progress of the announcement" clear.
verdict.better_correction: This was not so that they might escape the danger of persecution on their own account.

errors.english_quote: in the registers of beneficiaries and informers
errors.source_quote: in matricibus beneficiariorum et curiosorum
errors.why: Beneficiarii are soldiers on special police duty, not 'beneficiaries'. As English, 'beneficiaries' gives the reverse picture.
errors.corrected_english: in the registers of the police-soldiers and informers

verdict.reason: The claim matches the files. tofip_source.json §13 reads "cum in matricibus beneficiariorum et curiosorum inter tabernarios et (??)ianeos et fures balnearum et aleones et lenones Christiani quoque vectigales continentur", and tofip_english.json §13 has "Christians are listed as taxpayers in the registers of beneficiaries and informers". Here beneficiarii is a technical term. It means soldiers detached for special duty under a governor, who did police and extortion work at stations and checkpoints. They sit alongside the curiosi, the informers or secret police. To a modern reader, English "beneficiaries" means people who receive a benefit. That is a false friend: it hides the point that Christians were paying protection money to soldiers (compare "a militibus ... redimendam" at the end of the same section). A careful translator would fix it, so the claim is not a style preference. Severity low is right. The proposed fix "police-soldiers" is faithful. "Military police" reads a little more naturally, but either is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: in the registers of the military police and informers

errors.english_quote: And if you consult the Spirit, what does that saying of the Spirit prove more than anything?
errors.source_quote: Spiritum vero si consulas, quid magis sermone illo spiritus probat?
errors.why: Here 'probat' means 'approves', and the question is what the Spirit approves more than that saying (quoted next). The English makes no sense.
errors.corrected_english: And if you consult the Spirit, what does the Spirit approve more than that saying?

verdict.reason: The quote in tofip_source.json §9 is exact: "Spiritum vero si consulas, quid magis sermone illo spiritus probat?" Here "sermone illo" is an ablative of comparison, "spiritus" is the subject (it could also be read as a genitive), and "probat" means "approves". So the sense is "what does the Spirit approve more than that saying?" "That saying" points ahead to the oracle quoted next ("Publicaris... bonum tibi est"). The live English, "what does that saying of the Spirit prove more than anything?", makes the saying the subject, renders "probat" as "prove", and adds "than anything", which is not in the Latin. The result is garbled and loses the point of the comparison. This is a real error, not a style preference. The proposed fix is faithful. Thelwall's ANF reading is close ("what does He approve more than that utterance of the Spirit?"), but I recalled it from memory and did not check it against a copy. Reading "spiritus" as a genitive gives an equally good fix: "what does He approve more than that saying of the Spirit?"
verdict.better_correction: And if you consult the Spirit, what does He approve more than that saying of the Spirit?

works.notes: Read-only check of /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-idolatry/translations/toi_source.json against toi_english.json. CSEL 20 Latin, 24 sections. Sections 1, 5, 9, 11, 14, 15, 18 and 23 were compared sentence by sentence. Sections 14 and 18 are clean. The worst errors are in §9 and §11. In §9 the English makes Sergius Paulus an enemy of the apostles. In §11 a double negative is reversed, so the gladiator trainer 'does not commit the act himself'. Borderline readings not reported: §11 'sane non illa principalis idololatria?' rendered as a rhetorical question, which the text's punctuation allows; §23 'non ualet tacita uox in stilo' rendered as a positive claim; §5 'seorsum figurae' rendered 'set apart'. The Grok REPORT.md has no entry for this book (no matches for idolatry/toi).

errors.english_quote: Another magus, who opposed the apostles along with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his eyes.
errors.source_quote: alter magus, qui cum Sergio Paulo, quoniam isdem aduersabatur apostolis, luminum amissione multatus est
