errors.why: 'cum Sergio Paulo' means the magus (Elymas) was with Sergius Paulus, the proconsul who believed (Acts 13:7-12). The English makes Sergius Paulus an opponent of the apostles.
errors.corrected_english: Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight because he opposed those same apostles.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute it. The claim quotes the source (toi_source.json §9) exactly: "alter magus, qui cum Sergio Paulo, quoniam isdem aduersabatur apostolis, luminum amissione multatus est." The "quoniam" clause is a parenthesis. That leaves "qui cum Sergio Paulo [erat]", which places the magus in Sergius Paulus's company, as in Acts 13:7. ANF reads it the same way: "who dwelt with Sergius Paulus (since he was opposing himself to the same apostles)". The subject of "aduersabatur" is the magus alone, and "isdem" points back to the apostles who cursed Simon. The live English says "who opposed the apostles along with Sergius Paulus". That makes Sergius Paulus a co-opponent of the apostles, but in Acts 13:12 the proconsul believes. This is a real wrong-person error that changes the meaning. The proposed correction, "Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight because he opposed those same apostles," keeps "cum", "isdem" and "quoniam" (as "because"). "Loss of his sight" for "luminum amissione" is fine.
verdict.better_correction: Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight, since he opposed those same apostles.

errors.english_quote: he does not commit the act himself, but he supplies what another does.
errors.source_quote: nec per se non faciet quod faciendum alio subministrat
errors.why: Double negative: he will not fail to do himself what he supplies to another to do, so he too is guilty. The English says the opposite, that he does not commit it himself.
errors.corrected_english: for he himself is not innocent of doing what he supplies another to do.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json, Idolatry §11, reads: "sic et homicidii interdictio ostendit mihi lanistam quoque ab ecclesia arceri: nec per se non faciet quod faciendum alio subministrat." The "nec ... non" is a litotes meaning "nor will he fail to do himself what he supplies another to do." Tertullian's point is that the gladiator-trainer is guilty of the killing himself. The English in toi_english.json says "he does not commit the act himself, but he supplies what another does." That concedes the trainer's innocence and drops the second negative, which reverses the sense; ANF gives "he will not fail to do himself what he subministers to another to do." The proposed fix, "for he himself is not innocent of doing what he supplies another to do," gets the meaning right. Its "not innocent of" is a little loose for "non faciet" (he does it), so the alternative below is closer to the Latin.
verdict.better_correction: he too does himself what he supplies another to do.

errors.english_quote: it is still blotted out under the crime of idolatry.
errors.source_quote: in idololatriae tamen crimine expungitur
errors.why: 'expungitur' here is an accounting term: each sin is entered/settled under the account of idolatry. 'Blotted out' suggests the sin is erased or forgiven, the opposite of the argument that idolatry contains all sins.
errors.corrected_english: it is still charged to the account of the crime of idolatry.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source and English match the quotes exactly. In toi_source.json §1 the Latin reads "nam etsi suam speciem tenet unumquodque delictum, etsi suo quodque nomine iudicio destinatur, in idololatriae tamen crimine expungitur." In toi_english.json §1 the English reads "it is still blotted out under the crime of idolatry."

Tertullian often uses expungere in its late, bookkeeping sense: to check off, settle or reckon an account. Here it means each sin is entered and settled under the heading of idolatry. ANF (Thelwall) renders it "it is marked off under the general account of idolatry."

"Blotted out" uses the classical "strike out, erase" sense. An English reader takes it to mean the sin is wiped away or cancelled. That is the reverse of the argument, which is that idolatry contains and answers for every sin, as the next sentences show: "the idolater is also a murderer," and so on.

So this is a real sense error, not a style preference. The proposed "it is still charged to the account of the crime of idolatry" is faithful. "Yet it is reckoned to the account of the crime of idolatry" would be a slightly closer alternative.
verdict.better_correction: yet it is reckoned to the account of the crime of idolatry.

errors.english_quote: If he does anything for the ambition of praise, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.
errors.source_quote: si quid ad elogii ambitionem facit, non extraneum nec inimicum, sed ipsum se.
errors.why: 'elogium' is the written charge (indictment). The clause means 'if it adds to the grandeur of the charge': he has killed not a stranger but himself. 'He does anything for the ambition of praise' invents a motive and garbles the logic.
errors.corrected_english: If it adds anything to the weight of the charge, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.

verdict.reason: The source (toi_source.json §1) reads exactly as quoted: "quaeris quem occiderit? si quid ad elogii ambitionem facit, non extraneum nec inimicum, sed ipsum se." Here "elogium" is the legal term for the written charge, so "ad elogii ambitionem" means "to the grandeur (aggravation) of the charge". The verb "facit" is impersonal: "if it adds anything". The standard rendering agrees; ANF/Thelwall has "If it contributes aught to the aggravation of the charge, no stranger nor personal foe, but his own self." The live English, "If he does anything for the ambition of praise", turns this into a motive the idolater has, which is not in the source. It also breaks the logic: the point is that killing himself makes the charge worse. That is a real error of sense, not a style choice. The proposed fix, "If it adds anything to the weight of the charge, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself", is faithful. A tighter version could be "If it adds anything to the gravity of the charge: not a stranger or an enemy, but himself." That drops "it is", which the Latin does not need, and still answers "Whom has he killed?" Either wording works.
verdict.better_correction: If it adds anything to the gravity of the charge: not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.

errors.english_quote: If anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God.
errors.source_quote: artificum, quos numquam in domum dei admitti oportet si quis eam disciplinam norit
errors.why: The relative 'quos' refers to the idol-making craftsmen; they are the ones not to be admitted, as anyone who knows the discipline understands. The English makes the person who knows the discipline the one excluded.
errors.corrected_english: Anyone who knows that discipline knows that such craftsmen should never be admitted into the house of God.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json §5 reads "excusationes huiusmodi artificum, quos numquam in domum dei admitti oportet si quis eam disciplinam norit". "quos" (masculine plural accusative) can only refer back to "artificum", the craftsmen. So the people who must never be admitted are the craftsmen, and "si quis ... norit" is a side condition: anyone who knows the discipline would see that. The live English in toi_english.json §5 splits this off as its own sentence: "If anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God." The singular "they" most naturally points back to "anyone", so it says the person who knows the discipline is barred. That reverses the sense; it is not a style choice. The proposed fix is faithful. A smoother version keeps it in one sentence: "I will answer far more vigorously the excuses of such craftsmen, who, as anyone who knows that discipline is aware, should never be admitted into the house of God."
verdict.better_correction: I will answer far more vigorously the excuses of such craftsmen, who, as anyone who knows that discipline is aware, should never be admitted into the house of God.

errors.english_quote: But, someone says, that knowledge was permitted until the gospel, so that once Christ was born no one from then on would interpret anyone's birth from the heavens.
errors.source_quote: at enim scientia ista usque ad euangelium fuit concessa, ut Christo edito nemo exinde natiuitatem alicuius de caelo interpretetur.
errors.why: This is Tertullian's own answer to the magi argument, not an opponent's objection. 'Someone says' is added and assigns his thesis to the other side.
errors.corrected_english: But that knowledge was permitted only until the gospel, so that once Christ was born no one from then on should interpret anyone's birth from the heavens.

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source in toi_source.json §9 matches the quote exactly: "at enim scientia ista usque ad euangelium fuit concessa, ut Christo edito nemo exinde natiuitatem alicuius de caelo interpretetur." The English in toi_english.json §9 paragraph 4 begins "But, someone says, that knowledge was permitted until the gospel...". No word in the Latin means "someone says". "At enim" can open an objection, but here the context shows it is Tertullian's own answer, for three reasons. (1) The opponent's argument is the magi defence ("sed magi ab oriente uenerunt"), which Tertullian has just mocked ("de Christo scilicet est mathesis hodie"). (2) The sentence itself says astrology ended with Christ, which is Tertullian's thesis. An astrologer defending his trade would never argue it. (3) The next sentence, "nam et tus illud et myrram et aurum ... quasi clausulam sacrificationis et gloriae saecularis, quam Christus erat adempturus", is plainly Tertullian supporting that point, and paragraph 5 builds on it ("ut exinde aliter incederent"). So "someone says" adds words that are not in the source and gives Tertullian's own view to the opponent. That is a real wrong-speaker error. The proposed correction is faithful. It drops the invented attribution, and "only until" is a fair reading of "usque ad" together with the purpose clause ("so that from then on no one..."). "Should interpret" fits the purpose subjunctive "interpretetur".

errors.english_quote: I maintain that it still offends against idolatry, because it pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols and fattens every demon.
errors.source_quote: in crimen offendere idololatriae eam opinor, quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet, quae omne daemonium saginat.
errors.why: 'in crimen offendere idololatriae' means to fall into the charge of idolatry; 'offends against idolatry' says it opposes idolatry. Also 'eam ... quae' restricts the charge to the trade that serves the idols' soul (incense), not to all just profit.
errors.corrected_english: I think that trade still falls into the charge of idolatry which deals in the very soul and spirit of idols and fattens every demon.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. I checked §11 in toi_source.json and the Latin matches the quote: "sit nunc aliqua iustitia quaestus secura de cupiditatis et mendacii obseruatione, in crimen offendere idololatriae eam opinor, quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet, quae omne daemonium saginat."

There are two errors:

1. Wrong sense. "in crimen offendere idololatriae" means to run into, or fall under, the charge of idolatry. In English, "offends against idolatry" means breaking or opposing idolatry, which turns the meaning around. The Latin "crimen" (charge) is also left out.

2. Wrong scope. "eam ... quae" is restrictive: it means "that trade which serves the soul of idols", and the next sentences name it as incense ("tura dico"). The English "because it pertains" makes the clause a reason, so it condemns all just profit. Tertullian condemns only the trade that serves idols.

Standard renderings agree. Thelwall (ANF) has "that trade which pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols, which pampers every demon, falls into the crime of idolatry", and Waszink has the same sense.

The proposed fix is faithful. Its only problem is word order: the relative clause sits apart from "trade" ("that trade still falls ... which deals"), so the cleaner version below keeps them together.
verdict.better_correction: But suppose there is some just profit, free from the charge of desire and lying. I still think that the trade which concerns the very soul and spirit of idols, which fattens every demon, falls into the charge of idolatry.

errors.english_quote: So let them light their lamps daily—lamps that have no light. Let them fasten laurels to their doorposts, laurels that will soon burn, with fires hanging over them.
errors.source_quote: accendant igitur quotidie lucernas, quibus lux nulla est, affigant postibus lauros postmodum arsuras, quibus ignes imminent; illis competunt et testimonia tenebrarum et auspicia poenarum.
errors.why: Both 'quibus' clauses refer to the pagans (picked up by 'illis'): those who have no light, over whom fires of judgment hang. The English attaches them to the lamps and laurels and loses the point.
errors.corrected_english: So let those who have no light light lamps daily; let those over whom fires hang fasten to their doorposts laurels that will later burn. To them belong both the testimonies of darkness and the omens of punishment.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json matches the quote: "accendant igitur quotidie lucernas, quibus lux nulla est, affigant postibus lauros postmodum arsuras, quibus ignes imminent; illis competunt et testimonia tenebrarum et auspicia poenarum. Tu lumen es mundi et arbor uirens semper."

Each "quibus" clause belongs to the unstated subject of the verbs accendant and affigant, meaning the pagans: "those who have no light" and "those over whom fires hang." "illis" ("to them belong...") then refers back to those same people, not to the lamps. The next sentence, "Tu lumen es mundi et arbor uirens semper" ("You are the light of the world and a tree always green"), sets the Christian against those people. That contrast only works if they are the ones with no light and with fire over them: Christians have light and stay green, while pagans have no light and will burn. Thelwall's translation (ANF) reads it the same way: "Let, therefore, them who have no light, light their lamps daily; let them over whom the fires of hell are imminent, affix to their posts laurels doomed presently to burn."

The current English, "lamps that have no light", makes the lamps the ones without light. That is close to nonsense, since lit lamps give light. "With fires hanging over them" makes the threat fall on the laurels, so the reader loses Tertullian's warning that judgment hangs over the people. This is a wrong-sense error, not a style choice.

The proposed correction is faithful: "So let those who have no light light lamps daily; let those over whom fires hang fasten to their doorposts laurels that will later burn. To them belong both the testimonies of darkness and the omens of punishment." "Later" for postmodum is accurate. One small point outside this claim: the live English cites Matthew 5:14 after "a tree always green", but only "light of the world" comes from that verse.

errors.english_quote: When we borrow money from pagans, bound by pledges, we give security in writing under oath and deny ourselves. The pagans, of course, want to know the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.
errors.source_quote: pecuniam de ethnicis mutuantes sub pignoribus fiduciati iurati cauent et se negant; se scire uolunt scilicet tempus persecutionis et locus tribunalis et persona praesidis.
errors.why: The subject is 'those (Christians) who borrow', not 'we'. 'Se negant' means they deny that they are Christians, but English 'deny ourselves' reads as self-denial. 'Se scire uolunt' has the same borrowers as its subject (ironic: they want to pick the time and place of their own persecution); the English makes 'the pagans' the subject.
errors.corrected_english: Those who borrow money from pagans on pledges give written security under oath and so deny that they are Christians. They want, of course, to choose for themselves the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I checked toi_source.json and toi_english.json, §23. "mutuantes ... cauent et se negant" is third person plural. Its subject is the Christians who borrow, so "we" is the wrong person. Tertullian is describing others, not himself. With "we", "deny ourselves" reads as self-denial in the ascetic sense (Matt 16:24), but "se negant" means they deny that they are Christians. That reverses the sense. In "se scire uolunt", the reflexive "se" and the verb "uolunt" go back to the same borrowers. The pagans appear only in the ablative "de ethnicis", so the English is wrong to make "The pagans" the subject. The proposed fix gets the person and the denial right. But "to choose for themselves" adds a gloss: the source says "scire" (to know), not "choose". This passage is textually hard, so the fix should stay close to the Latin and not settle the reading by interpretation.
verdict.better_correction: Those who borrow money from pagans on pledges give written security under oath, and so deny that they are Christians. They wish, of course, to know for themselves the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.

errors.english_quote: For he does what belongs to the servants of idols.
errors.source_quote: id enim facit quod ad idolorum mancipes pertinet.
errors.why: 'mancipes' are the owners/proprietors of idols, i.e. the demons to whom idols are 'mancipantur' in the preceding sentence. 'Servants' reverses owner and slave.
errors.corrected_english: For he does what belongs to the owners of idols.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source quote is exact, from toi_source.json §1: "...non daemoniis et immundis spiritibus deputetur quibus idola mancipantur, sine dubio idololatrian admittit quicunque delinquit. id enim facit quod ad idolorum mancipes pertinet." A "manceps" is a purchaser, contractor or proprietor: the one who takes something in hand as property. The word never means a servant; the slave is "mancipium". Here the word picks up "quibus idola mancipantur" (the demons and unclean spirits to whom idols are made over as property). So "idolorum mancipes" means those demons, the owners of the idols. The argument runs: every sin is assigned to the demons, so a sinner does the demons' work, and that is idolatry. The English "For he does what belongs to the servants of idols" flips owner and slave. It also points the line at the wrong people, idol-worshippers instead of the demons, which breaks the argument's chain. The standard ANF rendering is "proprietors of idols". The proposed "For he does what belongs to the owners of idols" is faithful. "proprietors of idols" would also do.

errors.english_quote: any sophists or Chaldeans, by which I mean astrologers, or enchanters
errors.source_quote: aut sophistas aut Chaldaeos aut incantatores
errors.why: 'by which I mean astrologers' is an added gloss in Tertullian's voice; the Latin has only 'Chaldaeos'.
errors.corrected_english: any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim. The Latin of section 9 (toi_source.json) reads "post euangelium nusquam inuenias aut sophistas aut Chaldaeos aut incantatores aut coniectores aut magos, nisi plane punitos". It has no word or phrase meaning "by which I mean astrologers". The live English (toi_english.json, section 9, last paragraph) reads "any sophists or Chaldeans, by which I mean astrologers, or enchanters or diviners or magi". That inserts a first-person gloss in Tertullian's voice. "Chaldaei" did commonly mean astrologers, so the gloss is right about the meaning. But the text presents it as Tertullian's own words, so it is an addition and not a word choice. Low severity is right. The proposed fix "any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters" is faithful, and the rest of the sentence ("or diviners or magi, except plainly punished ones") should stay as it is. If a reader needs the sense, put it in a note, not in the text.
verdict.better_correction: After the gospel you will find nowhere any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters or diviners or magi, except plainly punished ones.

errors.english_quote: lovers of women, and betrayers also of this curiosity
errors.source_quote: amatores feminarum, proditores etiam huius curiositatis
errors.why: 'proditores' here means those who disclosed (revealed) this curious art to humans (the Enoch tradition). 'Betrayers of this curiosity' does not make sense in English.
errors.corrected_english: lovers of women, and also the revealers of this curious art

verdict.reason: The quotes are accurate. toi_source.json §9 reads "angelos esse illos desertores dei, amatores feminarum, proditores etiam huius curiositatis, propterea quoque damnatos a deo", and toi_english.json §9 reads "those angels were deserters of God, lovers of women, and betrayers also of this curiosity". Here "proditor" comes from prodo, "to bring forth" or "disclose". It refers to the Enoch tradition that the fallen angels taught humans astrology and the other arts. This is Tertullian's point: the angels are condemned, so astrology is condemned with them. English "betray" can still mean "reveal a secret", but a modern reader of "betrayers of this curiosity" will take it as "disloyal to this curiosity", which reverses the sense. "Curiosity" on its own also hides that "curiositas" here means a forbidden curious art, namely astrology. The claim stands as low severity. ANF (Thelwall) renders the phrase as "discoverers of this curious art". The proposed "and also the revealers of this curious art" is faithful. "Disclosers" would work equally well.
verdict.better_correction: lovers of women, and also the revealers of this curious art

errors.english_quote: if even now the work of idolatry is nearly accomplished without an idol through the burning of fragrances
errors.source_quote: si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur
errors.why: 'fere' goes with 'sine idolo': idolatry is now mostly carried out without an idol. 'Nearly accomplished' says the work is almost but not fully done.
errors.corrected_english: if even now the work of idolatry is mostly carried out without an idol, by the burning of fragrances

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against the source and it holds. In toi_source.json §11 the Latin reads exactly "si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur", and toi_english.json §11, paragraph 6, renders it as "the work of idolatry is nearly accomplished without an idol through the burning of fragrances". Here "fere" means "for the most part" or "generally" and goes with "sine idolo", not with "perpetratur". The Latin says idolatry is usually performed without an idol. The English says the work is almost but not quite finished, which is a different meaning and loses the point. The next sentence confirms the reading: "nam facilius sine idolo idololatria, quam sine turarii merce" ("idolatry is easier without an idol than without the incense-dealer's goods"). This is the standard reading; Thelwall (ANF) translates it as "perpetrated, for the most part, without the idol". The proposed fix, "mostly carried out without an idol, by the burning of fragrances", is faithful. "Generally carried out" would also work.

errors.english_quote: He should easily obtain victory over the one he feeds daily.
errors.source_quote: facile debuit de eo impetrare, quem cotidie pascit.
errors.why: 'impetrare de eo' means to get what he asked from him. The point is that the demon obliges its daily feeder. 'Victory over' is not in the source and flips the point.
errors.corrected_english: He could easily get what he asked from the one he feeds every day.

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against toi_source.json and toi_english.json for section 11, and it holds. The Latin reads "ille quidem si excluserit daemonium, non sibi placeat de fide. neque enim inimicum exclusit. facile debuit de eo impetrare, quem cotidie pascit." Here "impetrare de eo" means to get what you ask from someone. It is a word for a granted request, not for conquest. The ANF translation agrees: "he ought to have found it easy to get his request from one whom he daily feeds." Tertullian's point is that the exorcism proves nothing about the dealer's faith. The demon is no enemy to him, so it simply grants a favor to the man who feeds it. The English "obtain victory over" adds the idea of conquest. That turns a demon granting a favor into a struggle the dealer wins, which runs against the sentence just before it ("He has not cast out an enemy"). The error is small and low severity, but real. The proposed fix, "He could easily get what he asked from the one he feeds every day.", is faithful. A version closer to "debuit" would be: "It was easy for him to get his request granted by the one he feeds every day."
verdict.better_correction: It was easy for him to get his request granted by the one he feeds every day.

errors.english_quote: Since the same apostle calls desire idolatry
errors.source_quote: cum bis et idololatria ab eodem apostolo dicta sit cupiditas
errors.why: 'bis' (twice: Colossians 3:5, Ephesians 5:5) is dropped.
errors.corrected_english: Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. In toi_source.json section 11 the Latin reads exactly "cum bis et idololatria ab eodem apostolo dicta sit cupiditas", and toi_english.json section 11, paragraph 1, reads "Since the same apostle calls desire idolatry". The English drops "bis" (twice). Tertullian is pointing to Colossians 3:5 and Ephesians 5:5, so the word carries meaning: it shows how strongly Paul stated the point. The severity is low, but this is a real omission and not a style choice. The proposed fix, "Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry", is faithful, and "covetousness" is closer to "cupiditas" in the Pauline sense. One caution: the earlier sentence renders the same word as "desire, the root of all evils", and the paragraph uses "desire" four more times. Switching to "covetousness" in only one place would break that consistency. The smallest fix is to add "twice" and keep the paragraph's current word. Switching to "covetousness" throughout is also faithful.
verdict.better_correction: Since the same apostle has twice called desire idolatry (or, if the whole paragraph is changed to match, "Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry")

errors.english_quote: sealed with signs no longer of accusers but of angels.
errors.source_quote: signatae signis non iam aduocatorum, sed angelorum
errors.why: 'aduocati' are the witnesses/advocates who sealed the contract, not accusers.
errors.corrected_english: sealed with the seals no longer of witnesses but of angels.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked §23 of toi_source.json and toi_english.json, and both quotes match the files exactly. In Latin, "aduocati" are people called in to support a party, such as advocates or the witnesses who seal a document. They are not accusers. The English says nearly the opposite. That also flattens Tertullian's contrast: on earth, the pledge was sealed by human supporters, but at the judgment the same letters come sealed by angels. Thelwall's ANF translation reads "sealed with the seals no longer of advocates, but of angels." The proposed "witnesses" is faithful, since in Roman practice the signatories who sealed a pledge were witnesses. "Seals" for "signis" is also fine. "Advocates" would be a little closer to the word itself, but either fixes the error. The severity is low, and the claim is valid.
verdict.better_correction: sealed with the seals no longer of advocates (the witnesses who signed), but of angels.

works.notes: I checked 9 sections across the work (1, 4, 6, 11, 16, 18, 22, 25, 29) against top_source.json. Sections 11, 25 and 29 were clean except for the gloss in 29. The two medium errors are real meaning faults: in §4 a negated clause now reads as a positive claim, and in §6 'the bread of life' became 'life is bread'. The low ones are judgement calls but worth fixing. Near-misses I left out as defensible: §1 'looks upon us' for 'suis prospicere' (provides for his own); §25 'upper room' for 'superiora' (Acts 10:9 says housetop); §25 citing Acts 2:1-4 rather than Acts 2:15 for the third hour; §22 'Even if they cannot be compelled' for 'ne compellantur' (better as 'let them not be compelled'). errors.english_quote: We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God’s will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things.
errors.source_quote: non quod aliquis obsistat, quo minus uoluntas dei fiat, et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus, sed in omnibus petimus fieri uoluntatem eius
errors.why: Both clauses sit under the 'non quod' negation. Tertullian denies that we pray for success for God's will, as if it needed help. The English breaks the clause off and states it as fact: 'and we pray for the success of his will.' That reverses his point.
errors.corrected_english: We do not say this as though someone were resisting God’s will being done and we were praying that his will succeed. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things.

verdict.reason: The source in top_source.json §4 reads exactly as quoted: "non quod aliquis obsistat, quo minus uoluntas dei fiat, et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus, sed in omnibus petimus...". Both "obsistat" and "oremus" are subjunctive and joined by "et", so both sit under "non quod". Tertullian is denying the idea that we pray for God to succeed in his will, as if someone could stop him. The live English says "We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God's will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will." In that sentence, "and we pray for the success of his will" reads most naturally as a positive statement of what we do. That reverses the point the "sed" contrast is making. A reader could take it as part of the "because" clause, but the plain-indicative wording invites the wrong reading, so this is a real faithfulness error and not a style choice. The proposed correction ("as though someone were resisting God's will being done and we were praying that his will succeed") keeps both clauses under the negation and is faithful. Optionally, "praying that he succeed in his will" keeps "ei" (for him) a little closer.

errors.english_quote: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and life is bread.
errors.source_quote: Christus enim panis noster est, quia uita Christus et uitae panis.
errors.why: 'uitae panis' is genitive: 'the bread of life', a phrase that sets up the John 6:35 quote that follows. 'life is bread' misreads the grammar and states a claim Tertullian does not make.
errors.corrected_english: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and the bread of life.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The locked source for section 6 (top_source.json) reads "Christus enim panis noster est, quia uita Christus et uitae panis." "uitae" is genitive (or at most dative), so the clause cannot be read as "life is bread". The natural reading is "Christ is life and [Christ is] the bread of life", which sets up the next line, "ego sum, inquit, panis uitae". The English "and life is bread" (top_english.json §6) matches the variant "et uita panis" found in other editions (ANF follows that variant with "bread is life"), not the text this book uses. Even that variant would not give "life is bread". So this is a real wrong-sense error against the locked source. The proposed fix is faithful, but the comma before "and" makes it read like a fragment. Dropping it ties "the bread of life" to Christ more clearly.
verdict.better_correction: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life and the bread of life.

errors.english_quote: from the Spirit by which alone it has power
errors.source_quote: ex spiritu, quo tantum potest
errors.why: 'tantum potest' here means 'is so powerful' or 'has such great power', a statement of degree. 'alone' turns it into a limit ('only by the Spirit') that the Latin does not state.
errors.corrected_english: from the Spirit, by which it has such great power

verdict.reason: I checked the source and the English, and the quotes are accurate. Section 1 of top_source.json reads "ex sermone, quo enuntiatur, ex spiritu, quo tantum potest, ex ratione, qua docetur", and top_english.json has "from the Spirit by which alone it has power". The rendering is still sound. Tertullian often uses "tantum" as an adverb meaning "only". The same section has an example a few lines later: "neque enim propria tantum orationis officia complexa est", meaning "it has not only embraced the proper duties". The standard English translations also read it as "alone": the ANF (Thelwall) has "of the spirit, whereby alone it prevails", and Evans says much the same. The degree reading ("has such great power") is weaker. Latin would normally pair "tantum" with a matching "quantum" or "ut" clause for that sense, and none appears here. Even if the degree reading is arguable, the current English is a defensible rendering, not a faithfulness error. So the proposed correction is not an improvement and should not replace the current text.
verdict.better_correction: No change needed. Keep "from the Spirit by which alone it has power".

errors.english_quote: It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not receive from men what we hope for from God.
errors.source_quote: interest nostra, quod dei gratia exerceatur, solius dei conscientiae commendare, ne, quod a deo speramus, ab homine compensemus.
errors.why: 'quod dei gratia exerceatur' is the object of 'commendare': what is practiced by God's grace should be left to God's knowledge alone. The English makes 'that God's grace be exercised' the thing that matters, which changes the claim and leaves the sentence muddled.
errors.corrected_english: It is right for us to entrust what is practiced by God's grace to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not take our reward from men for what we hope for from God.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in top_source.json §22 reads: "interest nostra, quod dei gratia exerceatur, solius dei conscientiae commendare, ne, quod a deo speramus, ab homine compensemus." "quod ... exerceatur" is a relative clause, and that clause is the object of "commendare". The subject of "interest nostra" is the infinitive "commendare", so the sense is "it is in our interest to entrust what is practiced by God's grace to God's knowledge alone." The live English, "It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone", reads "quod" as "that". This makes "God's grace being exercised" the thing that matters, which misparses the sentence and blurs Tertullian's point: do the virtue in secret and leave it to God. Severity is low because "entrust it to God alone" still survives. The proposed correction fixes the structure but has two faults. "It is right for us" changes "interest nostra" ("it is to our advantage" or "it concerns us") into a moral claim. "take our reward from men" is fine for "ab homine compensemus" but drops the singular "man", which is minor. A closer rendering is below.
verdict.better_correction: It is in our interest to entrust what is done by God's grace to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not take from man the reward for what we hope for from God.

errors.english_quote: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, as in the story of Daniel's companions, or shut the mouths of lions
errors.source_quote: non roris angelum in mediis ignibus sistit nec ora leonibus obstruit
errors.why: The Latin has no 'as in the story of Daniel's companions'. It is a translator's gloss placed in the running text as if Tertullian wrote it. The identification is correct (Daniel 3), but it should be a reference in parentheses or a note.
errors.corrected_english: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames (Daniel 3), or shut the mouths of lions

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source quote is exact: top_source.json §29 reads "non roris angelum in mediis ignibus sistit nec ora leonibus obstruit nec esurientibus rusticorum prandium transfert". Nothing in it matches "as in the story of Daniel's companions". The English adds a gloss in the running text as if Tertullian had written it. The identification is right (the three youths of Daniel 3, with the dew-bringing angel of LXX Dan 3:49-50), so this is a low-severity addition, not a change of sense. The gloss is also lopsided: it names the source for the first allusion but not for the next two, the lions (Daniel 6) and the meal carried to the hungry (Habakkuk bringing food to Daniel, Bel and the Dragon 33-39). The proposed fix, "(Daniel 3)" inline, is better than the gloss, but it still puts an editor's reference in Tertullian's sentence and keeps the same lopsidedness. The section has no notes field, so the cleanest fix is to cut the gloss and leave the allusions as unglossed as the Latin does. If references are wanted, give all three in a note or footnote, not in the text.
verdict.better_correction: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace. (If references are wanted, put them in a note covering all three: Dan 3:49-50 LXX; Dan 6:22; Bel and the Dragon 33-39.)

errors.english_quote: sitting down after the appointed prayer
errors.source_quote: quod adsignata oratione assidendi mos est quibusdam
errors.why: 'adsignata oratione' (ablative absolute) means 'when prayer has been sealed' or 'concluded'. The custom under attack is sitting down once prayer is finished. 'Appointed' misreads 'adsignare' and hides that point. The next sentences ('after finishing prayer') confirm the intended sense.
errors.corrected_english: sitting down once prayer has been concluded

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote (top_source.json §16: "Item quod adsignata oratione assidendi mos est quibusdam"). "adsignata oratione" is an ablative absolute: "when the prayer has been signed off or sealed", that is, finished. ANF gives "when prayer is ended" and Evans "when prayer has been sealed". "Appointed" reads adsignare in its "assign or allot" sense. That sense does not fit here. It also adds the idea of a set or scheduled prayer, which is not in the text. Tertullian's point is about sitting down at the close of any prayer, and "transacta oratione" ("after finishing prayer") in the next sentence confirms this. The error is minor because the English already says "after", but it is a real wrong sense a careful translator would fix. The proposed "sitting down once prayer has been concluded" is faithful. "Once prayer has been sealed" is a more literal option.
verdict.better_correction: I do not see the reason why some people have a custom of sitting down once prayer has been concluded (literally "sealed")

errors.english_quote: So also on the day of Easter, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance
errors.source_quote: sic et die paschae, quo communis et quasi publica ieiunii religio est
errors.why: For Tertullian, 'dies paschae' is the paschal fast day before the resurrection feast. Rendering it 'Easter' tells a modern reader that the whole church fasted on Easter Sunday, which is wrong and makes the passage confusing.
errors.corrected_english: So also on the day of the Pascha, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance

verdict.reason: The claim holds, at low severity. The quotes match the files. In top_source.json §18 the Latin reads "sic et die paschae., quo communis et quasi publica ieiunii religio est, merito deponimus osculum", and top_english.json §18 has "So also on the day of Easter, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance". "Easter" is the only place this book renders pascha. In Tertullian, "dies paschae" means the paschal fast day before the resurrection feast (Good Friday or Holy Saturday). It does not mean Easter Sunday: he says elsewhere (De corona 3) that fasting on the Lord's day is forbidden. The sentence itself names the day as one of public fasting, so "Easter" gives a modern reader the wrong day and contradicts Tertullian. This is a real error of sense, not a matter of style. Standard English versions avoid "Easter" here. Thelwall (ANF) uses "the day of the passover", and others use "Pascha" or "Good Friday". I checked this from memory, not against those texts in this session. The proposed "So also on the day of the Pascha" is faithful. It could be made clearer as "So also on the day of the Pascha (the paschal fast)", but the correction as given is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: So also on the day of the Pascha, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance

works.notes: Read-only check of tertullian-on-the-shows. I compared these sections line by line: 2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 17, 23 and 30. Sections 5, 12 and 17 are clean. The worst error is §30: 'a Iuda redemistis' is translated as 'you redeemed from the Jews'. It means 'you bought from Judas'. Recurring pattern: the translator adds short glosses not in the Latin, all accurate: 'Timaeus, the Greek historian' and 'Varro, the Roman scholar' (§5), explanations of the dissignator and haruspex (§10), 'the political offices under which such shows were given' (§12), and 'I will say to the persecutors, whom you called' (§30). They read as house style for orientation, so I did not count them as errors. Source data issue, not a translation error: the locked _source.json §10 begins with a stray copy of the Virgil couplet 'Primus Erichthonius currus...', which also appears in §9. The English rightly leaves it out of §10, but the source file should be cleaned. Borderline items I did not count: §12 'humaniore atrocitate' rendered as 'a semblance of humanity' (loses 'atrocitate'); §17 'plurimum' rendered as 'entirely'; §30 'utraque cauea' rendered as 'both tiers of seats' (more likely 'both theaters', i.e. theater and amphitheater).
