errors.english_quote: this is the one you redeemed from the Jews
errors.source_quote: hic est quem a Iuda redemistis
errors.why: 'a Iuda' is Judas (singular), not 'the Jews', and 'redemistis' here means 'you bought', the price paid to Judas. 'Redeemed' also reads as the theological word for salvation, which reverses the irony.
errors.corrected_english: this is the one you bought from Judas

verdict.reason: I checked translations/tots_source.json for section 30. The Latin reads exactly "hic est quem a Iuda redemistis". "Iuda" is the ablative of Iudas, meaning Judas. The word for "the Jews" would be "Iudaeis", which is the form Tertullian uses elsewhere in this work ("Iudaeorum"). Here "redimo" means "to buy or purchase", and the line points to the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas. The ANF translation reads "This is He whom you purchased from Judas." The live English, "this is the one you redeemed from the Jews", gets the source person wrong and gives the verb its theological sense. It also makes no sense in context, because the people being addressed are the persecutors, that is, the Jews, so they cannot have redeemed him from themselves. This is a real error. The proposed fix, "this is the one you bought from Judas", is faithful and fits the parallel "this is the one..." clauses around it.

errors.english_quote: all the kinds of evils which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted consist of the works of God
errors.source_quote: omnes species malorum, quae etiam ethnici ut indubitata et prohibent et defendunt, ex operibus dei constant
errors.why: 'defendunt' here has its legal sense, to punish or guard against. 'Defend' makes the pagans uphold the evils, the opposite of the point.
errors.corrected_english: all the kinds of evils which even the pagans, treating them as undoubted, both forbid and punish, consist of the works of God

verdict.reason: The quotes match. The Latin in tots_source.json reads "ceterum omnes species malorum, quae etiam ethnici ut indubitata et prohibent et defendunt, ex operibus dei constant", and the English in tots_english.json, section 2, paragraph 6, reads "which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted". In Tertullian and other late Latin, "defendere" often means to ward off, avenge or punish (as in "defendere iniuriam"). It is paired here with "prohibent", and both verbs act on "malorum" (evils). Standard translations agree: Thelwall (ANF) has "prohibit and guard against", and Glover (Loeb) has "forbid and punish". In English, "defend" an evil means to uphold or justify it. That reverses Tertullian's point that even pagans treat these evils as wrongs. The error is real and changes the meaning; it is not a matter of style. The proposed fix, "both forbid and punish", is faithful. Its phrase "treating them as undoubted" correctly makes "ut indubitata" ("as undoubted evils") describe the evils, not the verbs. Minor polish is optional, for example "which even the pagans forbid and punish as undoubted evils".
verdict.better_correction: Besides, all the kinds of evils which even the pagans forbid and punish as undoubted evils consist of the works of God.

errors.english_quote: whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns
errors.source_quote: quaecumque condidit non in exitum operum constat condidisse quae damnat
errors.why: 'in exitum operum quae damnat' means 'to issue in (result in) the works he condemns'. The English says God did not create things to destroy evil works, which reverses the argument.
errors.corrected_english: whatever he created he certainly did not create to issue in the works he condemns

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim, so it stands. In tots_source.json, section 2 reads: "indubitate quaecumque condidit non in exitum operum constat condidisse quae damnat[at]". (The source has a typo here, "damnatat" for "damnat".) The phrase "in exitum operum quae damnat" means "to issue in / result in the works he condemns", with "exitus" meaning outcome. Thelwall's standard rendering agrees: "whatever He has made He has not made to issue in deeds which He condemns". The live English says "whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns". That makes "exitum" mean "destruction" and says God did not create things to destroy evil works. This wrecks Tertullian's argument. His point is that creation was not meant to lead to sin, even though sin is carried out through created things. The next clause, "licet eadem opera per ea quae condidit administrentur", only makes sense with that reading. The proposed fix is faithful. Its "certainly" stands for "constat", but in the full sentence it repeats "undoubtedly" (indubitate). Dropping it reads more cleanly, as in the version below.
verdict.better_correction: then undoubtedly whatever he created he did not create to issue in the works he condemns, even though those same works are carried out through the things he created

errors.english_quote: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants
errors.source_quote: Apollines et Musas et Mineruas et Mercurios mancipes habent
errors.why: 'mancipes' are owners/proprietors (patrons). Tertullian's point is that these gods own the arts; 'servants' turns them into subordinates.
errors.corrected_english: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their owners

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I could not refute it. The source quote is exact (tots_source.json §10): "quae uero uoce et modis et organis et litteris transiguntur, Apollines et Musas et Mineruas et Mercurios mancipes habent." The English in tots_english.json §10 is "have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants." A manceps is a contractor, purchaser or proprietor: the one who holds the title, not a servant. The context settles it. Tertullian has just said "est plane in artibus quoque scaenicis Liberi et Veneris patrocinium" (the stage arts are under the patronage of Bacchus and Venus). Then he gives the voice and music arts to Apollo, the Muses, Minerva and Mercury as their proprietors or patrons. His next words are "oderis, Christiane, quorum auctores non potes non odisse": the gods are the authors and owners of these arts. "Servants" reverses who rules whom, and so it breaks the argument. The standard translations agree. Glover's Loeb has "for their proprietors", and Thelwall's ANF puts these arts "in the domain of" those gods. The proposed fix, "as their owners", is faithful. "As their proprietors" or "as their patrons" would match the legal flavor of mancipes and the parallel patrocinium a little more closely, but "owners" is an acceptable fix.
verdict.better_correction: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their proprietors

errors.english_quote: They cast forth dolphins to Neptune.
errors.source_quote: delphines Neptuno uomunt
errors.why: The dolphins are the subject: the dolphin figures spout water in Neptune's honor. The English has people throwing dolphins.
errors.corrected_english: The dolphins spout in honor of Neptune.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in tots_source.json §8 reads "delphines Neptuno uomunt, columnae Sessias ... sustinent". "delphines" is nominative plural and the subject of "uomunt", in the same pattern as "columnae ... sustinent" right after it. The sentence means "the dolphins spout (water) for Neptune". This refers to the dolphin-shaped water spouts on the circus spina, which the next clause lists as ornaments along with the columns. The English "They cast forth dolphins to Neptune." wrongly makes "they" (the people) the subject and the dolphins the thing thrown, so the meaning is wrong. The proposed fix "The dolphins spout in honor of Neptune." is faithful. "The dolphins spout water for Neptune." would also be acceptable.

errors.english_quote: Consus, as we said, is hidden underground at the turning posts; Murcia is there too. He made even them into an idol:
errors.source_quote: Consus, ut diximus apud metas, sub terra delitescit Murcias. eas quoque idolum fecit
errors.why: 'Murcias' modifies the turning posts (the Murcian metae), and 'eas quoque idolum fecit' means an idol gave these posts their name too. The English invents a separate 'Murcia is there too' and an unclear 'He made even them into an idol'.
errors.corrected_english: Consus, as we said, lies hidden underground at the Murcian turning posts. These too an idol named:

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In tots_source.json §8 the Latin reads "Consus, ut diximus apud metas, sub terra delitescit Murcias. eas quoque idolum fecit: Murciam enim deam amoris uolunt, cui in illa parte aedem uouerunt." "Murcias" is an accusative plural adjective that agrees with "metas": the Murcian turning posts. Nothing in the Latin says "Murcia is there too", so the English invents a separate claim. In "eas quoque idolum fecit", "idolum" is the subject: an idol made these posts too. The next clause explains that the idol is Murcia, the goddess of love who has a temple there. The live English, "He made even them into an idol", makes Consus the subject and reverses the relation, which leaves the sentence unclear. Glover's Loeb version agrees with this reading: "lurks underground at the Murcian Turning-posts. Those, too, are the work of an idol." The proposed fix gets the first sentence right. Its second sentence, "These too an idol named", adds a meaning the Latin lacks: "fecit" means "made", not "named". The naming link is only implied by the next clause. A plainer, more literal second sentence is better.
verdict.better_correction: Consus, as we said, lies hidden underground at the Murcian turning posts. These too are the work of an idol: for they claim Murcia is a goddess of love, to whom they dedicated a temple in that part.

errors.english_quote: For they used to call other theatrical games properly Liberalia, devoted to Bacchus beyond the rest—those which among the Greeks are Dionysia, also instituted by Bacchus.
errors.source_quote: nam et alios ludos scaenicos Liberalia proprie uocabant, praeterquam Libero deuotos, quae sunt Dionysia penes Graecos, etiam a Libero institutos
errors.why: 'praeterquam Libero deuotos ... etiam a Libero institutos' means 'besides being devoted to Liber, also as instituted by Liber'. 'Devoted to Bacchus beyond the rest' misreads 'praeterquam', and the sentence loses its two reasons.
errors.corrected_english: For they used to call the theatrical games properly Liberalia: besides being devoted to Bacchus (these are the Dionysia among the Greeks), they were also instituted by Bacchus.

verdict.reason:
The claim stands. I checked tots_source.json and tots_english.json for section 10, and both quotes match the files. The error is real. "praeterquam Libero deuotos" means "besides / apart from those devoted to Liber". It does not mean "devoted to Bacchus beyond the rest". The current English also makes the Dionysia the subject of "also instituted by Bacchus", which loses the reason: the games were called Liberalia because they too were instituted by Liber.

The proposed fix reads the sentence the way the ANF translator (Thelwall) did: besides being devoted to Bacchus, they were also instituted by him. That reading is defensible, but the fix drops "alios" ("other") and turns "etiam ... institutos" into a second, separate fact. The more literal reading, which is also the one the Loeb translator (Glover) follows as I recall it, keeps "alios". On that reading, other stage games, apart from those devoted to Liber (the Greek Dionysia), were also properly called Liberalia because Liber instituted them too. That reading accounts for both "alios" and "etiam", so the better correction keeps "other".

I quoted both earlier translations from memory and did not check them against a copy, so treat those attributions as unverified.
verdict.better_correction: For they also used to call other theatrical games, apart from those devoted to Bacchus (which among the Greeks are the Dionysia), properly Liberalia, since these too were instituted by Bacchus.

errors.english_quote: what will he judge of the pantomime, who is even bent into women's garments?
errors.source_quote: quid de pantomimo iudicabit, qui etiam muliebribus curuatur?
errors.why: 'muliebribus curuatur' means he bends his body in womanish movements. Being 'bent into garments' makes no sense; Tertullian is escalating from wearing women's clothes to moving like a woman.
errors.corrected_english: what will he judge of the pantomime, who even bends himself in womanish ways?

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this claim. In tots_source.json, §23 reads exactly as quoted: "cum in lege praescribit maledictum esse qui muliebribus uestietur, quid de pantomimo iudicabit, qui etiam muliebribus curuatur?" In tots_english.json, the live English reads exactly "what will he judge of the pantomime, who is even bent into women's garments?"

The translator carried "garments" over from the first "muliebribus", where "uestietur" (will be clothed) makes it right. In the second clause the verb is "curuatur" (is bent or curved), so "muliebribus" means womanly postures or movements, not clothes. Tertullian's point is that the pantomime goes past dressing as a woman and shapes his body like one; that is what "etiam" (even) marks. "Bent into women's garments" makes no sense and loses that step up.

Thelwall's standard rendering, "who is even brought up to play the woman", supports the claim's reading. I recalled it from memory and did not check it here. Thelwall's "brought up" leans on §17, which says the pantomime is trained "from boyhood". The proposed fix, "who even bends himself in womanish ways", is faithful and keeps the bodily sense of "curuatur" and the force of "etiam".
verdict.better_correction: what will he judge of the pantomime, who even bends his body into a woman's postures?

errors.english_quote: whom the devil adorned to be carried off in a chariot, unlike Elijah
errors.source_quote: quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit
errors.why: 'aduersus Elian' means 'in rivalry with Elijah'. The devil dressed him up as a parody of Elijah's chariot ascent; 'unlike' drops that point.
errors.corrected_english: whom the devil decked out to be carried off in a chariot, in rivalry with Elijah

verdict.reason: The source (tots_source.json, §23) reads exactly as quoted: "quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit". The live English (tots_english.json) has "whom the devil adorned to be carried off in a chariot, unlike Elijah". Here "aduersus" means "against" or "in rivalry with". The devil decks out the charioteer as a counterfeit of Elijah's ascent in a chariot. This fits Tertullian's theme that the devil imitates holy things, and the Loeb (Glover) rendering is close to "to rival Elijah". "Unlike Elijah" states only a contrast and loses the point that the devil is aping Elijah. It is a real, though minor, error of sense, not a style choice. The proposed correction is faithful. "To rival Elijah" or "in mockery of Elijah" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: whom the devil decked out to be carried off in a chariot, in rivalry with Elijah

errors.english_quote: so that in the very creation granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion
errors.source_quote: ut, quam doluerat homini concessam, non sibi, in ea ipsa et hominem reum deo faceret et suam dominationem collocaret
errors.why: 'doluerat' (he had resented) is dropped, so the angel's envy, the motive the clause gives, disappears.
errors.corrected_english: so that in the very creation he had resented seeing granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion

verdict.reason: The source quote is exact. tots_source.json §2 reads "ut, quam doluerat homini concessam, non sibi, in ea ipsa et hominem reum deo faceret et suam dominationem collocaret". The live English renders this as "so that in the very creation granted to man and not to himself", which leaves out the main verb of the relative clause, "doluerat" ("he had grieved / resented"). With that verb gone, the clause loses the angel's envy, the motive Tertullian gives for why the devil corrupted creation. The phrase "not to himself" only hints at it. This is a real omission of meaning, not a style choice, though a small one, so low severity fits. The proposed fix is faithful. It reads a little awkwardly, and the better correction below is smoother.
verdict.better_correction: so that in the very creation which he had resented being granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion

errors.english_quote: this universe is as good as it is handed over to man
errors.source_quote: eamque uniuersitatem tam bonam quam homini mancipatam
errors.why: 'tam ... quam' here means 'both ... and': the universe is both good and made over to man. The English reads as a comparison of degree.
errors.corrected_english: this universe is both good and made over to man

verdict.reason: I checked tots_source.json §2. It reads "deum esse uniuersitatis conditorem eamque uniuer sitatem tam bonam quam homini mancipatam". The "uniuer sitatem" split is an OCR break and changes nothing. The live English is "that this universe is as good as it is handed over to man". Here "tam ... quam" pairs two equal predicates, "bonam" and "mancipatam": the universe is both good and made over to man. Thelwall reads it the same way ("both good and man's by gift"). The current English can be read two wrong ways. One is a comparison of degree: it is good only to the extent it is handed over. The other is "as good as" meaning "practically", which turns the line into "the universe is practically handed over to man". Both distort the plain sense, so this is garbled English and should be fixed. The proposed "this universe is both good and made over to man" is faithful. "Made over" correctly carries mancipare as a legal transfer of property.

errors.english_quote: For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness.
errors.source_quote: nam saepe censores nascentia cum maxime theatra destruebant moribus consulentes, quorum scilicet periculum ingens de lasciuia prouidebant
errors.why: 'moribus consulentes' (out of concern for public morals) is omitted, and so is the reference of 'quorum': the danger was to those morals.
errors.corrected_english: For often the censors, out of concern for public morals, destroyed theaters just as they were being born, foreseeing the immense danger to those morals from their wantonness.

verdict.reason: I checked tots_source.json §10. The Latin reads "nam saepe censores nascentia cum maxime theatra destruebant moribus consuentes, quorum scilicet periculum ingens de lasciuia prouidebant". "consuentes" is an OCR slip for "consulentes". The live English, "For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness.", leaves out "moribus consulentes" entirely. That phrase gives the censors' motive, and Tertullian's next clause builds on it: pagan judgment agrees with Christian discipline. So the omission is real, though low severity. The English also hangs "their wantonness" on the theaters, but "de lasciuia" has no possessive. The nearest antecedent for "quorum" is "moribus", so "the danger to morals from wantonness" is the natural reading. Thelwall's ANF takes "quorum" as the theaters, so the referent is open to debate. The proposed correction is faithful. A tighter version would keep the imperfect's sense of repeated action and render "cum maxime" exactly.
verdict.better_correction: For often the censors, out of concern for public morals, would tear down theaters at the very moment they were rising, foreseeing, of course, the immense danger to those morals from wantonness.

works.notes: I checked 8 sections from the beginning, middle and end against the Oehler Latin: 3, 7, 8, 14, 22, 30, 39 and 43. Only §14 had no errors. The source section labeled 39 holds the text of Oehler chapters 39 and 40 (the second paragraph starts 'Sequetur a quo...'), and the English covers both paragraphs. There are no source sections numbered 40 or 42, so 41 entries map to 43 chapters. I did not flag places where the Oehler text itself is corrupt or differs from other editions: §8 'Et hoc ergo illo facit', §14 'novissime ignorare te melius sciet', §43 'scilicet cum vos non crederetis' and §43 'Agnoscent suam potius culpam'. The two high errors, §8 'vacabat' and §39 'nec periclitor', both reverse Tertullian's argument. They should be fixed first. Files: /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-prescription-against-heretics/translations/tpah_english.json and tpah_source.json. Read-only check: nothing was edited.

errors.english_quote: then far more, “Seek, and you will find,” was fitting for us, since teaching was about to come to us unsought
errors.source_quote: multo magis vacabat erga nos, Quaerite et invenietis, quibus ultro erat obventura doctrina
errors.why: vacabat means the saying was void or had no place for us. The whole chapter argues that 'Seek and you will find' does not apply to Christians, because teaching came to them without seeking. 'Was fitting for us' says the opposite.
errors.corrected_english: then far less did “Seek, and you will find” apply to us, since teaching was to come to us unsought

verdict.reason: I checked the source and could not refute the claim. In tpah_source.json §8 the Latin reads "multo magis vacabat erga nos, Quaerite et invenietis, quibus ultro erat obventura doctrina per apostolos et ipsis apostolis per spiritum sanctum", exactly as quoted. The English in tpah_english.json §8, paragraph 4, reads: "then far more, “Seek, and you will find,” was fitting for us, since teaching was about to come to us unsought". "Vacare" means "to be empty, void or idle". "Vacabat erga nos" says the saying had no force for us. "Was fitting for us" says the reverse. The whole chapter argues that "Seek" was meant for the Jews, not for Gentile Christians, who received teaching "ultro" (without seeking). The live English contradicts both that argument and its own orientation note. The ANF (Holmes) translation agrees with the claim: "far more needless to us was the expression, 'Seek, and ye shall find'". The proposed correction is faithful. It also needs to keep the rest of the sentence: "then far less did “Seek, and you will find” apply to us, since teaching was to come to us unsought through the apostles, and to the apostles themselves through the Holy Spirit." A wording closer to the Latin: "then all the more did “Seek, and you will find” have no bearing on us...".
verdict.better_correction: But if the apostles were appointed as teachers for the Gentiles, and they themselves were also about to receive the Holy Spirit as their teacher, then far less did “Seek, and you will find” apply to us, since teaching was to come to us unsought through the apostles, and to the apostles themselves through the Holy Spirit.

errors.english_quote: Nor do I risk saying that the Scriptures themselves were arranged by God's will so that they might supply materials for heretics
errors.source_quote: Nec periclitor dicere ipsas quoque scripturas sic esse ex dei voluntate dispositas ut haereticis materias subministrarent
errors.why: 'Nec periclitor dicere' means 'I do not hesitate to say' (I run no risk in saying). Tertullian affirms the claim, and backs it with 'since I read that there must be heresies'. The English reads as if he declines to say it.
errors.corrected_english: Nor do I hesitate to say that the Scriptures themselves were arranged by God's will so that they might supply materials for heretics

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source quote matches tpah_source.json §39 word for word: "Nec periclitor dicere ipsas quoque scripturas sic esse ex dei voluntate dispositas ut haereticis materias subministrarent, cum legam oportere haereses esse". The live English in tpah_english.json §39 has "Nor do I risk saying...". "Nec periclitor dicere" means "I run no risk in saying", so "I do not hesitate to say". Tertullian is stating the claim as his own, and the "cum legam oportere haereses esse" clause (1 Cor 11:19) gives his reason for it. In English, "Nor do I risk saying X" means the speaker will not say X. That reverses his meaning, and the "since I read..." clause no longer makes sense after it. This is a real error of sense, not a style choice. The proposed fix "Nor do I hesitate to say that the Scriptures themselves were arranged by God's will..." is faithful. One optional change: "were so arranged" would also carry the Latin "sic".
verdict.better_correction: Nor do I hesitate to say that the Scriptures themselves were so arranged by God's will as to supply materials for heretics, since I read that there must be heresies, which cannot exist without the Scriptures.

errors.english_quote: and he shows the last to be first
errors.source_quote: et de primis novissimos ostendit
errors.why: 'Out of the first he shows the last' means he shows the first to be last. That is the point here: people once first in the church fall away. The English reverses it.
errors.corrected_english: and he shows the first to be last

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim; it's a real error. The quotes in the claim match the files. tpah_source.json §3 reads "et plantam, quam non plantavit, eradicat, et de primis novissimos ostendit". tpah_english.json §3, paragraph 4, reads "and he shows the last to be first". In the Latin, "de primis" means "from among the first" and "novissimos" ("the last") is the object of "ostendit" ("he shows"). So God shows that some of the first are really last. The line echoes Matt 19:30 ("many that are first shall be last"). This is also the whole point of the chapter: bishops, deacons, virgins and martyrs who were once prominent fall away, and that proves nothing for heresy. The current English turns this into the opposite saying ("the last shall be first"), which reverses the meaning. The proposed fix "and he shows the first to be last" restores the right sense and is acceptable. "De primis" literally means "some out of the first", not all of them, so the better rendering below states that.
verdict.better_correction: and he shows that some of the first are last

errors.english_quote: But he became involved with a woman who had abandoned Marcion's discipline of continence, and withdrew
errors.source_quote: sed lapsus in feminam desertor continentiae Marcionensis ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit
errors.why: desertor is masculine and goes with Apelles, the subject of lapsus and secessit. Apelles is the one who abandoned Marcionite continence; the English gives that to the woman.
errors.corrected_english: But falling into sin with a woman, he deserted Marcion's discipline of continence and withdrew

verdict.reason: I checked section 30 in tpah_source.json and tpah_english.json, and the claim holds. The Latin reads "sed lapsus in feminam desertor continentiae Marcionensis ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit." "Desertor" is a masculine nominative noun, and it stands beside "lapsus", whose subject is Apelles, the same subject as "secessit". So Apelles is the one who deserted Marcionite continence. "Feminam" is accusative after "in" and has nothing describing her. The live English says "he became involved with a woman who had abandoned Marcion's discipline of continence". That moves the desertion from Apelles to the woman, which is a wrong-person error. It also undercuts Tertullian's point: Apelles broke his own sect's rule of celibacy. "Lapsus" (fell, lapsed) also implies moral failure, which "became involved with" softens. The proposed correction is faithful. Keep the rest of the sentence when applying it: "But falling into sin with a woman, he deserted Marcion's discipline of continence and withdrew from the eyes of his most holy teacher to Alexandria." A version closer to the Latin structure is also acceptable: "But having fallen with a woman, a deserter of Marcionite continence, he withdrew from the eyes of his most holy teacher to Alexandria."
verdict.better_correction: But falling into sin with a woman, he deserted Marcion's discipline of continence and withdrew from the eyes of his most holy teacher to Alexandria.

errors.english_quote: with the two hundred sesterces he had brought into the church
errors.source_quote: cum ducentis sestertiis quae ecclesiae intulerat
errors.why: sestertia (neuter plural) are units of 1,000 sesterces, so ducenta sestertia is 200,000 sesterces, the standard reading. 'Two hundred sesterces' cuts the gift a thousandfold and loses the point that it was a large donation returned to him.
errors.corrected_english: with the two hundred thousand sesterces he had brought into the church

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source quote is exact (tpah_source.json §30: "Marcion quidem cum ducentis sestertiis quae ecclesiae intulerat"), and so is the English ("was expelled with the two hundred sesterces he had brought into the church"). The ablative "ducentis sestertiis" taken alone could come from either sestertius (one coin) or sestertium (1,000 sesterces). The relative pronoun settles it: "quae" is neuter plural, while the masculine would be "quos". So the noun is the neuter sestertia, and ducenta sestertia means 200,000 sesterces. This is the standard scholarly reading (Harnack, Evans), and it fits Adv. Marc. IV.4, where Marcion's money is presented as a large gift returned to him. ANF renders it "two hundred sesterces", but that is the inherited error. As currently worded, the English cuts the amount a thousandfold and loses the point. The proposed correction is faithful. "Brought into the church" is fine for "intulerat"; "given to the church" would also do.
verdict.better_correction: Marcion, indeed, was expelled with the two hundred thousand sesterces he had brought into the church

errors.english_quote: And if we have not brought it forward, let us for the moment give room to the opposing side
errors.source_quote: ac si prolata non sit a nobis, locum interim demus diversae parti
errors.why: 'ac si' means 'as if'. Tertullian proposes to argue as though the proof had not been offered yet. 'And if we have not' turns this into a condition and breaks the logic.
errors.corrected_english: let us, as if it had not been brought forward by us, give room for the moment to the opposing side

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The quote matches the source exactly: tpah_source.json §22 reads "Sed quoniam tam expedita probatio est, ut, si statim proferatur, nihil iam sit retractandum, ac si prolata non sit a nobis, locum interim demus diversae parti, si quid putant ad infirmandam hanc praescriptionem movere se posse". Here "ac si" with the subjunctive means "as if". Tertullian is saying that, although the proof is ready, he will argue as though he had not yet given it. The ANF translation (Holmes) reads it the same way: "just as if no proof were forthcoming from us". The live English says "And if we have not brought it forward", which wrongly turns a pretence into a real condition. It also breaks off the "quoniam" (since) clause into its own sentence. The proposed fix is faithful. It works better as one sentence that keeps "since", as below.
verdict.better_correction: But since the proof is so ready to hand that, if it were brought forward at once, nothing would remain to be reconsidered, let us for the moment give room to the opposing side, as if we had not brought it forward, in case they think they can raise anything to weaken this legal objection.

errors.english_quote: Brothers, there are spirits of wickedness with whom we wrestle. They deserve our attention, and they are necessary for faith
errors.source_quote: Erant ingenia de spiritalibus nequitiae, cum quibus luctatio est nobis, fratres, merito contemplanda, fidei necessaria
errors.why: The subject is ingenia, the clever devices that come from the spiritual forces of wickedness (the scripture-twisting just described). Those devices deserve attention and are 'necessary for faith'. The English drops ingenia and says the evil spirits themselves are necessary for faith.
errors.corrected_english: Such are the clever devices of the spiritual forces of wickedness with which we wrestle, brothers. They rightly deserve our attention, and they are necessary for faith

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In tpah_source.json §39, the Latin reads "Erant ingenia de spiritalibus nequitiae, cum quibus luctatio est nobis, fratres, merito contemplanda, fidei necessaria, ut electi manifestentur...". The neuter plural gerundive "contemplanda" and the adjective "necessaria" agree with "ingenia", not with "spiritalibus nequitiae", which is ablative after "de". So it is the devices or clever schemes that come from the spiritual forces of wickedness that deserve attention and are "necessary for faith". The English in tpah_english.json §39 drops "ingenia" completely. It reads "Brothers, there are spirits of wickedness with whom we wrestle. They deserve our attention, and they are necessary for faith". That makes the evil spirits themselves "necessary for faith", which changes the meaning. The English also drops "merito" ("rightly"). The proposed correction fixes the subject and restores "rightly", so it is faithful. One small point: "Erant" is past tense ("These were"), which fits a look back at the Scripture-twisting just described. "Such are" is still defensible.
verdict.better_correction: These were the clever devices of the spiritual forces of wickedness with which we wrestle, brothers. They rightly deserve our attention, and they are necessary for faith

errors.english_quote: He promises an exposition of sins from the washing.
errors.source_quote: expositionem delictorum de lavacro repromittit
errors.why: expositio here means 'putting away, removal' (the devil's imitation of baptismal forgiveness), not 'exposition'. The English calque means explanation, which makes no sense.
errors.corrected_english: He promises the putting away of sins through the washing.

verdict.reason: I checked tpah_source.json §39. The Latin reads exactly "expositionem delictorum de lavacro repromittit". Here "expositio" means setting aside or removal (from "exponere", to put out or away). The passage lists the devil's copies of Christian rites: baptism, forgiveness of sins, sealing the forehead, the bread offering. So the copied rite is the washing away of sins, and the standard rendering (ANF: "promises the putting away of sins by a laver") agrees. The live English, "He promises an exposition of sins from the washing.", copies the Latin word letter for letter, means "an explanation of sins", and makes no sense here. That is a real wrong-sense error, not a style choice. The proposed fix, "He promises the putting away of sins through the washing.", is faithful. "Remission of sins" or "forgiveness of sins through the washing" would also be correct.

errors.english_quote: What of the fact that he also established a high priest for the marriage of one man?
errors.source_quote: Quid, quod et summum pontificem in unius nuptiis statuit?
errors.why: in unius nuptiis statuit means he requires his high priest to marry only once, imitating the church rule for clergy. 'A high priest for the marriage of one man' is garbled and loses the point.
errors.corrected_english: What of the fact that he also restricts his high priest to a single marriage?

verdict.reason:
The quote matches the source exactly. Section 39 of tpah_source.json reads "Quid, quod et summum pontificem in unius nuptiis statuit?" and tpah_english.json reads "What of the fact that he also established a high priest for the marriage of one man?"

"In unius nuptiis" means "in one marriage" ("unius" goes with "nuptiis"). The phrase says the devil sets his high priest within a single marriage, so the priest may marry only once. Tertullian is pointing to the pagan rule that copies the Church rule that clergy marry only once (compare his Exhortation to Chastity 13).

The current English reads as if the priest were appointed to serve at, or because of, some man's wedding. That is a wrong sense, not a style choice. The next sentence makes the meaning clear: "he has virgins too, and he has the continent." It lists counterfeit forms of chastity.

The proposed correction, "restricts his high priest to a single marriage," is faithful. A slightly closer rendering of "statuit" is "What of the fact that he also appoints his high priest from among the once-married?" or "...also requires his high priest to marry only once?"
verdict.better_correction: What of the fact that he also requires his high priest to marry only once?

errors.english_quote: Their dealings with itinerants, with wandering charlatans, with astrologers, with philosophers
errors.source_quote: commercia haereticorum cum magis quam pluribus, cum circulatoribus, cum astrologis, cum philosophis
errors.why: magis quam pluribus means 'with very many magicians'. The English drops the magicians and adds 'itinerants', which is not in the source.
errors.corrected_english: Their dealings with a great many magicians, with wandering charlatans, with astrologers, with philosophers

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. In tpah_source.json §43 the Latin reads "commercia haereticorum cum magis quam pluribus, cum circulatoribus, cum astrologis, cum philosophis". Here "magis" is the ablative plural of "magus" (magician), not the adverb "more". "Quam pluribus" (in some editions "quamplurimis") means "very many", so the phrase means "with a great many magicians". The ANF translation reads it the same way: "with very many magicians, mountebanks, astrologers, philosophers". The live English says "Their dealings with itinerants, with wandering charlatans, with astrologers, with philosophers". That drops the magicians entirely. It also adds "itinerants", which nothing in the source supports, since the wandering idea is already in "circulatoribus" (rendered as "wandering charlatans"). This is a real omission plus an invented word, not a style choice. The proposed fix, "Their dealings with a great many magicians, with wandering charlatans, with astrologers, with philosophers", matches the Latin and keeps the rest of the sentence. It should go in front of the existing tail, "—all people devoted to curiosity—have also been noted."

errors.english_quote: For this we believe first: that there is nothing beyond which we ought to believe.
errors.source_quote: Hoc enim prius credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debeamus.
errors.why: The Latin says there is nothing further we ought to believe. 'Nothing beyond which we ought to believe' is garbled and suggests a limit past which belief goes, which changes the meaning of a famous line.
errors.corrected_english: For this we believe first: that there is nothing further that we ought to believe.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute the claim. The source (tpah_source.json §7) reads exactly "Hoc enim prius credimus, non esse quod ultra credere debeamus." The relative clause "quod ... credere debeamus" means "something that we ought to believe", and "ultra" means "further" or "beyond this". So the sense is "there is nothing further that we ought to believe", which is the standard reading (ANF: "that there is nothing which we ought to believe besides"). The live English (tpah_english.json §7) says "that there is nothing beyond which we ought to believe". That makes "nothing" the limit that belief goes beyond, so it reads as "belief has no limit", close to the opposite of Tertullian's point. It also clashes with the sentence just before it: "When we believe, we desire nothing beyond belief." This is a real error of sense, not a style preference. It is also a famous line, so the low severity undersells it a little. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly tighter version that keeps "ultra" as "beyond" is: "For this we believe first: that there is nothing beyond this that we ought to believe."
verdict.better_correction: For this we believe first: that there is nothing further that we ought to believe.

errors.english_quote: when the very things we suffer as Christians show us to be following the example of Christ himself
errors.source_quote: cum ea nos ostendunt Christianos quae patimur ad exemplum ipsius Christi
errors.why: The Latin says the things we suffer after Christ's example show us to be Christians. The English swaps the predicate and the qualifier, so suffering now proves imitation of Christ, not Christian identity.
errors.corrected_english: when the things we suffer after the example of Christ himself are what show us to be Christians

verdict.reason: The claim stands, though it is minor. The source in tpah_source.json §3 reads exactly "cum ea nos ostendunt Christianos quae patimur ad exemplum ipsius Christi". Here "Christianos" is the predicate of "nos ostendunt" ("show us to be Christians"), and "ad exemplum ipsius Christi" goes with "patimur" ("the things we suffer after the example of Christ himself"). The live English reads "when the very things we suffer as Christians show us to be following the example of Christ himself". That turns "Christians" into a label on the sufferers and makes "following the example of Christ" the thing proved. Tertullian's point is the other way round: being deserted, as Christ was deserted by Judas, proves we are truly Christians. The overall sense is close, so this is low severity, but the English swaps what is being proved. The proposed fix is faithful. A slightly smoother version that keeps the question form: "Are we surprised when his churches are deserted by certain people, when the very things we suffer after the example of Christ himself show us to be Christians?"
verdict.better_correction: when the very things we suffer after the example of Christ himself show us to be Christians

errors.english_quote: lest the tracings of the things they falsely claim be admitted along with them
errors.source_quote: ne pariter admittantur traductiones eorum quae mentiuntur
errors.why: traductiones means public exposures or convictions, not 'tracings'. As written the clause is unclear.
errors.corrected_english: lest the exposure of their lies be admitted along with them

verdict.reason: I read section 22 in tpah_source.json and tpah_english.json, and the claim holds. The Latin matches the quote exactly: "Tanti est enim illis non habere probationes eorum quae defendunt, ne pariter admittantur traductiones eorum quae mentiuntur." In Tertullian, traducere means to expose or convict, and traductio means a public exposure or refutation. It does not mean a tracing. The English "lest the tracings of the things they falsely claim be admitted along with them" uses the wrong sense of the word and leaves the sentence's point unclear. The point is that the heretics would rather have no proofs at all, because once proofs are allowed, the proofs that expose their lies come in with them. This is a real error, though a minor one. The proposed fix, "lest the exposure of their lies be admitted along with them", says what the Latin says. Two notes on it: "along with them" stands for "pariter" (at the same time), which is fine, and "their lies" is a fair way to put "eorum quae mentiuntur" (the things they lie about). A more literal option is "lest the refutation of their falsehoods be admitted at the same time."
verdict.better_correction: For it matters so much to them to have no proofs for what they defend, lest the exposure of their lies be admitted along with them.

kept.english_quote: For what did Christ not endure on our account, that he should be called Christ?
kept.source_quote: Τί γὰρ δι' ἡμᾶς οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν κληθῆναι Χριστός;
kept.why: Χριστός is the subject; τί is what he submitted to be called (κληθῆναι depends on ὑπέμεινεν). The line introduces the list of names that follows. The English invents a purpose clause about being called 'Christ' and breaks the link to the list.
kept.corrected_english: For what did Christ not submit to be called for our sake?

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the claim. The source is quoted correctly. In section u01-rem-mid of translations/adrb_u01_rem_source.json, the Greek reads "Τί γὰρ δι' ἡμᾶς οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν κληθῆναι Χριστός;". The live English in translations/adrb_u01_rem_english.json reads "For what did Christ not endure on our account, that he should be called Christ?"

The natural parse makes Χριστός the subject of ὑπέμεινεν. κληθῆναι is the infinitive that completes it ("submit to be called"), and τί stands for what he was called. The next sentence confirms this reading: "We cannot count his names..." followed by a list that includes humble ones (sheep, worm, stone). The point is that Christ let himself be called even "worm" for our sake.

The live English takes Χριστός as the name he was called and turns κληθῆναι into a purpose clause ("that he should be called Christ"). kept.english_quote: But do not think, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them.

verdict.reason:
The source matches the quote, in antimont_u2_source.json §2.1: "ἀλλὰ μὴ ἄνευ τοῦ ἰδεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐπίστασθαί τῶν τοιούτων νομίζομεν ὦ μακάριε." The author is warning himself and his own side not to claim knowledge of things they did not witness. The next sentence ("ἴσως μὲν γὰρ οὕτως, ἴσως δὲ οὐχ' οὕτως", "perhaps so, perhaps not") confirms this.

The live English, "But do not think, blessed one, that we know such things without having seen them", has two problems:
1. It changes the subject to "you" (an order to the reader).
2. It reads naturally as "don't assume our knowledge is second-hand", which suggests the author did see these things. That is the opposite of the author's disclaimer, and it clashes with the "perhaps ... perhaps not" that follows.

So the claim stands: wrong person, with a sense that flips in normal reading.

The proposed fix ("But we do not suppose ...") puts back "we", but the dangling "without having seen them" keeps the same double meaning. It also misses an omission in the same spot: the sentence just before, "φασὶ γοῦν τοῦτο οὕτω γεγονέναι" ("At any rate, they say this is how it happened"), is missing from the English altogether.

But let us not suppose, blessed one, that we have knowledge of such things when we did not see them. For perhaps Montanus and Theodotus and the woman mentioned above died in this way, and perhaps not."

kept.english_quote: that I might seem to some people to be adding to or taking away from the word of the new covenant of the gospel
kept.source_quote: μή πῃ δόξω τισὶν ἐπισυγγράφειν ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι τῷ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου καινῆς διαθήκης λόγῳ
kept.why: Both verbs mean adding: writing additions and adding new provisions, as with a codicil (compare Gal 3:15). Nothing in the clause means 'taking away'. That idea appears only in the next clause (μήτε προσθεῖναι μήτ’ ἀφελεῖν), so the English moves it forward and loses the author's point.
kept.corrected_english: that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to, or adding new provisions to, the word of the new covenant of the gospel

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against the source and the English in antimont_u1_source.json and antimont_u1_english.json, section 1.1, and it holds. The Greek reads "μή πῃ δόξω τισὶν ἐπισυγγράφειν ἢ ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι τῷ τῆς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου καινῆς διαθήκης λόγῳ". Both verbs mean adding. ἐπισυγγράφειν means to write something more onto a document. ἐπιδιατάσσεσθαι means to add provisions to a will, as with a codicil; Gal 3:15 uses the same verb for adding to a ratified covenant. Nothing in this clause means "take away". The live English, "adding to or taking away from the word of the new covenant", takes the idea of removing from the next clause, "ᾧ μήτε προσθεῖναι μήτ’ ἀφελεῖν δυνατὸν", and puts it here too early. The author's worry is that a new treatise could look like a supplement to the gospel. Standard English versions agree: McGiffert has "add to the writings or injunctions of the word of the new covenant". This is a small error of sense, so severity low is right. The proposed correction is faithful but a little clumsy. A smoother faithful version: "that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to the word of the new covenant of the gospel, or adding new provisions to it".
verdict.better_correction: that I might seem to some people to be writing additions to the word of the new covenant of the gospel, or adding new provisions to it

kept.english_quote: Then again, after saying other things in between to refute the false prophecies of Maximilla,
kept.source_quote: ἐν ταυτῷ δὲ πάλιν ἕτερα μεταξὺ πρὸς ἔλεγχον τῶν τῆς Μαξιμίλλης ψυδοπροφητειῶν εἰπὼν

kept.english_quote: but let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon.
kept.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ προσδράμωμεν

kept.corrected_english: but let us run to the one who forgives sins.

The English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json says "but let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon." kept.english_quote: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters? Rise, take up your mat and walk."
kept.source_quote: τί περιμένεις τὰ μικρά; τί ζητεῖς ὑδάτων ἰατρείαν; ἔγειραι, ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν.
kept.why: The Greek says only 'Rise,' and adds 'the Resurrection said to you,' a deliberate wordplay naming Christ as the Resurrection (it sets up the list 'resurrection to the dead' that follows). The English drops that title and adds 'take up your mat and walk', which the source does not have here. The full command first appears in the next paragraph (§10).
kept.corrected_english: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this claim. The source matches the quote exactly. cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, §9 of section u01-rem-early, reads: "ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· τί περιμένεις τὰ μικρά; τί ζητεῖς ὑδάτων ἰατρείαν; ἔγειραι, ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν. πανταχοῦ γὰρ ... νεκροῖς ἀνάστασις ...". The live English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, paragraph 5, reads: 'And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters? Rise, take up your mat and walk."'

The English makes two errors:
1. It drops "ἡ ἀνάστασίς σοι εἶπεν" ("the Resurrection said to you"). This is the play on ἔγειραι/ἀνάστασις, naming Christ as the Resurrection, and it sets up "resurrection to the dead" in the very next sentence.
2. It adds "take up your mat and walk", which the Greek does not have here. That phrase first appears at the start of §10 ("Ἔγειραι, ἆρόν σου τὸν κράββατον καὶ περιπάτει"), and the English already renders it there as paragraph 6, so it now appears twice.

This is a real omission plus an addition, not a style choice. The proposed correction is faithful. It should keep the lead-in "And he says to him:", giving: And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.
verdict.better_correction: And he says to him: "Why do you wait for small things? Why do you seek healing from waters?" "Rise," the Resurrection said to you.

kept.english_quote: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and he was bound by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.
kept.source_quote: καὶ εἰ ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, ἀλλὰ στέφανος, καὶ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος. βασιλεῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν ἀναγορεύονται.
kept.why: δεδεμένος agrees with στέφανος: the crown was plaited (bound) by soldiers. The point is that soldiers crowned him, as soldiers proclaim kings. The English makes Christ the one 'bound', which breaks the argument.
kept.corrected_english: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and one plaited by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.

verdict.reason: The quote matches the locked source exactly (cjhp_u01_rem_source.json and cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-mid, §12). In Greek "καὶ εἰ ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, ἀλλὰ στέφανος, καὶ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν δεδεμένος", the masculine nominative δεδεμένος matches ὁ στέφανος, which is the only nominative subject in that clause. Christ is not named in the nominative anywhere nearby; the last mention is "βασιλεὺς γὰρ ἦν", two sentences earlier. The words read as "a crown, and [a crown] bound by soldiers", which echoes Matthew 27:29, where the soldiers plait the crown of thorns. The next sentence, "βασιλεῖς γὰρ ὑπὸ στρατιωτῶν ἀναγορεύονται", only follows if soldiers crowning him is the royal sign, in line with the purple robe before it. Christ being tied up is not a sign of kingship, so "he was bound by soldiers" gives the wrong referent and breaks the argument. This is a real faithfulness error, not a style preference. The proposed fix "and one plaited by soldiers" is faithful. δέω means bind or tie, and "plaited" or "woven" is a normal English word for making a wreath. A closer literal option would be "and one bound together by soldiers", but the proposed wording is fine.
verdict.better_correction: And if the crown was of thorns, still it was a crown, and one plaited by soldiers. For kings are proclaimed by soldiers.

kept.english_quote: For the apostle does not want us to take ourselves completely out of the world and do no evil; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh
kept.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀπόστολος τελείως ἑαυτοὺς ἐξαγαγόντας ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι φαῦλον
kept.why: The participle gives the means: the apostle does not want us to avoid evil by leaving the world entirely. As written, the English reads as if the apostle does not want us to 'do no evil'.
kept.corrected_english: For the apostle does not want us to avoid doing evil by taking ourselves completely out of the world; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh

verdict.reason: The quotes match. The Greek in u01-rem-close §18 (cjhp_u01_rem_source.json) reads: "οὐ γὰρ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀπόστολος τελείως ἑαυτοὺς ἐξαγαγόντας ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι φαῦλον, ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντας ἡμᾶς καταδουλῶσαι τὴν σάρκα". The aorist participle ἐξαγαγόντας tells how: the apostle does not want us to keep from doing evil by leaving the world entirely. He wants us to master the flesh while still in it, and the ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντας contrast confirms this. The live English (cjhp_u01_rem_english.json) has "does not want us to take ourselves completely out of the world and do no evil". Joining the two with "and" makes them two separate things the apostle does not want. The plain reading is then that he does not want us to "do no evil", which is close to the reverse of the sense. This is a real error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction, "does not want us to avoid doing evil by taking ourselves completely out of the world; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh", keeps the participle as the means and is faithful. When applied, the edit should keep the existing "and not be ruled by it" (καὶ μὴ ἄρχεσθαι ὑπ' αὐτῆς) that follows.

kept.english_quote: Train the passions away from the passionless text.
kept.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε.
kept.why: Cyril tells the reader to use the passionless (chaste) words to retrain the passions, that is, to read the bridal language chastely. 'Away from the passionless text' suggests turning away from the text, which is the opposite.
kept.corrected_english: Use what is free of passion to retrain the passions.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly: the Greek in cjhp_u01_rem_source.json reads "μηδὲ ἐμπαθῶς ἄκουε ταῦτα, ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν τὰ πάθη μεταγύμναζε". μεταγυμνάζω means "train differently, retrain". ἐκ τῶν ἀπαθῶν means "out of / by means of the passionless things", meaning the chaste bridal words Cyril has just described as "nuptial, sober, chaste". The Greek has no idea of moving "away from" the text. The live English, "Train the passions away from the passionless text", invents that direction. A reader can take it to mean "train your passions to leave the text", which turns Cyril's point upside down: he wants the reader to stay with the chaste words and let them reshape the passions. This is garbled, not a matter of style, so the claim stands. The proposed fix, "Use what is free of passion to retrain the passions", is faithful, but it drops the word for "words/text". It also hides a likely pun: the section opens with "τοῦ πάθους ... τὰ σύμβολα" (the symbols of the Passion), and the next sentence speaks of the songs "τοῦ πάθους Χριστοῦ μηνυτικά" (revealing Christ's Passion). So τὰ πάθη may also hint at reading Christ's sufferings out of passionless words. A closer rendering keeps the "from ... words" frame and leaves that double sense open.
verdict.better_correction: From the passionless words, retrain the passions.

kept.english_quote: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions were at work in our members."
kept.source_quote: ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν
kept.why: The English drops τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ('aroused through the law') from Romans 7:5. There is also no citation for this quotation, though others in the text have one.
kept.corrected_english: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members" (Romans 7:5).

The English, "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions were at work in our members.", leaves out τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου. The proposed fix, "the sinful passions aroused through the law were at work in our members", is faithful ("aroused by the law" or "that came through the law" would also do). The missing citation is a minor consistency point, not a faithfulness error. The book does cite references inline elsewhere (John 5:6, John 7:38 and others), but this same paragraph also leaves James 1:13 and Gen 6:3 uncited. Adding "(Romans 7:5)" is optional. The required fix is restoring the law phrase.

kept.english_quote: Let our soul follow the great physician who gives knowledge.
kept.source_quote: τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν·
kept.why: τὴν ψυχήν is the accusative of respect that ends the clause 'εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν τὴν ψυχήν' ('if we are in pain in soul'). The section split cut off 'εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν', and the English made 'soul' the subject of 'follow'. 'Great' is not in the source; it is simply 'the physician of knowledge'. This section repeats the source of u02-open, which renders the same words correctly (except for 'great').
kept.corrected_english: [If we are in pain] in soul, let us follow the physician of knowledge.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked both files in cjhp_u02_rem_*.json. The source for u02-rem-early starts mid-clause with "τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν·". In u02-open, the words before it are "εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν", so "τὴν ψυχήν" is an accusative of respect: "if we are in pain in soul". The English "Let our soul follow" makes "soul" the subject of a first-person-plural verb (ἐξακολουθήσωμεν, "let us follow"). That is a grammatical misreading caused by the bad section split, not a defensible choice. "Great" has no source word; the Greek says only "τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως". "Who gives knowledge" reads more into the genitive than it says but is a minor point. The same section text is already covered, nearly correctly, in u02-open ("If our soul is in pain, let us follow the great physician of knowledge"). kept.english_quote: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one my Father has revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters"
kept.source_quote: εἰ σὺ εἶ ὃν ἐγὼ οἶδα, μᾶλλον δὲ ὃν ὁ πατήρ μοι ἐμήνυσεν
kept.why: μοι is the dative 'to me' and is already rendered by 'revealed to me'. ὁ πατήρ is 'the Father' (echoing Matthew 16:17), not 'my Father'. As written, Peter calls God 'my Father'.
kept.corrected_english: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters"

verdict.reason:
The source quote is accurate. cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, §8 reads "ὁ δὲ Πέτρος πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγει· εἰ σὺ εἶ ὃν ἐγὼ οἶδα, μᾶλλον δὲ ὃν ὁ πατήρ μοι ἐμήνυσεν, κέλευσόν μοι ἐλθεῖν πρὸς σὲ ἐπὶ τὰ ὕδατα." The English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json, paragraph 4, has "the one my Father has revealed to me".

Nothing in the Greek supplies "my". The only first-person word in that clause is μοι, and the English already uses it for "to me". A Greek article can sometimes stand in for a possessive with kinship nouns. But when ὁ πατήρ names the divine Father in a Christological passage, the standard reading is "the Father". Cyril is pointing to Matthew 16:17, where Christ says the Father revealed this to Peter. In the current English, Peter instead calls God "my Father", a phrase the Gospels give to Christ.

This is a small addition, not a reversal of sense, so "low" severity is right. Still, it is a real addition that a careful translator would remove, not a style preference.

The proposed fix is faithful: "If you are the one I know, or rather, the one the Father revealed to me, command me to come to you on the waters". The simple past "revealed" matches the aorist ἐμήνυσεν better than "has revealed", though both are acceptable.

kept.english_quote: The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste.
kept.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα.
kept.why: σοφά means 'wise', which completes the contrast with κατὰ σοφίαν. 'Chaste' (σώφρονα) is a different word and loses the wordplay.
kept.corrected_english: For the passions are not in keeping with wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The locked source in translations/cjhp_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-mid, reads exactly "οὐ γὰρ κατὰ σοφίαν τὰ πάθη, ἀλλὰ σοφὰ τὰ νοήματα." The live English in cjhp_u01_rem_english.json renders it as "The passions are not according to wisdom; rather, the thoughts are chaste."

σοφά means "wise", not "chaste". The chastity words in this passage are σωφρονικοῖς and σωφροσύνης, and σοφά is not one of them. The sentence sets κατὰ σοφίαν ("in keeping with wisdom") against σοφά ("wise"), and "chaste" breaks that contrast. The English also drops γάρ ("for"), so the sentence no longer reads as the reason for the line before it.

The error is minor, since the general sense is still close, but it is a real wrong word. The proposed correction is faithful to the Greek: "For the passions are not in keeping with wisdom; rather, the thoughts are wise." It restores both "for" and "wise".

kept.english_quote: with you is the fountain of life (Psalm 36:9 LXX)

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against both files and it holds. In translations/cjhp_u02_open_source.json, the Greek reads "εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν".
