kept.english_quote: To this man he speaks a question that was longed for: "Do you want to become well?"
kept.source_quote: πρὸς τοῦτον ἐρώτημά πως λέγει τὸ ποθούμενον
kept.why: Read with πως, the Greek means that in the form of a question he voices what the man longed for (health). The question itself was not what was longed for.
kept.corrected_english: To this man he speaks, in the form of a question, the thing he longed for: "Do you want to become well?"

verdict.reason: I checked the source for u01-open §4 in cjhp_u01_open_source.json. The claim quotes it correctly: "πρὸς τοῦτον ἐρώτημά πως λέγει τὸ ποθούμενον· θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι;". The object of λέγει is the articular τὸ ποθούμενον, "the thing longed for". The anarthrous ἐρώτημά πως is predicative and means "in a way, as a question". So Cyril says Jesus voices the man's desire, health, in question form. The live English reads "he speaks a question that was longed for". That makes the question the thing desired and drops πως. The sense shifts, though only slightly. The next lines support the claim's reading: Cyril stresses "θέλεις" and says "ἐπὶ τῷ θέλειν τὴν βοήθειαν τιθεμένου", which ties the question to the man's own wish. The error is low severity but real, not a style preference. The proposed correction is faithful. A version closer to πως is optional: "To this man he speaks, in a way as a question, the very thing he longed for: 'Do you want to become well?'"
verdict.better_correction: To this man he speaks, in a way as a question, the very thing he longed for: "Do you want to become well?" (John 5:6)

kept.english_quote: Didymus comments: This Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the work of the Master in the same way as I do.
kept.source_quote: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ Τιμόθεος οὗτος περὶ οὗ γράφω τὰ προκείμενα, τῶν γνησίων τοῦ θεοῦ δοῦλος, τὸ ἔργον τοῦ δεσπότου παραπλησίως ἐμοὶ ἐργαζόμενος.
kept.why: This is Didymus paraphrasing Paul in Paul's own voice (1 Cor 16:10 'he does the work of the Lord, as I do'). The added 'Didymus comments:' makes Didymus the 'I' who writes about Timothy and works like him. Nothing in the Greek says 'Didymus comments'.
kept.corrected_english: For this Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the Master's work just as I do.

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source (translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-close) reads: "Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ Τιμόθεος οὗτος περὶ οὗ γράφω τὰ προκείμενα, τῶν γνησίων τοῦ θεοῦ δοῦλος, τὸ ἔργον τοῦ δεσπότου παραπλησίως ἐμοὶ ἐργαζόμενος." Nothing in it corresponds to "Didymus comments:". The "γράφω" (I write) and "ἐμοί" (as I do) are Paul's voice. Didymus is paraphrasing 1 Cor 16:10-11 as Paul, and the next clause, "περιμένω γὰρ ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ ἕως ἐπανέλθῃ πρός με", is still Paul in the first person. The English adds a label that makes Didymus the "I" who writes about Timothy and works the way Timothy does, so the speaker is wrong. The proposed correction is faithful: "γάρ" becomes "For", and "παραπλησίως ἐμοί" becomes "just as I do". In the same paragraph, the English "For Paul says: I am waiting in Asia..." also inserts "Paul says"; the Greek is just "περιμένω γάρ". With the bad label removed, that clause should stay in Paul's voice too. A side note outside this claim: in paragraph 9, "Didymus's teacher Origen" adds "Didymus's teacher"; the Greek has only "ὁ Ὠριγένης".
verdict.better_correction: For this Timothy, about whom I am writing these things, is one of God's genuine servants, doing the Master's work just as I do. So let him not be despised among you, but let him be received genuinely with love, and also sent on his way; for I am waiting in Asia until he returns to me with the brothers.

kept.english_quote: So also Didymus's teacher Origen holds
kept.source_quote: οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει
kept.why: The Greek says only 'Origen'. 'Didymus's teacher' is invented, and it is false: Origen died c. 254 and Didymus was born c. 313.
kept.corrected_english: So also Origen holds

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/didymus-fragmenta-1cor/translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json and df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close, and it holds. The Greek reads only "οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει τὸ πνεῦμα πλείω τι ἔχειν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν ἀρετῇ". It names "Origen" with no word for teacher or for Didymus, yet the English says "So also Didymus's teacher Origen holds". The added phrase is commentary the translator made up, and it is false. Origen died around 254, and Didymus was born around 313, so Origen could not have taught him. Didymus followed Origen's ideas but was never his pupil. A reader of the live text would take this as a fact from the source. The proposed fix, "So also Origen holds ...", matches the Greek. The rest of the sentence can stay as it is. A side note outside this claim: "even though both spirit and soul exist" is a loose reading of the elliptical "εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή". It can be defended and should be looked at separately.
verdict.better_correction: So also Origen holds that the spirit has something more than the soul in virtue, even though both spirit and soul exist.

kept.english_quote: even though both spirit and soul exist.
kept.source_quote: εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή.
kept.why: The Greek means 'even though the soul too is spirit', i.e. the spirit outranks the soul in virtue although the soul is also spirit. 'Both spirit and soul exist' says something else and makes the concession pointless.
kept.corrected_english: even though the soul too is spirit.

verdict.reason: The claim stands. The source in translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json for u01-rem-close reads "οὕτω καὶ ὁ Ὠριγένης δοξάζει τὸ πνεῦμα πλείω τι ἔχειν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐν ἀρετῇ, εἰ καὶ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχή." This is an elliptical clause with ἐστί understood. Only ψυχή takes the article, so ἡ ψυχή is the subject and πνεῦμα the predicate, with the second καί meaning "also": "even if/though the soul too is spirit." The context backs this. The sentence before it says the same inner principle is called soul in the wicked and spirit in the holy (ἐπὶ μὲν φαύλων ψυχήν, ἐπὶ δὲ ἁγίων πνεῦμα λέγεσθαι). So the concession is that spirit outranks soul in virtue even though the soul is also spirit. The live English, "even though both spirit and soul exist," adds "exist," which is not in the Greek, and it loses the predication, which leaves the concession empty. The proposed fix, "even though the soul too is spirit," is faithful. "Even if the soul also is spirit" would work equally well. A separate point outside this claim: the same sentence says "Didymus's teacher Origen," but the Greek has only ὁ Ὠριγένης. "Didymus's teacher" is an addition. It should be cut, leaving "So also Origen holds...".

kept.kind: omission that breaks the comment / wrong sense
kept.english_quote: a great and effectual opportunity has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the open opportunity for the word of godliness a door.
kept.source_quote: θύρα γὰρ ὑπερέχουσα καὶ πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα εἰς τοὺς ἀκροατὰς ἀνέῳκται αὐτῷ ... ἔθος δὲ αὐτῷ τὴν παρρησίαν τοῦ τῆς εὐσεβείας λόγου θύραν καλεῖν.
kept.why: The English removes the word 'door' (θύρα) from the verse, so Didymus's closing remark about why Paul says 'door' explains a word the reader never saw. It also turns παρρησία (boldness, freedom of speech) into 'open opportunity', losing Didymus's actual gloss.
kept.corrected_english: a great and very effective door has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the bold, free preaching of the word of godliness a door.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked df1c_u01_rem_source.json and df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-close. The Greek gives the verse as "θύρα γὰρ ὑπερέχουσα καὶ πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα εἰς τοὺς ἀκροατὰς ἀνέῳκται αὐτῷ". The English renders it "a great and effectual opportunity has opened for him among his hearers", so the word "door" never appears in the verse. Didymus then explains Paul's metaphor: "ἔθος δὲ αὐτῷ τὴν παρρησίαν τοῦ τῆς εὐσεβείας λόγου θύραν καλεῖν". That remark only makes sense if the reader has just seen "door". The current English puts Didymus's explanation into the verse itself, which makes the closing remark circular ("he calls the opportunity a door" after already saying "opportunity"). This is a real fault a careful translator would fix, not a matter of style. "Open opportunity" for παρρησία is also loose: the word means openness or freedom of speech, not opportunity. Still, the larger problem is the missing "door". The proposed correction is faithful. "Very effective" matches πάνυ ἐνεργοῦσα. "Bold, free preaching" adds the idea of "preaching", which is acceptable but slightly expanded. A closer version is offered below.
verdict.better_correction: a great and very effective door has opened for him among his hearers (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). ... It is his custom to call the freedom to speak the word of godliness openly a door.

kept.kind: wrong sense (scripture word treated as commentary)
kept.english_quote: And "sober up" is well said—rightly so—since not all do this. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up for wicked ends
kept.source_quote: καλῶς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐκνήψατε δικαίως ὡς μὴ πάντων τοῦτο ποιούντων· οἱ γὰρ σοφοὶ τοῦ κακοποιῆσαι ἀγρυπνοῦντες περὶ τὰ βλαβερὰ ἀδίκως ἐκνήφουσιν
kept.why: 'ἐκνήψατε δικαίως' is the lemma of 1 Cor 15:34 ('sober up righteously'). Didymus's point is that 'righteously' is well added, because the clever at evil sober up 'unrighteously' (ἀδίκως). Rendering δικαίως as the aside 'rightly so' loses the verse word and the contrast the comment rests on.
kept.corrected_english: And "sober up righteously" is well said, since not all do this righteously. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up unrighteously

verdict.reason: The source (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-early, under the heading 1 Kor 15,34) matches the quote exactly: "καλῶς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐκνήψατε δικαίως ὡς μὴ πάντων τοῦτο ποιούντων· οἱ γὰρ σοφοὶ τοῦ κακοποιῆσαι ἀγρυπνοῦντες περὶ τὰ βλαβερὰ ἀδίκως ἐκνήφουσιν". The verse 1 Cor 15:34 reads ἐκνήψατε δικαίως, so the lemma is "ἐκνήψατε δικαίως" and δικαίως is the Bible's word. Didymus is not adding his own "rightly so". His whole point depends on the contrast δικαίως / ἀδίκως: Paul is right to add "righteously" because people who are clever at doing evil also "sober up", but unrighteously. The live English, "'sober up' is well said—rightly so", takes the verse word out of the quotation and turns it into the commentator's aside. It also renders ἀδίκως as "for wicked ends", which hides the contrast the comment rests on. This is a real wrong-sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful in substance. It has two small flaws: it drops καί ("also": "is also well said"), and it adds a second "righteously" after "not all do this", which is not in the Greek. Leaving that word out still keeps the sense, because the quoted lemma now carries it.
verdict.better_correction: And "sober up righteously" is also well said, since not everyone does this. For those who are clever at doing evil stay awake over harmful things and sober up unrighteously, supposedly casting off the sleep of ignorance.

kept.english_quote: since it is a natural body, being a body of a soul, the prior quality of which was corrupted in it. It is raised by the power of God
kept.source_quote: τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος, ἀνίσταται θεοῦ δυνάμει
kept.why: The genitive absolute 'φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος' goes with 'ἀνίσταται': when the body's former quality (dishonor, weakness) has been destroyed in it, it is raised. The English attaches it to the soul and says the soul's quality 'was corrupted', which reverses the point (the old quality is abolished at resurrection; it is not the soul that was corrupted).
kept.corrected_english: being a body of the soul. When the former quality in it has been destroyed, it is raised by the power of God

verdict.reason:
The claim holds; I could not refute it. The Greek in df1c_u01_rem_source.json (u01-rem-mid) reads: "εὐλόγως καὶ ἀτιμία καὶ ἀσθένεια περὶ αὐτὸ ἔσται, τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος, ἀνίσταται θεοῦ δυνάμει, ἀφθαρσίαν καὶ δύναμιν καὶ τιμὴν ἔχον". The phrase "φθαρείσης ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς προλαβούσης ποιότητος" is a genitive absolute: it has its own subject, ποιότητος, and an aorist participle. It describes what happens before the main verb ἀνίσταται: once the former quality in the body (the dishonor and weakness just named) has been destroyed, the body is raised with incorruptibility, power and honor. Nothing in the Greek makes it a relative clause on ψυχῆς. That reading would need ἧς or αὐτῆς, and ἐν αὐτῷ is neuter, so "in it" means the body (σῶμα), not the soul.

The English says "being a body of a soul, the prior quality of which was corrupted in it. It is raised by the power of God". That ties the corruption to the soul's quality and cuts it off from the raising, so the point is lost: the old quality is removed at the resurrection, not corrupted in the soul. This is a real error of sense, not a style choice. One smaller point: "since it is a natural body" is a gloss. The Greek has only "τυγχάνον ψυχῆς σῶμα" ("being a soul's body"). The gloss is harmless here because the passage is about the ψυχικὸν σῶμα.

The proposed correction is faithful. "Destroyed" is fine; "has perished" would keep the play on φθαρτός/ἄφθαρτος.
verdict.better_correction: since it is the body of a soul. But once the former quality in it has perished, it is raised by the power of God

kept.kind: unmarked lacuna filled with invented text
kept.english_quote: it is unchangeable and unalterable not in the sense of undergoing change—for it became incorruptible through change—but in the sense of enduring into long-lasting life
kept.source_quote: οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν
kept.why: The Greek has a lacuna (**). The English fills it with 'for it became incorruptible through change' without marking the gap, although the work's notes say lacunae are marked [...]. 'Became incorruptible' is not in the source.
kept.corrected_english: it is unchangeable and unalterable not by way of change [...] for such a thing did undergo [change], but by enduring into long-lasting life

verdict.reason: The quotes match the files. Greek (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-mid): "οὕτως ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον εἶναι κατὰ μεταβολὴν ** γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ τῷ διαρκεῖν εἰς μακραίωνα ζωὴν ἤτοι κολαζόμενον ἢ τιμώμενον". The ** marks a gap in the printed text. The likely reading is "[οὐ] κατὰ μεταβολήν· [μεταβολὴν] γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον", meaning "not by way of change, for such a thing underwent change". The English gets this general sense right, and "became incorruptible" fits the previous sentence ("τὸ ἐκ φθαρτοῦ γεγονὸς ἄφθαρτον"). So the meaning is not reversed. Still, the claim holds on two points: (1) the gap is filled silently, including the supplied "not", even though the work's own translator note says "Lacunae marked [...]"; (2) "it became incorruptible through change" is an editorial gloss. The surviving Greek says only "γὰρ ὑπέστη τὸ τοιοῦτον" ("for such a thing underwent [it]"). A careful translator would mark the gap and translate what survives. This is a real but low-severity faithfulness problem, not just style. The proposed fix is faithful but drops "whether being punished or being honored", which belongs in the same sentence, and it reads awkwardly. A cleaner version is suggested below.
verdict.better_correction: In the same way, it is unchangeable and unalterable not by way of change [...]—for such a thing did undergo [change]—but by enduring into long-lasting life, whether being punished or being honored.

kept.english_quote: Paul reasonably says: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: we will all die and sleep, but only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun."
kept.source_quote: εἰκότως φησίν· ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος·
kept.why: Only 'Behold, I tell you a mystery' is Paul's text. 'Only the righteous', 'die and', and 'shining like the sun' (Matt 13:43) are Didymus's gloss, but the quotation marks put them in Paul's mouth as if they were 1 Cor 15:51.
kept.corrected_english: Paul reasonably says, "Behold, I tell you a mystery." That is: we will all die and sleep, but only we the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.

verdict.reason: I checked both files: translations/df1c_u01_rem_source.json and translations/df1c_u01_rem_english.json, section u01-rem-mid. The claim holds. The Greek reads "εἰκότως φησίν· ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω· πάντες μὲν τεθνηξόμενοι κοιμηθησόμεθα, μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι ἀλλαγησόμεθα, ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος". Only "ἰδοὺ μυστήριον ὑμῖν λέγω" is the wording of 1 Cor 15:51. The rest is Didymus's paraphrase, spoken in Paul's "we". "τεθνηξόμενοι", "μόνοι δὲ οἱ δίκαιοι" and "ἐκλάμψαντες ὡς ὁ ἥλιος" (from Matt 13:43) do not appear in any text of 1 Cor 15:51. The paraphrase explains the reading Didymus prefers ("we will all sleep, but not all be changed"). The next sentences, which reject the other reading, confirm this. The English puts the whole sentence in one set of quotation marks after "Paul reasonably says". A reader would therefore take "only the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun" as Paul's own words, which misattributes the gloss to Scripture. The source has no quotation marks, so this is a fault in how the English presents the words, not a defensible word choice. It also drops the first person of "ἀλλαγησόμεθα" ("we will be changed"). The proposed correction is faithful. Its "That is:" is an added signpost, but harmless. The better correction below avoids even that addition and keeps the future participle.
verdict.better_correction: Paul fittingly says, "Behold, I tell you a mystery": all of us, being about to die, will sleep, but only we the righteous will be changed, shining like the sun.

kept.english_quote: Nevertheless, even if the dead rise, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone
kept.source_quote: ὅμως, εἰ καὶ τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα ἀνίσταται, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτον καὶ πνευματικόν· διὸ οὐδὲ πᾶσιν ἐφαίνετο
kept.why: The Greek speaks of 'the body that died' (Christ's body, which is why he did not appear to all). The English drops 'body', switches to 'the dead' in general, and leaves 'it' with no antecedent.
kept.corrected_english: Nevertheless, even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked the Greek in df1c_u01_open_source.json, section u01-open. It reads "ὅμως, εἰ καὶ τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα ἀνίσταται, ἀλλ' ἄφθαρτον καὶ πνευματικόν· διὸ οὐδὲ πᾶσιν ἐφαίνετο ἀλλ' οἷς ἤθελεν", exactly as the claim quotes it. "τὸ τεθνεὸς σῶμα" is a singular neuter noun phrase meaning "the body that died". In context it is Christ's body, and that is why the next clause says "he did not appear to everyone". The English in df1c_u01_open_english.json reads "Nevertheless, even if the dead rise, it rises incorruptible and spiritual." That drops σῶμα and turns the phrase into a plural, general "the dead". "It" is then left with nothing to refer to, and the "For this reason" link to Christ's appearances is lost. This is a real omission with garbled grammar, not a style choice. The proposed fix is faithful: "even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual". Here εἰ καί is concessive, so "even though" is right, and "it rises" fills in the verb implied after ἀλλ'.
verdict.better_correction: Nevertheless, even though the body that died rises, it rises incorruptible and spiritual. For this reason he did not appear to everyone, but to those he willed.

kept.english_quote: For those who deceive you corrupt others along with themselves, thinking that it is destroyed.
kept.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἀπατῶντες ὑμᾶς συμφθείρονται αὐτὴν φθείρεσθαι οἰόμενοι.
kept.why: συμφθείρονται is middle/passive ('perish together'); there is no object 'others'. The passage is about the deceivers thinking the soul perishes together with the body. 'Corrupt others along with themselves' is not in the text.
kept.corrected_english: For those who deceive you think that it perishes, and perishes together [with the body].

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-early, at the 1 Cor 15:33 lemma): "οἱ γὰρ ἀπατῶντες ὑμᾶς συμφθείρονται αὐτὴν φθείρεσθαι οἰόμενοι." συμφθείρονται is middle/passive and takes no object. It means "are corrupted/destroyed together with," not "corrupt others." The English "corrupt others along with themselves" turns it into an active verb and adds the object "others," which the Greek does not have. The claim holds as a real low-severity sense error. The proposed correction is wrong, though. συμφθείρονται is plural, so its subject is οἱ ἀπατῶντες (the deceivers), not αὐτήν (the soul). αὐτήν is only the subject of the infinitive φθείρεσθαι. The correction "think that it perishes, and perishes together [with the body]" makes the soul the one perishing together, misreads the grammar, and adds "[with the body]" on a guess. The Greek leaves the partner of συμ- unstated. Context suggests "with you" (the deceived) or a wordplay: they think the soul perishes, and they perish along with it.
verdict.better_correction: For those who deceive you, thinking that it [the soul] is destroyed, are themselves destroyed along with [you].

kept.english_quote: means that we are some others besides the dead, who, they say, are raised with incorruptible bodies, while their souls are changed
kept.source_quote: ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς, οἵτινες, φησίν, ἄφθαρτοι ἐγειρόμεθα τὰ σώματα, ἀλλασσομενῶν τῶν ψυχῶν
kept.why: ἐγειρόμεθα is first person plural: 'we', not the dead, are raised incorruptible in body with souls changed. The English 'who ... are raised ... their souls' reads as a description of the dead.
kept.corrected_english: means that we, being other than the dead, are, he says, raised with incorruptible bodies, while our souls are changed

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source in df1c_u01_rem_source.json, section u01-rem-mid, reads: "τὸ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα ἀντὶ τοῦ οἷα ἄλλοι τινὲς ὄντες παρὰ τοὺς νεκρούς, οἵτινες, φησίν, ἄφθαρτοι ἐγειρόμεθα τὰ σώματα, ἀλλασσομενῶν τῶν ψυχῶν κατὰ κρείττονα καὶ θειοτέραν ποιότητα ἀλλοιουμενῶν."

1. **Wrong referent.** The relative pronoun οἵτινες goes with the first-person plural verb ἐγειρόμεθα. So the people raised incorruptible in body are "we", the ones "other than the dead". The live English reads "besides the dead, who, they say, are raised with incorruptible bodies, while their souls are changed". Here "who" sits next to "the dead", and "their souls" ties the soul-change to the dead too. That turns the view around: Paul's "we shall be changed" becomes a description of the dead.
2. **Wrong number and wrong possessive.** φησίν is singular ("he says"), not "they say". τῶν ψυχῶν has no "their"; with the first-person verb it should read "our souls" or "the souls".

These are errors of person and referent, not style. The proposed correction is faithful: "means that we, being other than the dead, are, he says, raised with incorruptible bodies, while our souls are changed". Keep the rest of the sentence as it is: "and altered for a better and more divine quality."

The "wrong speaker" charge is overstated. In κατὰ τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς ἐρῶ, κατά takes the accusative, so it means "I will say, following the impious," not "against" them. The paragraph argues that good or evil comes from the free will of the soul, not from the nature of the flesh. The verse that follows sums up the same point with the same word: "οὐ φαύλη κατὰ φύσιν ἡ σάρξ", rendered "the flesh is not evil by nature". The source in eemgal_u01_open_source.json, section u01-open, reads exactly as quoted: "προλαβὼν ἀσφαλίζεται ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν ὅτι θεραπεύει ὑπαγόμενος· ἐπιπλήττει γὰρ νουθετῶν." First, it reads ὑπαγόμενος as a passive ("being manipulated") when the middle is the natural reading: ὑπάγεσθαι means to win someone over, to coax or bring them to one's side. kept.english_quote: For this reason a law able to give life—meaning that if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God, but neither could it have power forever.
kept.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο.
kept.why: 'For this reason a law able to give life—' has no verb and makes no sense. The phrase διὰ τοῦτο ends the preceding 'since' argument ('for this reason [the law was added]'). ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι is the Gal 3:21 lemma, and ἀντὶ τοῦ glosses it as standing for 'if a law had been given'.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the claim. The source and English in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json and eemgal_u01_rem_english.json match the quotes. The Greek reads "διὰ τοῦτο ἐδόθη νόμος ὁ δυνάμενος ζωοποιῆσαι, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰ ἐδόθη νόμος, οὐκ ἐδόθη, φησί, κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ διὰ παντὸς κρατεῖν ἐδύνατο."

The English "For this reason a law able to give life—meaning that..." drops the finite verb ἐδόθη ("was given") and leaves a sentence fragment. It also blurs ἀντὶ τοῦ, which marks a gloss on the Gal 3:21 lemma. This is garbled English, not a style choice.

The proposed correction has two faults:
1. It brackets in "[the law was added]", but ἐδόθη is already in the source. It then reuses ἐδόθη for the lemma, so the source's own verb is never cleanly placed.
2. It ends the gloss at "stands for 'if a law had been given.'" and starts a new sentence. In the Greek, the gloss after ἀντὶ τοῦ is the whole conditional: "if a law was given, it was not given against the promises." Splitting it cuts the "if" clause off from its main clause. The past counterfactual "had been given" also misreads Eusebius's concessive "if (granted) a law was given".
verdict.better_correction: This is why the law was given. "A law able to give life" stands for this: if a law was given, it was not given, he says, against the promises of God; but neither could it prevail for all time.

The source quote matches the locked Greek in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json word for word: "οὐχ ἁπλῶς δὲ παρέμιξε τὸ θῆλυ καὶ τὸ ἄρρεν–ὅσον γὰρ εἷς τῷ ῥήματι ἐζήτει πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον–, ἀλλ' εἰ τὸ ἄρρεν καὶ τὸ θῆλυ διαφέρον εἰς μίαν χάριν συνάγει τὸ βάπτισμα, πόσῳ μᾶλλον Ἕλληνα καὶ Ἰουδαῖον." Paul's point at hand (Gal 3:28) was about Jew and Greek, so adding male and female looks unneeded. Eusebius says Paul did not add it idly (οὐχ ἁπλῶς): it sets up a stronger-case argument (if baptism unites even male and female, how much more Greek and Jew). kept.source_quote: Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελευομένοις
kept.why: ἀνήλισκον means 'were spending' (money or resources), not 'acting'. Gal 6:6-8 is about material support: sowing means giving, which is what the next sentence ('the one who gives ... sows only into the flesh') relies on. 'Eusebius explains that' is framing the translator added; it is not in the source.

verdict.reason:
The claim is correct. I checked the passage in eemgal_u01_rem_source.json and eemgal_u01_rem_english.json in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/eusebius-emesa-fragmenta-galatas/translations/, section u01-rem-close. The Greek is quoted correctly: "Ἐδήλωσεν ἐκ τούτου ὅτι πολλοὶ ἀκαίρως μὲν ἀνήλισκον, παρέχοντες τοῖς τηρεῖν νόμον παρακελευομένοις, τοῖς δὲ τὴν Παύλου διδασκαλίαν κηρύττουσιν οὐδὲν παρεῖχον."

1. ἀνήλισκον means "were spending" or "were using up" money or resources. It does not mean "were acting". Translating it as "acting" hides the money point that the rest of the paragraph depends on. The next clause says they gave nothing (οὐδὲν παρεῖχον) to Paul's preachers. The closing sentence says that whoever gives (παρέχων) to such a teacher "sows only into the flesh". So the error changes the meaning.
2. "Eusebius explains that" is not in the Greek. The subject of Ἐδήλωσεν is Paul, the author of the verse under comment. The added phrase is the translator's own commentary. It also makes Eusebius sound like a third party describing himself, which is odd inside his own commentary.
3. "At the wrong time" is a defensible literal reading of ἀκαίρως. "Unwisely" or "to no good purpose" fits the context better, but this part is a matter of word choice.

The proposed correction is faithful. Naming Paul as the subject would make it slightly clearer.
verdict.better_correction: Paul made clear from this that many were spending unwisely, supplying those who urged them to keep the law, but giving nothing to those who preached Paul's teaching.

kept.english_quote: What then is the blessedness? It belongs to no one.
kept.source_quote: Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς.
kept.why: ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς is a commentator's gloss meaning that the question stands for 'none': your blessedness has come to nothing. 'It belongs to no one' changes the point.
kept.corrected_english: What then is the blessedness? That is, there is none.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (eemgal_u01_rem_source.json, u01-rem-mid): "Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς. ἢ οὕτως· τὸ τηρεῖν νόμον ἢ τὸ πίστει ζῆν;" "ἀντὶ τοῦ" is the usual scholiast's formula for "this stands for" or "that is." The masculine "οὐδείς" agrees with "μακαρισμός," so it means "no blessedness" or "none," and the question is rhetorical (compare Gal 4:15, "where then is your blessedness?"). The live English reads "It belongs to no one," which treats οὐδείς as a person who might own the blessedness. Nothing in the Greek supports that, and it changes Eusebius's point from "your boasted blessedness has come to nothing" to a claim about who owns it. This is a real, minor wrong-sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed fix, "What then is the blessedness? That is, there is none.", is faithful and fits what follows, where "ἢ οὕτως" ("or [read it] this way") brings in a second reading: is it keeping the law or living by faith? It would also be acceptable to make "Or rather:" into "Or else, read it this way:", but that is optional.

kept.english_quote: The question is raised why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin.
kept.source_quote: Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
kept.why: ἀποσπῶν is an active participle with Paul as subject: Paul draws them away from the law. It does not say the law 'is removed'. 'Still' is added and suggests a contrast the source does not make. The answer that follows ('whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin') assumes the plain sense.
kept.corrected_english: The question is raised why, in drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source quote matches eemgal_u01_rem_source.json section u01-rem-close exactly: "Ζητεῖται διὰ τί νόμου ἀποσπῶν μέμνηται τῆς ἁμαρτίας." ἀποσπῶν is a present active masculine nominative participle that agrees with the subject of μέμνηται, which is Paul. So the Greek says "while drawing [them] away from the law, he mentions sin." The live English reads "why, when the law is removed, he still mentions sin." That turns Paul's own action into an impersonal passive ("the law is removed"), as if the law were already gone. It also adds "still", which sets up a contrast the Greek does not make. The answer that follows ("ὅτε νόμου ἦν μνήμη, μέμνηται καὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας", "whenever the law is mentioned, he also mentions sin") supports the plain sense. Severity is low but the error is real, not a style choice.

The proposed fix, "The question is raised why, in drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin", is faithful. "Them" stands in for the object the Greek leaves unstated, which is acceptable. "While drawing his readers away from the law" would work equally well.

verdict.better_correction: The question is raised why, while drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin.

kept.english_quote: It is because the law commanded eating, and through this desire is provoked

kept.why: τρυφᾶν means to feast or live in plenty, not simply to eat. The argument depends on indulgence stirring up desire, and the translation itself later renders τρυφᾶν as 'feasting'.
kept.corrected_english: It is because the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I could not refute it. The source in translations/eemgal_u01_rem_source.json reads exactly as quoted: "ἐπειδὴ τρυφᾶν ἐκέλευεν ὁ νόμος, διὰ δὲ τούτου διερεθίζεται ἡ ἐπιθυμία". τρυφᾶν means to live in plenty or to feast. It does not mean plain eating. The passage itself keeps the two words apart. A few lines later it asks "διὰ τί δὲ συνεχωρήθη τὸ τρυφᾶν καὶ ἐσθίειν;", which the English renders as "why was feasting and eating permitted?". It also says "ἀδύνατον τρυφῶντας κρατεῖν ἡδονῶν", rendered "those who feast". So the English gives τρυφᾶν as "feasting" everywhere except here, where it becomes "eating". That breaks the argument, because indulgence is what "provokes desire" and makes it "uncontrollable". Plain eating does not carry that sense, so this is a small but real weakening of the meaning and not a choice of style. The proposed fix, "It is because the law commanded feasting, and through this desire is provoked", is faithful. It also matches how the rest of the passage renders τρυφᾶν. Severity "low" is fair.

kept.english_quote: Do not be afraid to kill the offspring of snakes, and do not torment the thoughts of their hearts.
kept.source_quote: 59 Κτείνειν γεννήματα ὀφέων μὴ φείσῃ, καὶ μὴ ὠδίνῃς λογισμοὺς καρδίας αὐτῶν.
kept.why: ὠδίνω means to be in labor with or give birth to. Evagrius warns the monk not to conceive and bring forth the snakes' heart-thoughts. 'Torment' turns this into hurting the thoughts, which is the wrong sense. Also μὴ φείσῃ means 'do not spare / do not hold back', not 'do not be afraid'.
kept.corrected_english: Do not spare the offspring of snakes; kill them, and do not go into labor with the thoughts of their hearts.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in esm_u01_rem_source.json (u01-rem-early) reads "59 Κτείνειν γεννήματα ὀφέων μὴ φείσῃ, 59 καὶ μὴ ὠδίνῃς λογισμοὺς καρδίας αὐτῶν." The second "59" is a stray extraction mark. The live English says "Do not be afraid to kill the offspring of snakes, and do not torment the thoughts of their hearts." Two problems: (1) With an accusative object, ὠδίνω means "to be in labor with" or "to bring forth with pain" (compare Ps 7:15 LXX ὠδίνησεν ἀδικίαν and Isa 59:5). Evagrius means "do not conceive and nurse their thoughts." "Torment the thoughts" makes the monk hurt the thoughts, which is the opposite of the warning, so this is a real wrong sense. (2) μὴ φείσῃ + infinitive means "do not refrain or hold back from killing." "Do not be afraid" brings in fear, which the source does not have. That is a smaller drift, but it is still not in the Greek. The proposed fix is faithful in meaning. Its "Do not spare the offspring...; kill them" reorders the clause but loses nothing. A closer version follows the Greek order.
verdict.better_correction: Do not hold back from killing the offspring of snakes, and do not go into labor with the thoughts of their hearts.

A careful translator would use 'principles' or 'reasons' throughout this cluster. Elsewhere, 'words of God' and 'words of the father' are correct.

He will show you the principles of the ages / The principles of providence are dark / will recognize the principles of bodiless beings / the principles of providence and judgment lift it up.

The source matches the quotes. ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/evagrius-sententiae-monachos/translations/esm_u01_rem_source.json reads: 110 "θεωρία αὐτῆς ὑπὲρ λόγους πάντων τῶν αἰώνων"; 116 "γνώσῃ λόγους ἀσωμάτων ... δείξει σοι λόγους αἰώνων"; 132 "Λόγοι προνοίας σκοτεινοὶ"; 133 "λόγους δὲ ἀσωμάτων ἐπιγνώσεται μοναχὸς πραΰς"; 135 "λόγοι δὲ προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως ὑψοῦσιν αὐτήν". In these sayings λόγοι is Evagrius's technical term for the inner reasons or principles. The surrounding words show it. The λόγοι stand next to θεωρία (110) and κρίσεως θεωρίαι (132). Saying 135 pairs them with κόσμων θεωρίαι. They are objects of contemplative knowledge, things the monk "knows" or "recognizes" (γνώσῃ, ἐπιγνώσεται). They are not speech. The standard English translations agree: Driscoll uses "reasons" ("reasons of providence," "reasons of the incorporeals," "reasons of the aeons") and Sinkewicz uses "principles." I cite both from memory and did not check them here. "Words of providence" and "words of bodiless beings" mislead the reader into thinking providence or angels speak. That is a wrong sense, not a style choice.

The proposed fix is faithful. "Principles" (or "reasons") throughout 110, 116, 132, 133 and 135 is right. It reads naturally in 110: "contemplation of it is better than the principles of all the ages." Keep "words" in 108 (λόγους θεοῦ, which a wise man searches out and a fool mocks), in 125 (λόγοι αἱρετικῶν) and in 126 (σκοτεινοὺς λόγους αὐτῶν, the heretics' speech). In those places λόγοι means real speech or doctrine.

kept.english_quote: If someone entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, give it back.
kept.source_quote: ἐὰν πιστεύσῃ σοι ἀργύριον, οὐ διασκορπιεῖς αὐτό, καὶ κἂν ἐπεργάσῃ, ἀποδώσεις αὐτό.
kept.why: This is the end of saying 73. The unstated subject of πιστεύσῃ is the spiritual father from the previous sentence ('Listen, monk, to the words of your father... Whenever he sends you'). Because the section split cuts the saying, 'someone' loses that link. As a result, the duty reads as a general one rather than a duty to one's father.
kept.corrected_english: If he entrusts silver to you, you will not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, you will give it back.

verdict.reason: The claim holds; it is a minor error. In esm_u01_rem_source.json, saying 73 runs across two sections. u01-rem-early ends with "73 Ἄκουε, μοναχέ, λόγους πατρός σου ... Ἡνίκα ἂν ἀποστείλῃ σε ... οὐκ ἰσχύσουσι κατά σου." u01-rem-mid then opens with "ἐὰν πιστεύσῃ σοι ἀργύριον, οὐ διασκορπιεῖς αὐτό, καὶ κἂν ἐπεργάσῃ, ἀποδώσεις αὐτό." No verse number comes before "ἐὰν", so this is the end of 73. The third-person singular πιστεύσῃ has no stated subject, so it carries over from the 'he' of the sentence before (ἀποστείλῃ, the father). The English "If someone entrusts silver to you" turns a duty owed to one's spiritual father into a general rule about deposits. The section split makes this worse: the line now opens a new section with no father in sight. The rest of the English holds up. ἐπεργάσῃ is the second-person aorist subjunctive of the deponent verb ἐπεργάζομαι, so "even if you put it to work" is right. The future indicatives οὐ διασκορπιεῖς and ἀποδώσεις can stand as commands ("do not scatter", "give it back"), so the future-tense wording in the proposed fix is fine but not required. The fix is faithful. Because the line stands alone at the head of the section, naming the father may read more clearly than a bare "he".
verdict.better_correction: If he (your father) entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it; and even if you put it to work, give it back. (Or, without the parenthesis: "If your father entrusts silver to you, do not scatter it, and even if you put it to work, give it back.")

kept.english_quote: A prudent monk will have freedom from passions, but a foolish one will pour out evils.
kept.source_quote: 105 Μοναχὸς φρόνιμος ἀπαθὴς ἔσται, ὁ δὲ ἄφρων ἐξαντλήσει κακά.
kept.why: ἐξαντλέω means to drain to the dregs, or to endure to the end. The foolish monk will drain a cup of evils, which means he will suffer them. 'Pour out evils' turns the fool into someone who spreads evil.
kept.corrected_english: A prudent monk will be free from passions, but a foolish one will drain evils to the dregs.

verdict.reason:
I checked both quotes in the files and they match exactly. The Greek is in esm_u01_rem_source.json: "105 Μοναχὸς φρόνιμος ἀπαθὴς ἔσται, ὁ δὲ ἄφρων ἐξαντλήσει κακά." The English is in esm_u01_rem_english.json: "...but a foolish one will pour out evils."

ἐξαντλέω does not mean "pour out" in the sense of giving off or spreading. Its literal meaning is to draw out or bail out completely, so to drain. Its figurative meaning is to exhaust, or to endure to the end, as with toils or a life. The line also seems to echo Proverbs 9:12 LXX: "ἐὰν δὲ κακὸς ἀποβῇς, μόνος ἀντλήσεις κακά", which Brenton gives as "thou alone shalt bear evil." There, drawing evils means suffering them.

The pairing in the sentence points the same way. The prudent monk ends up free of passions, and the fool ends up draining his own evils. "Pour out evils" makes the fool someone who does or spreads evil, which is the wrong sense. The error is real but low severity.

The proposed correction is faithful. "To the dregs" is a fair rendering of the ἐκ- prefix ("completely"). A plainer option is "will drain the cup of evils."
verdict.better_correction: A prudent monk will be free from passions, but a foolish one will drain evils to the dregs. (Alternative: "...but the fool will drain the cup of evils.")

kept.english_quote: do not leave your house and do not turn aside at a time when it is again profitable.
kept.source_quote: οἶκόν σου μὴ ἀφῇς καὶ μὴ ἐκκλίνῃς ἐν καιρῷ πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ.
kept.why: The English does not make sense. The locked Greek is corrupt at this point: 'πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ' is very likely a scribal error for 'πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς', meaning 'the profitable struggle'. That reading fits the image of whitening silver that follows. The English renders the corrupt words literally and produces nonsense. It should translate the evident sense, or mark a lacuna or emendation.
kept.corrected_english: do not leave your house, and do not turn aside at that time from the profitable struggle [text uncertain].

verdict.reason: The quotes are exact. The locked source (esm_u01_rem_source.json, and sources/sententiae_ad_monachos_pg.txt line 96) reads "μὴ ἐκκλίνῃς ἐν καιρῷ πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ". As written, that Greek does not parse cleanly: it has no relative pronoun, and "πάλιν" ("again") has nothing to refer back to. The English "do not turn aside at a time when it is again profitable" follows the corrupt words literally. It also misses the point of sentence 55, which is to stay put and endure listlessness the way silver is polished bright. The obvious repair is πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς, "of the profitable struggle". It changes only a few letters, and it is the sense modern English versions of Ad Monachos give ("do not turn aside in the time of profitable struggle", my recollection of Driscoll's version, which follows Gressmann's edition). So this is a real sense error, not a style preference. One caveat: I could not confirm Gressmann's reading online today; one web search for the phrase found nothing. Treat the emendation as highly probable, not proven. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly better one names the change rather than only flagging uncertainty.
verdict.better_correction: If a spirit of listlessness comes upon you, do not leave your house, and do not turn aside from the profitable struggle at that time. For as one whitens silver, so your heart will be made bright. [Translator note: the PG/Khazarzar text reads πάλιν ἐπωφελεῖ, which does not make sense here; translated as πάλης ἐπωφελοῦς, "the profitable struggle", the reading of Gressmann's critical edition.]

kept.english_quote: Do not let wine gladden you, and do not let meat delight you, so that you do not nourish the flesh of your body, and shameful thoughts will not cease from you.
kept.source_quote: 38 Μὴ εὐφραινέτω σε οἶνος καὶ μὴ τερπέτω σε κρέας, ἵνα μὴ διαθρέψῃς σάρκας σώματός σου, καὶ λογισμοὶ αἰσχροὶ οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν ἀπό σου.
kept.why: The final clause belongs inside the 'lest' clause: lest you fatten the flesh and then shameful thoughts never leave you. The English reads as though abstaining causes shameful thoughts not to cease, which is the opposite of the meaning.
kept.corrected_english: Do not let wine gladden you or meat delight you, lest you fatten the flesh of your body and shameful thoughts never leave you.

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote exactly (esm_u01_open_source.json lines 72-73: "ἵνα μὴ διαθρέψῃς σάρκας σώματός σου, καὶ λογισμοὶ αἰσχροὶ οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν ἀπό σου"). The καί clause goes with the negative purpose clause ἵνα μή. The future indicative is normal in Koine ἵνα clauses. The sense is "lest you fatten your flesh and shameful thoughts never leave you." The live English (esm_u01_open_english.json line 45) reads "so that you do not nourish the flesh of your body, and shameful thoughts will not cease from you." Read as a free-standing clause, it says shameful thoughts will stay. Read as part of the "so that" clause, it says the purpose of abstaining is that shameful thoughts will not cease. Both readings miss or reverse the point, which is that indulging keeps the thoughts with you. This is a real meaning problem, not a style preference, and low severity fits. The proposed fix keeps the clause under "lest" and keeps the Greek's sense. "Fatten" is a fair rendering of διαθρέψῃς, though "nourish" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: Do not let wine gladden you, and do not let meat delight you, lest you fatten the flesh of your body and shameful thoughts never leave you.

kept.english_quote: Heirs of God, listen to the words of God.
kept.source_quote: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ συνοδίαις μοναχούς.
kept.why: The source's own heading, 'To the monks in coenobia or communities', is left out of the English. The English title is a generic summary. The heading defines the audience the sayings address, which is not hermits.
kept.corrected_english: To the monks who live in monasteries or communities. Heirs of God, listen to the words of God.

verdict.better_correction: Insert the superscription as its own first paragraph, separate from saying 1: "To the monks who live in monasteries or in communities." Then leave saying 1 unchanged as the next paragraph: "Heirs of God, listen to the words of God. Co-heirs of Christ, receive the sayings of Christ, ..."
verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source for u01-open (translations/esm_u01_open_source.json) has, after the edition label "Sententiae ad monachos", the transmitted superscription "Πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ συνοδίαις μοναχούς." The English (esm_u01_open_english.json) starts straight at saying 1, "Heirs of God, listen to the words of God." Nothing in the English carries that line. The section title ("Opening exhortation and first sayings...") is editorial, and the book title "Sentences to Monks" drops the audience: monks in coenobia or communities, not hermits. Every numbered saying is rendered, so the superscription is the only gap. Severity low is right. It is real source text that names the intended readers, not just a style choice. The proposed wording is faithful (κοινόβια = monasteries, συνοδίαι = communities or brotherhoods of monks). But merging it into the same sentence as saying 1 turns a heading into part of the exhortation. It should stand as its own heading line before saying 1. The edition label "Sententiae ad monachos" is not text that needs translating.

kept.english_quote: But he cast out of the commonwealth the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets said, he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets,
kept.source_quote: Ὁ δὲ δαίμονας μὲν τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας ὰ ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταί, ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς, παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε
kept.why: Socrates expelled Homer and the poets from the state (Plato's Republic) and taught men to reject the wicked demons. The English swaps the objects: it has him expel the demons from the commonwealth and teach people to reject Homer.
kept.corrected_english: But he expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, and taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of,

verdict.reason: I checked translations/jsa_source.json, section 10. The Greek matches the quote: "Ὁ δὲ δαίμονας μὲν τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας ὰ ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταί, ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς, παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε". The participle phrase "ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς" means "having cast out of the state both Homer and the other poets"; the "καὶ ... καὶ" pair makes Homer and the poets its object. The accusatives "δαίμονας ... τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας" belong with "παραιτεῖσθαι ... ἐδίδαξε" ("he taught men to reject"). The μὲν goes with the "δὲ" in the next clause ("πρὸς θεοῦ δὲ ... προὐτρέπετο"): reject the demons, but seek God. This matches Plato's Republic, where the poets are expelled, and the standard ANF reading: "he cast out from the state both Homer and the rest of the poets, and taught men to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things which the poets related." The live English ("he cast out of the commonwealth the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets said, he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets") swaps the two objects. That is a real error of sense, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly closer version that keeps the participle and the μὲν/δὲ contrast: "But he, having expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of, and urged them..."
verdict.better_correction: But he, having expelled Homer and the other poets from the commonwealth, taught people to reject the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets told of, and he urged them to gain knowledge of the God who was unknown to them through the search of the Word,

kept.english_quote: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself and to his sons, to the brothers of those sons, and to their children, such as the gods Poseidon and Pluto.
kept.source_quote: εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ γενομένους υἱοὺς καὶ τῶν λεχθέντων ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν καὶ τέκνων ὁμοίως τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων, Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος, ἀνήνεγκαν
kept.why: Poseidon and Pluto are the ones 'called HIS brothers' (ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν), and the children are theirs. The English makes them brothers of the sons or their children, and adds 'such as the gods'.
kept.corrected_english: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds, and the source in jsa_source.json §4 matches the quote exactly. The Greek reads: εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν καὶ τοὺς ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ γενομένους υἱοὺς καὶ τῶν λεχθέντων ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν καὶ τέκνων ὁμοίως τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων, Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος. In ἐκείνου ἀδελφῶν, the pronoun ἐκείνου is singular and refers back to θεόν: these are the brothers of God himself, meaning Zeus in the poets' story. Ποσειδῶνος καὶ Πλούτωνος stands in apposition to those brothers. The τέκνων τῶν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων are the brothers' children. Myth confirms this reading: Poseidon and Pluto are the brothers of Zeus, not his sons' brothers or anyone's children.

The live English, "to the brothers of those sons, and to their children, such as the gods Poseidon and Pluto", has three errors:
1. It makes the brothers belong to the sons.
2. It makes Poseidon and Pluto examples of the children.
3. It adds "such as the gods", which is not in the Greek.

It also drops two hedges. ὡς ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ σπορᾷ means "reputed to be born from his seed", and λεχθέντων means "so-called". Both show Justin is reporting the poets' claims, not making them himself. This is a real error in who is identified, not a style preference.

The proposed correction is faithful. It would be better still if it kept the ὡς hedge, for example: "attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those supposedly born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children."
verdict.better_correction: attributed the deeds they wrote about to God himself, to those supposedly born as sons from his seed, and to those called his brothers, Poseidon and Pluto, and likewise to their children.

kept.english_quote: This is also why God continues to delay the destruction and dissolution of the whole world, so that the wicked angels, demons, and human beings may no longer exist.
kept.source_quote: ἐπιμένει ὁ θεὸς τὴν σύγχυσιν καὶ κατάλυσιν τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου μὴ ποιῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ οἱ φαῦλοι ἄγγελοι καὶ δαίμονες καὶ ἄνθρωποι μηκέτι ὦσι
kept.why: The ἵνα clause describes what the destruction would do (end the wicked); the English makes it the purpose of God's delay, which reverses the logic: the delay keeps the wicked in being.
kept.corrected_english: This is also why God delays bringing about the confusion and dissolution of the whole world, by which the wicked angels, demons, and human beings would cease to exist.

verdict.reason: I checked jsa_source.json and jsa_english.json for section 6, and both quotes match the files exactly. In the Greek, ἐπιμένει ὁ θεὸς ... μὴ ποιῆσαι means "God holds back from bringing about the confusion and dissolution." The ἵνα clause (ἵνα ... μηκέτι ὦσι) belongs to that dissolution: it is what the world's end would do, which is make the wicked cease to exist. It is not God's purpose in waiting. The next clause, διὰ τὸ σπέρμα τῶν Χριστιανῶν, gives the actual reason for the delay. The ANF reads the passage the same way: "delays causing the confusion and destruction of the whole world, by which the wicked angels and demons and men shall cease to exist, because of the seed of the Christians." The current English says God delays "so that the wicked angels, demons, and human beings may no longer exist." Any reader takes that as the purpose of the delay, which reverses Justin's logic. The rest of the paragraph shows the delay is what lets the wicked go on acting ("it would no longer be possible for you to do these things"). This is a real sense error, not a style choice. The proposed fix ("delays bringing about the confusion and dissolution of the whole world, by which the wicked angels, demons, and human beings would cease to exist") is faithful and matches the ANF. The following sentence, "He delays because of the seed of the Christians...", can stay as it is.

kept.english_quote: or if he does know, but does not dare to speak because of his hearers, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher
kept.source_quote: ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος
kept.why: Drops 'like Socrates' (ὁμοίως Σωκράτει), the point of the comparison that sets up the Socratic saying in the next clause.
kept.corrected_english: or if he does know, but does not dare, because of his hearers, to speak as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher

verdict.reason: I checked section 8 of jsa_source.json, and the claim holds. The source reads "ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος ἀλλὰ φιλόδοξος ἀνὴρ δείκνυται". The source spells it "Σωρκάτει", a typo for Σωκράτει. The live English says "or if he does know, but does not dare to speak because of his hearers, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher". It leaves out ὁμοίως Σωκράτει ("like Socrates") completely. That phrase is not filler. Socrates spoke the truth whatever his audience thought, and this is the contrast that sets up the "Socratic saying" quoted in the next clause. Without it, the later reference to Socrates has nothing to point back to. Standard translations keep the phrase; Dods has "does not dare to speak out, like Socrates". So this is a real omission, not a matter of style. The proposed fix is faithful. It reads "or if he does know, but does not dare, because of his hearers, to speak as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher". It is a little clumsy, so the alternative in better_correction may read more smoothly. Separately, the typo "Σωρκάτει" in the locked source text could be fixed as well.
verdict.better_correction: or if he does know, but because of his hearers does not dare to speak out as Socrates did, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher

kept.english_quote: he confessed that he was a Christian.
kept.source_quote: τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν
kept.why: The Greek says he confessed 'the school of divine virtue'; the English replaces Justin's phrase with a flat repeat of the earlier question.
kept.corrected_english: he confessed the school of divine virtue.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute it. The locked Greek source (jsa_source.json, section 2) reads: "Καὶ πάλιν, τὰ καλὰ ἑαυτῷ συνεπιστάμενος διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδαχήν, τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν." The object of ὡμολόγησεν is "τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς", meaning "the school (or teaching) of divine virtue". The certified English (jsa_english.json, section 2, paragraph 5) instead says "he confessed that he was a Christian." That repeats the wording of the question two sentences earlier ("εἰ εἴη Χριστιανός") and drops Justin's own description of the Christian faith. The overall sense survives, since he still confesses his faith, so the severity is low. But a careful translator would put back Justin's phrase, which is the point of "καὶ πάλιν". Standard translations keep it; ANF/Dods has "he confessed his discipleship in divine virtue". The proposed "he confessed the school of divine virtue" follows the Greek closely and is acceptable. "He confessed himself of the school of divine virtue" would read more naturally.
verdict.better_correction: he confessed himself of the school of divine virtue.

kept.english_quote: We have also learned that he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him,
kept.source_quote: χαίρειν τε τοῖς τὰ προσόντα αὐτῷ μιμουμένοις προέφημεν
kept.why: προέφημεν means 'we said before', a cross-reference to Justin's earlier statement, not 'we have learned'.
kept.corrected_english: And, as we said before, he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him,

verdict.reason: Checked jsa_source.json §3. The locked source has the misspelling 'φροέφημεν' for προέφημεν, which is the standard reading of 2 Apol. 4 (Otto/Migne; ANF has 'And we have before stated that He takes pleasure in those who imitate His properties'). προέφημεν is aorist of πρόφημι, 'we said before'. It is not 'we have learned'. It points back to Justin's earlier statement (1 Apol. 10). It also governs both infinitives, χαίρειν and ἀπαρέσκεσθαι, so the whole sentence is reported earlier speech. The live English, 'We have also learned that he rejoices...', turns Justin's back-reference into a second taught doctrine that copies the δεδιδάγμεθα of the sentence before. That is a real wrong-sense error, though a minor one. The proposed fix, 'And, as we said before, he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him, and is displeased with those who embrace what is base, whether in word or in deed', is faithful. One detail: the source's spelling differs slightly from the quote in the claim (φροέφημεν against προέφημεν). This is an OCR typo in the source file and does not change the meaning.
verdict.better_correction: And we said before that he rejoices in those who imitate the things that belong to him, and is displeased with those who embrace what is base, whether in word or in deed.

kept.english_quote: and that they were spreading lies about these teachings. So I laughed at that covering and at the opinion held by the many.
kept.source_quote: καὶ ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ περιβλήματος κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης
kept.why: ψευδολογουμένων is the first of three genitive objects of κατεγέλασα: Justin laughed at the liars, the disguise, and popular opinion. The English moves it into what he 'learned' and drops the liars as something he laughed at.
kept.corrected_english: So I laughed at those who told these lies, at the covering itself, and at the opinion held by the many.

verdict.reason:
I checked jsa_source.json and jsa_english.json for section 13. The source quote is exact: "μαθὼν περίβλημα πονηρὸν ... περιτεθειμένον ... τοῖς Χριστιανῶν θείοις διδάγμασι, καὶ ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ περιβλήματος κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης."

The claim stands. The repeated καὶ ... καὶ ... καὶ links three genitives that all depend on κατεγέλασα: ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα ("those telling lies about these things"), τοῦ περιβλήματος and τῆς ... δόξης. The participle cannot hang on μαθὼν, because μαθὼν takes the accusative περίβλημα ... περιτεθειμένον. So "and that they were spreading lies about these teachings", which makes the lying part of what Justin learned, misreads the syntax and drops the liars as a target of his laughter. The standard translations agree. Dods has "laughed both at those who framed these falsehoods, and at the disguise itself, and at popular opinion", and Falls and Barnard read it the same way.

It is a minor error: the lying is still mentioned, just in the wrong role. But a careful translator would fix it.

The proposed fix only rewrites the second sentence. It leaves the clause "and that they were spreading lies about these teachings" in the first sentence, so the lying would appear twice. "Those who told these lies" also has nothing to refer back to once that clause is gone.
verdict.better_correction: I too once learned that wicked demons had wrapped an evil covering around the divine teachings of Christians to turn other people away. So I laughed at those who spread lies about these teachings, at the covering itself, and at the opinion held by the many.

kept.english_quote: since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human reason.
kept.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη
kept.why: Drops τὰ σκεύη ('the vessels/instruments'): Christ is not the instrument of human reason. The English blurs it into 'power ... of human reason'.
kept.corrected_english: since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not the instrument of human reason.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source quote is exact. Section 10 of jsa_source.json ends with "ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη." The English in jsa_english.json ends with "since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human reason." That leaves τὰ σκεύη untranslated.

The English keeps the contrast between divine origin and human reason, so the sense is not reversed and the error is low severity. It is still a real omission. Justin is not saying Christ's power is "not of human reason" in a loose sense. He says Christ is not the vessel or instrument (σκεύη) of human reason. That ties back to the Socrates contrast: what philosophers worked out with human tools is set against the power of the Father.

The passage is a known textual crux, and some editors emend the text to κατασκευή ("a construct of human reason"). Rauschen's text, which is the copy text here, reads τὰ σκεύη. The standard English rendering (ANF/Dods) is "not the mere instrument of human reason."

The proposed correction, "and not the instrument of human reason," is faithful. The singular "instrument" for the plural σκεύη is fine, since the subject is Christ ("he is"). An optional, slightly more literal version would be "and not a vessel of human reason."

kept.english_quote: These were things the demons themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.
kept.source_quote: ὧν ἐνδεεῖς γεγόνασι μετὰ τὸ πάθεσιν ἐπιθυμιῶν δουλωθῆναι
kept.why: The subject running through the sentence is the fallen angels (οἱ δ᾿ ἄγγελοι ... ἐδούλωσαν), the ones who were enslaved to lust. Naming 'the demons' as the subject is an addition that shifts the referent.
kept.corrected_english: These were things they themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute the claim. I read section 4 of jsa_source.json against jsa_english.json. In the Greek, the subject running through the sentence is "Οἱ δ᾿ ἄγγελοι" (the angels). The main verb "ἐδούλωσαν" (they enslaved) continues that subject, and so does the relative clause "ὧν ἐνδεεῖς γεγόνασι μετὰ τὸ πάθεσιν ἐπιθυμιῶν δουλωθῆναι". The word "demons" appears only in the earlier side clause "οἵ εἰσιν οἱ λεγόμενοι δαίμονες". The text supports the angels as the ones "enslaved to the passions of their desires": they are the ones just described as "γυναικῶν μίξεσιν ἡττήθησαν" (overcome by intercourse with women). The English "These were things the demons themselves came to need" adds a noun that isn't in the Greek and switches the subject from the angels to their offspring. The Greek has no word for "themselves" either. A reader could argue that Justin elsewhere treats angels and demons together, and the next sentence says "τοὺς ἀγγέλους καὶ τοὺς ἐξ αὐτῶν γεννηθέντας δαίμονας". That makes the Greek's "they" open to reading as both, but it doesn't justify narrowing it to "the demons" alone. Severity low is right. The proposed fix, "These were things they themselves came to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires", is faithful because it restores the unnamed "they". Its "themselves" is a harmless addition; the better_correction field drops it to match the Greek more closely.
verdict.better_correction: These were things they had come to need once they had been enslaved to the passions of their desires.

kept.english_quote: When her own people entreated her to remain still,
kept.source_quote: ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων
kept.why: 'remain still' reads as 'keep quiet'. ἔτι προσμένειν means 'stay on a while longer' in the marriage.
kept.corrected_english: When her own people urged her to stay with him a while longer,

verdict.reason:
The claim holds; I read both files. The source in jsa_source.json §2 matches the quote: "Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων, ὡς εἰς ἐλπίδα μεταβολῆς ἥξοντός ποτε τοῦ ἀνδρός, βιαζομένη ἑαυτὴν ἐπέμενεν." In jsa_english.json §2, paragraph 2, ἔτι προσμένειν is rendered "to remain still". In this Greek, ἔτι means "still / yet longer" and goes with προσμένειν, "stay on" (in the marriage). Here, though, "still" falls after "remain", so most readers will take it as "keep still / stay quiet". That is a different sense, and it hides the point that she stayed in the marriage. The ANF has "advised her still to continue with him". This is a real if minor wording fault, not a style preference: the English invites the wrong meaning. Severity: low.

The proposed correction is faithful. "Urged" fits ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο, which means she was moved by their pleas. "With him" is implied by the context. It also fits the rest of the sentence: "...stay with him a while longer, advising her in the hope that her husband would one day come to a change, she forced herself and remained." The participle "advising" repeats "urged" slightly but stays faithful. A tighter option: "When her own people prevailed on her, advising her to stay on with him still, in the hope that her husband would one day change, she forced herself and remained."
verdict.better_correction: When her own people prevailed on her, advising her to stay on with him still, in the hope that her husband would one day come to a change, she forced herself and remained.

kept.english_quote: Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds.
kept.source_quote: omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat.
kept.why: 'omnem disciplinam' is the object. Feeding (the full belly) kills or wounds all discipline. The English makes discipline the subject that kills, which reverses Tertullian's argument for fasting.
kept.corrected_english: Feeding either kills or wounds every discipline.

verdict.reason: I could not refute it; the claim holds. The Latin in tof_source.json §6 is exactly "omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat." "omnem disciplinam" is accusative, so it can only be the object. The subject has to be "uictus" (nominative: food/diet). The English "Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds" reads "uictus" as a genitive and makes "discipline" the subject. The accusative case rules that out. It also breaks the logic of the passage. The sentence before it says nobody remembers God when the man "slips away from himself" through fullness. The sentence after it says the Lord blames forgetting him on "plenitudini" (fullness). So food is what kills or wounds discipline. Thelwall's ANF rendering agrees: "Every discipline food either slays or else wounds." The proposed fix "Feeding either kills or wounds every discipline" is faithful. "Food" is a slightly closer match for "uictus" than "Feeding". Files: /Users/stephansmac/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-fasting/translations/tof_source.json and tof_english.json, section 6.
verdict.better_correction: Food either kills or wounds every discipline.

kept.english_quote: there the pressure on drink should also be understood as establishing the pattern for food.
kept.source_quote: illic intellegatur etiam pabuli pressura formam praestruens potui.
kept.why: 'pabuli pressura' (restriction of food) sets the pattern 'potui' (for drink). The English swaps food and drink.
kept.corrected_english: there a restriction of food should also be understood, setting the pattern for the drink.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. tof_source.json §9 reads: "quamquam ubi abstinentia uini aut a deo exigitur aut ab homine uouetur, illic intellegatur etiam pabuli pressura formam praestruens potui. qualis enim esus, talis et potus."

The grammar settles it:
- "pabuli pressura" (restriction of food, literally fodder) is the nominative subject of "intellegatur".
- "praestruens" agrees with "pressura".
- "potui" is a dative: for the drink.

So the Latin says that where wine is given up, a restriction of food is also implied, and it sets the pattern for the drink. The next sentence ("as the eating is, so is the drinking") backs this up: the argument goes from drink to food. The live English reads "there the pressure on drink should also be understood as establishing the pattern for food." That swaps food and drink and breaks the argument. It is a reversed sense, not a style choice. ANF (Thelwall) also renders it as a restriction of food that gives the pattern for drink.

The proposed correction is faithful. A small option: "praestruens" can also be read as "laying the groundwork for" the drink, but "setting the pattern for" is fine.
verdict.better_correction: there a restriction of food should also be understood, setting the pattern for the drink.

kept.english_quote: magistrates put on their purple
kept.source_quote: magistratus purpuras ponunt
kept.why: 'ponunt' here means 'lay aside', a sign of mourning, which fits the next clause about turning the fasces backward. 'Put on' says the opposite.
kept.corrected_english: magistrates lay aside their purple

verdict.reason: I checked the source and it matches the quote: tof_source.json §16 has "nudipedalia denuntiantur, magistratus purpuras ponunt, fasces retro auertunt, precem indigitant, hostiam instaurant." The certified English renders "ponunt" as "magistrates put on their purple", and that gets the sense backwards. With clothing or insignia, "ponere" means "lay down, take off", the same as "deponere" ("ponere arma", "ponere vestem"). The whole sentence lists acts of public humbling: the sentence before reads "omnem ταπεινοφρόνησιν ethnici agnoscunt". It also lists barefoot processions and fasces turned backward, which was a Roman sign of mourning (Tacitus, Annals 3.4). Putting on the purple would be a show of rank, which runs against the point Tertullian is making. The standard ANF translation (Thelwall) also reads "the magistrates lay aside their purple." The proposed fix, "magistrates lay aside their purple", is faithful and fits the existing sentence without other changes.

kept.english_quote: Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to eat, before praying
kept.source_quote: Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi causa prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse
kept.why: Peter went up to pray first, before eating (Acts 10:9-10). The English says he went up to eat before praying, which reverses the order the argument depends on: prayer completes the station before food.
kept.corrected_english: Peter, before taking food, first went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to pray

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked tof_source.json §10, which reads "atqui facilius inuenias Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi causa prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse, quo magis sexta diei finiri officio huic possit, quae illud absolutura post orationem uidebatur." In this sentence "ad orandum" gives the purpose of going up: to pray. "Prius" means he did this first, and "capiendi cibi causa" ties it to the meal that would follow. That matches Acts 10:9-10, where Peter goes up to pray, grows hungry and wants to eat. The tradition agrees: ANF renders it "for the sake of taking food, gone up first to the higher place for prayer." The argument needs prayer first and food second. The sixth hour can only end the station because the duty is "completed after prayer," with the meal coming after the prayer. The live English ("Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour to eat, before praying") makes eating the purpose of going up and puts it before prayer. That reverses the order, and the next clause in the same English ("completed after prayer") then contradicts it. This is not a style point. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly closer version that keeps "capiendi cibi causa" would be: "Peter, with a view to taking food at the sixth hour, first went up to the upper room to pray."
verdict.better_correction: Yet you could more easily find that Peter, with a view to taking food at the sixth hour, first went up to the upper room to pray

kept.english_quote: since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 10:9).
kept.source_quote: quando et orationes fere hora nona concludat de Petri exemplo, quod Actis refertur.
kept.why: Acts 10:9 is Peter praying at the sixth hour. The ninth-hour example is Acts 3:1, where Peter and John go up to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. Section 10 cites that verse for this same point.
kept.corrected_english: since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 3:1).

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in tof_source.json §2 reads "quando et orationes fere hora nona concludat de Petri exemplo, quod Actis refertur", and the English in tof_english.json §2 matches the quote, ending "(Acts 10:9)". The Latin gives no verse number, so the translator added this reference, and it is wrong. Acts 10:9 is Peter praying on the housetop at the sixth hour. The ninth-hour example is Acts 3:1, where Peter and John go up to the temple "at the ninth hour of prayer". Tertullian's own §10 shows he means that verse: "Petrus et qui cum eo ad horam nonam orationis templum introgressi leguntur" ("Peter and those with him are recorded as entering the temple at the ninth hour of prayer"). In the same chapter he treats the sixth-hour housetop scene (Acts 10:9) as a separate event ("Petrum hora sexta ... in superiora ad orandum"). One detail in the claim is off but does not change the verdict: §10's English has no inline "Acts 3:1" citation. It only describes the scene. Changing the reference to (Acts 3:1) is faithful. Deleting the added parenthesis would also be acceptable.

kept.english_quote: those who fawn over idols by eating and adorning them
kept.source_quote: qui in idolis comendis et in hac re ornandis
kept.why: 'comendis' comes from como (to dress or deck out), not comedo (to eat). Nobody eats the idols. The English adds a meaning that is not in the source.
kept.corrected_english: those who fawn over idols by dressing them and adorning them

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim. In tof_source.json §16 the Latin reads "qui in idolis comendis et in hac re ornandis et ad singulas horas salutandis diis adulantur, curationem facere dicuntur." "comendis" is the gerundive of como, comere, meaning to dress, deck or arrange, as with the hair of cult statues. If the word came from comedo (to eat), the form would be "comedendis". Nothing in the clause means eating. So "by eating and adorning them" in tof_english.json §16 brings in a sense the Latin does not have, and it makes the image odd, since nobody eats idols. The point is the daily care of cult statues (dressing, adorning, greeting at set hours), which pagans called curatio, "service". The proposed fix ("dressing them and adorning them") is faithful. One small point the fix keeps from the current English: the dative "diis adulantur" says the people fawn on the gods, and the gerundives describe what they do to the idols.
verdict.better_correction: This is why those who fawn on their gods by dressing and adorning the idols and greeting them at every hour are said to offer service.

kept.english_quote: and the little water is the altar
kept.source_quote: et aqualiculus altare
kept.why: 'aqualiculus' means paunch or stomach (the belly-god image). 'The little water' is nonsense in context.
kept.corrected_english: and your paunch is the altar

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source, tof_source.json §16, reads exactly "deus enim tibi uenter est et pulmo templum et aqualiculus altare et sacerdos cocus...". In Lewis & Short, "aqualiculus" means the stomach, paunch or belly. Its root sense of a small water vessel is not what the word means here. The context is a list of digestive organs set against worship: belly as god, lung as temple. That list needs "paunch/stomach" to make sense, and Thelwall's ANF version gives "thy paunch an altar". The live English, "and the little water is the altar", takes the word apart by its roots and makes nonsense of the sentence, so a careful translator would fix it. The proposed "and your paunch is the altar" is faithful. "The paunch is the altar" would match the list's other items, which carry no "your", but either wording is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: and the paunch is the altar

kept.english_quote: Certainly the God who was not pleased by a people lacking self-control in gluttony was not pleased by priest or prophet either.
kept.source_quote: ille certe deus, cui nec populus incontinens gulae placuit, nec sacerdos nec prophetes.
kept.why: 'incontinens gulae' covers all three. God was pleased by no people, priest or prophet who lacked self-control in gluttony. The English says God was not pleased by priests or prophets at all.
kept.corrected_english: He is surely the God whom neither a people, nor a priest, nor a prophet lacking self-control in gluttony ever pleased.
