verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source in tof_source.json matches the quote exactly: "ille certe deus, cui nec populus incontinens gulae placuit, nec sacerdos nec prophetes." The three subjects share one verb, "placuit", in a nec...nec...nec series. "incontinens gulae" sits next to "populus", but the passage reads it with all three. The examples that follow prove this. The people are the quail-gluttons. The priest is Eli, whose house "cheated the fleshly sacrifices", a matter of greed for meat. The prophet is Shemaiah, who broke his fast by eating. The paragraph then sums up: "examples both to the people and to bishops ... if they admit any lack of self-control in gluttony." The current English attaches the qualifier only to the people. "was not pleased by priest or prophet either" then reads as God disliking priests and prophets as such. That is a real change of sense, not a style point, though "low-medium" fits it better than "medium". The proposed fix gets the sense right but has two flaws. It adds "ever", which is not in the Latin. And with "lacking self-control in gluttony" placed after "prophet", it can read as qualifying only the prophet, which is the same kind of ambiguity in reverse. The smallest faithful fix keeps the current sentence and adds "such", so the qualifier covers all three.
verdict.better_correction: Certainly the God who was not pleased by a people lacking self-control in gluttony was not pleased by such a priest or prophet either.  (A closer alternative: "Surely this is the God whom no people, no priest and no prophet lacking self-control in gluttony pleased.")

kept.english_quote: I do not mean from the business of collecting contributions, as you are quick to point out
kept.source_quote: non dico de industria stipium conferendarum, ut uestrae capturae est
kept.why: 'ut uestrae capturae est' is Tertullian's jab: 'as is your way of making gain', meaning the psychic bishops call fasts to raise money. The English turns his charge into an objection from the opponents.
kept.corrected_english: I do not mean for the business of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In tof_source.json §13 the Latin reads exactly: "bene autem, quod et episcopi uniuersae plebi mandare ieiunia adsolent, non dico de industria stipium conferendarum, ut uestrae capturae est, sed interdum et ex aliqua sollicitudinis ecclesiasticae causa." "captura" means gain, a catch, or profit, and "ut uestrae capturae est" means "as is your way of making gain". It is Tertullian's own jab: the psychic bishops call fasts to raise collections. Thelwall reads it the same way ("as your capturing policy has it"). The live English, "as you are quick to point out", makes it a remark by the opponents. That reverses whose charge it is and drops the accusation of profiteering. Nothing in "capturae" means pointing anything out, so this is a wrong sense, not a matter of word choice. The proposed correction is faithful. A slightly smoother version that keeps the idiom "de industria" ("on purpose, for the purpose of") would be: "I do not mean for the purpose of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain, but sometimes also from some cause of concern for the church."
verdict.better_correction: I do not mean for the purpose of collecting contributions, as is your way of making gain, but sometimes also from some cause of concern for the church

kept.english_quote: if you conduct a gathering of everyone together even at a human edict
kept.source_quote: si et ex hominis edicto et in unum omnes ταπεινοφρόνησιν agitatis
kept.why: The Greek word (garbled in the source, = tapeinophronesis, 'humiliation') is the object. They practise a common self-humbling or fast, not just 'a gathering'. Losing it drops the parallel to 'unitatem ieiunationum' in the next clause.
kept.corrected_english: if you all practise a common humiliation (fasting) together, and at a human edict

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in tof_source.json §13 reads "itaque si et ex hominis edicto et in unum omnes 'tCl'itEtVoą'póV'tjatv agitatis". The garbled OCR token stands for ταπεινοφρόνησιν (humiliation, self-abasement), and it is the object of "agitatis". "In unum omnes" means "all together as one"; it does not mean "a gathering". The live English reads "if you conduct a gathering of everyone together even at a human edict". That turns the adverbial phrase into an invented object and drops ταπεινοφρόνησιν altogether. As a result the reader loses the point: the bishops' commanded common fast is the parallel to the "unitatem ieiunationum et xerophagiarum et stationum" that Tertullian is defending. Thelwall also renders this as "all unanimously practise humiliation". The proposed correction is close but not fully faithful. It adds "(fasting)" as a gloss that is not in the source. It also turns "et ... et" (even/both) into "and at a human edict", which weakens the concession that this happens even at a mere man's edict.
verdict.better_correction: Therefore, if even at a human edict you all practise humiliation together as one, how do you censure in us that very unity of fasts, dry-food fasts, and station fasts?

kept.english_quote: equal in truth to his equal, as far as fasting makes them so.
kept.source_quote: parem reuera pari.
kept.why: 'as far as fasting makes them so' has no counterpart in the Latin. It is an added gloss.
kept.corrected_english: equal in truth to his equal.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin at the end of section 6 (tof_source.json) reads exactly: "tanta est circumscripti uictus praerogatiua, ut deum praestet homini contubernalem, parem reuera pari." Nothing in it limits the equality, so "as far as fasting makes them so" is the translator's own hedge. The next sentence already says how man becomes equal to God ("hoc erit tempus, quo homo deo adaequetur, cum sine pabulo uiuit"), so the hedge is not needed and blunts Tertullian's deliberately bold claim. It is a real addition, though small. I would rate it low to medium rather than medium, because it softens the meaning without reversing it. The proposed fix, "equal in truth to his equal.", is faithful: reuera means "in truth" or "in fact", and parem ... pari means "equal to equal". The full corrected sentence would read: "So great is the prerogative of a restricted diet, that it makes God a tent-companion to man, equal in truth to his equal."

kept.english_quote: fed by God and fattened in name by his fasting
kept.source_quote: Moysen deo pastum inediamque eius nomine saginatam
kept.why: The Latin says Moses was fed by God and his fasting was fattened (enriched) by God's name. 'Fattened in name by his fasting' makes no sense and loses the paradox.
kept.corrected_english: Moses, fed by God, his fasting fattened by God's name

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source (tof_source.json, §6) reads: "cum quidem nec ipsum Moysen deo pastum inediamque eius nomine saginatam constanter contemplari ualeret pinguior populus." Grammatically, "pastum" goes with Moses, and "saginatam" goes with "inediam" (his fasting). So "deo pastum" means "fed by God", and the second phrase means "his fasting, fattened by [God's] name". It is the fasting that is fattened, by the name. The English "fed by God and fattened in name by his fasting" makes Moses the one fattened, and it turns "fasting" into the cause instead of the thing fattened. That reverses the structure and loses Tertullian's deliberate paradox: the fatter people cannot look at a man whose very fasting is "fattened". It is a real sense error, not a matter of style. The proposed correction is faithful. "eius" most naturally points to God (deo), but "His name" would keep the slight ambiguity of the Latin. The suggested phrasing also drops the "-que" link, which is minor.
verdict.better_correction: although indeed the fatter people could not steadily look upon even Moses himself, fed by God, and his fasting fattened by God's name.

kept.english_quote: equate them with those of chaste Isis and Cybele
kept.source_quote: casto Isidis et Cybeles eas adaequas
kept.why: 'castus' is a noun here: the ritual abstinence of Isis and Cybele. The goddesses are not called chaste. The point is that the rites are compared.
kept.corrected_english: equate them with the abstinence rites of Isis and Cybele

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in tof_source.json, section 16, reads "sed bene quod tu nostris xerophagiis blasphemias ingerens casto Isidis et Cybeles eas adaequas." "casto" is masculine or neuter singular. It cannot agree as an adjective with "Isidis" and "Cybeles", which are feminine genitives. It is the cult noun castum/castus (dative after adaequas): the set period of ritual abstinence, as in Festus and Arnobius's "castum Cereris". So the Latin says "you equate them [our dry-food fasts] with the abstinence-rite of Isis and Cybele". The English, "equate them with those of chaste Isis and Cybele", misreads "casto" as an epithet of the goddesses and drops the noun that names the rite. This is a grammar error, not a style choice, though it is minor because the point that fasts are being compared survives. The proposed correction, "equate them with the abstinence rites of Isis and Cybele", is faithful. The singular, "the sacred abstinence of Isis and Cybele", would also work.

kept.english_quote: "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a healing" (Joel 2:15, LXX)
kept.source_quote: sancite ieiunium et praedicate curationem
kept.why: 'curatio' renders LXX therapeia, meaning service or worship. The next sentences use the same word for 'services that care for God' and the pagans' 'curationem facere' (rendered 'offer service'). 'Healing' breaks that link.
kept.corrected_english: "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a service" (Joel 2:15, LXX)

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. tof_source.json §16 reads: "nam et Iohel exclamauit: sancite ieiunium et praedicate curationem, prospiciens ... praedicaturos officia curantia deum. unde et qui in idolis comendis ... diis adulantur, curationem facere dicuntur." The LXX of Joel 2:15 (and 1:14) has κηρύξατε θεραπείαν, where θεραπεία means service or worship, not medical healing. Tertullian's whole point depends on that sense. The prophets will proclaim "officia curantia deum", and "unde" ("this is why") pagans who attend to idols are said to "curationem facere". The English already gives those two later uses as "services that care for God" and "offer service". Rendering the quotation itself as "proclaim a healing" therefore breaks the chain of reasoning, so the "This is why..." sentence no longer follows. That is a real sense error inside the argument, not a style choice. Low severity is right. The citation (Joel 2:15, LXX) is valid. The proposed fix, "Sanctify a fast and proclaim a service", is faithful and restores the link. "Proclaim a service of worship" would be an acceptable alternative.

I also noticed two other errors in the same section while checking. They are outside this claim but worth logging. (1) "magistratus purpuras ponunt" is rendered "magistrates put on their purple". "Ponunt" here means "lay aside", which is the mourning gesture, so the English reverses the sense. It should read "magistrates lay aside their purple". (2) "aqualiculus altare" is rendered "the little water is the altar". "Aqualiculus" means paunch or belly, so it should read "the paunch is the altar".

kept.english_quote: For he had been guilty of gluttony, even if innocent.
kept.source_quote: gulae enim licet simplicis reus fuerat.
kept.why: 'simplicis' describes the gluttony as simple or unwitting. Jonathan is not called innocent. 'Guilty ... even if innocent' contradicts itself.
kept.corrected_english: For he had been guilty of gluttony, though an unwitting one.

verdict.reason: The claim stands, as a low-severity error. The source quote is exact. The Latin in tof_source.json, §10 reads: "gulae enim licet simplicis reus fuerat." Here "simplicis" is genitive and agrees with "gulae", so it describes the gluttony, not Jonathan. The meaning is "guilty of a gluttony, albeit a simple/guileless one." The live English, "For he had been guilty of gluttony, even if innocent," moves the innocence onto Jonathan, so the sentence says he was both guilty and innocent. A careful translator would fix that. The intended sense (no guilty intent) can still be recovered, which is why the severity is low. This is not a style preference: the English changes what the adjective describes and produces a contradiction the Latin does not have. The proposed fix, "For he had been guilty of gluttony, though an unwitting one," is faithful. "Unwitting" fits the context ("quamquam ignarus ieiunationis"), and it keeps simplicis attached to the gluttony. A slightly more literal option: "For he had been guilty of gluttony, though of an innocent sort." The ANF translation is similar: "although of a simple kind."
verdict.better_correction: For he had been guilty of gluttony, though of an innocent (unwitting) sort.

kept.english_quote: For they say that where they wish, they recognize what the law and the prophets mean, up to John
kept.source_quote: ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem.
kept.why: This is Tertullian's own sarcastic aside that they invoke 'until John' only when it suits them. 'They say' turns it into the opponents' own claim.
kept.corrected_english: For where it suits them, they recognize what 'the law and the prophets until John' means

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I could not refute it. The Latin in tof_source.json §2 reads exactly as quoted: "ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem." The verb is a plain indicative (adgnoscunt), and the sentence has no verb of saying. The opponents' views around it are given in reported speech: "illos dies ... determinatos putant", "hos esse ... solos legitimos", then "itaque ... ieiunandum" and "sic et apostolos obseruasse". This one sentence breaks out of that pattern, so it is Tertullian's own jab: they invoke "until John" (Matthew 11:13) only when it suits them. The English adds "they say that", which turns the jab into the opponents' own statement. That also makes no sense, because no one would boast that they read the law selectively. The error is real but minor, so "low" severity fits. The proposed fix is faithful: it drops the invented "they say", keeps "ubi uolunt" as "where it suits them", and quotes "the law and the prophets until John" as the phrase they appeal to. Keep the (Matthew 11:13) reference after it.
verdict.better_correction: For where it suits them, they recognize what "the law and the prophets until John" means (Matthew 11:13).

kept.english_quote: your young men recline with the sisters
kept.source_quote: adulescentes tui cum sororibus dormiunt
kept.why: 'dormiunt' (sleep with) is a sexual charge, and the next sentence ties it to wantonness (lasciuia). 'Recline' turns it into table posture and drops the charge.
kept.corrected_english: your young men sleep with the sisters

verdict.reason: I read the Latin source at §17 of ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-fasting/translations/tof_source.json. It says "sed maioris est agape, quia per hanc adulescentes tui cum sororibus dormiunt. appendices scilicet gulae lasciuia atque luxuriae", which matches the claim's quote. The live English in tof_english.json says "because through it your young men recline with the sisters". "Dormiunt" means "sleep", not "recline". Latin's word for reclining at table would be "accumbunt" or "discumbunt". The next sentence makes the sexual meaning plain: lust and luxury follow gluttony, and Paul's "nec in cubilibus et libidinibus" (not in beds and lusts, Romans 13:13) is cited as the proof. "Recline" drops Tertullian's charge of sexual misconduct at the love-feast and makes the "beds and lusts" citation pointless. Thelwall's ANF translation also reads "sleep with". The claim stands. The fix, "your young men sleep with the sisters", is faithful and keeps "tui" (your). "The sisters" means the women of the congregation and is a fair choice for "sororibus".

kept.english_quote: without assessing my opponents
kept.source_quote: sine taxatione aduersariorum
kept.why: Here 'taxatio' means censure or reproach. Tertullian cannot defend chastity without attacking his opponents. 'Assessing' misses that.
kept.corrected_english: without censuring my opponents

verdict.reason: The source quote is exact. In tof_source.json §1 the Latin reads: "piget iam cum talibus congredi, pudet etiam de eis altercari quorum nec defensio uerecunda est. quomodo enim protegam castitatem et sobrietatem sine taxatione aduersariorum?" In classical Latin, "taxatio" means a valuation or appraisal. Tertullian, though, regularly uses taxare/taxatio to mean "censure, reproach". From memory, Lewis & Short gives that late sense for "taxatio" and may cite this very passage (Tert. Jejun. 1); I could not check that here. The context requires the reproach sense. He has just said it is shameful even to argue with these people, and he is explaining why he must attack them anyway. "Assessing my opponents" uses the classical sense. It reads as a neutral evaluation and loses the point that defending chastity forces him to rebuke them. The error is minor, but it is a real wrong sense, not a style preference, so low severity is right. "Without censuring my opponents" is faithful. "Without rebuking my opponents" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: How am I to protect chastity and sobriety without censuring my opponents?

kept.english_quote: But if you were not handed over, were you going to be handed over? Therefore, by not wanting to be handed over, you did not want to be exposed; by not wanting it, you denied what you did not want to be handed over as. But, you say, by not wanting to be handed over as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I do not want to be handed over as—that is, a Christian.
kept.source_quote: Non traditus autem traduci habebas? Ergo dum nolendo tradi non vis traduci, nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti. Immo, inquis, dum nolo traduci quod sum, sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci, id est Christianum.
kept.why: Tertullian contrasts tradi (be handed over) with traduci (be paraded, publicly exposed). The English renders traduci as 'handed over' too, so the argument collapses and the first question becomes nonsense. A prior review (reviews/justifications/12.json) wrongly ruled that 'traduci means to be handed over'. Lewis & Short give traduco as 'to expose, parade, disgrace publicly'.
kept.corrected_english: But if you were not handed over, would you have been publicly exposed? So while, by refusing to be handed over, you refuse to be exposed, by that refusal you have denied what you refused to be exposed as. 'No,' you say, 'by refusing to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I refuse to be exposed as, that is, a Christian.'

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked the Latin in tofip_source.json §12 and it matches the quote word for word: "Non traditus autem traduci habebas? Ergo dum nolendo tradi non vis traduci, nolendo negasti, quod te esse traduci noluisti. Immo, inquis, dum nolo traduci quod sum, sum confessus id esse quod nolo traduci, id est Christianum." Tertullian sets two verbs against each other here: tradi (to be handed over to the authorities) and traduci (to be publicly exposed or paraded as something). Lewis & Short gives traduco as "to expose, parade, disgrace publicly", and Thelwall's ANF translation also uses "publicly exhibited/exposed" for this passage. The live English uses "handed over" for traduci three out of four times and "exposed" once. That turns the first question into nonsense ("if you were not handed over, were you going to be handed over?") and breaks the argument: refusing to be handed over means refusing to be exposed as a Christian, and that refusal is a denial. The English also contradicts itself, using "exposed" in one clause and "handed over" for the same verb in the next. This is a real error of sense and garbled English, not a matter of style. The earlier review in reviews/justifications/12.json, which treated traduci as meaning "handed over", was wrong. The proposed correction gives tradi and traduci each the right meaning and follows the Latin. One small improvement is optional: "habebas" with an infinitive reads more exactly as "would you have had to be publicly exposed?"
verdict.better_correction: But if you had not been handed over, would you have had to be publicly exposed? So while, by refusing to be handed over, you refuse to be exposed, by that refusal you have denied what you refused to be exposed as. 'No,' you say, 'by refusing to be exposed as what I am, I have confessed that I am what I refuse to be exposed as, that is, a Christian.'

kept.english_quote: we confess that it comes from him from whom we beg its pardon
kept.source_quote: ab eo illam profitemur accidere a quo veniam eius deprecamur
kept.why: Here 'venia eius' means being spared or let off from the temptation. 'Beg its pardon' is meaningless English and loses the logic: we ask God to spare us, so the temptation must come from him.
kept.corrected_english: we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin is quoted correctly. In section 2 of tofip_source.json it reads: "Sed in legitima oratione, cum dicimus ad patrem, Ne nos inducas in temptationem (quae autem maior temptatio, quam persecutio?), ab eo illam profitemur accidere a quo veniam eius deprecamur." The pronoun "eius" refers to the temptation (persecution). "Veniam ... deprecamur" means we beg to be let off or spared it, not forgiveness for it. The argument depends on this: we ask the Father not to lead us into temptation, so we admit that temptation comes from him. The certified English is in tofip_english.json, section 2, paragraph 6: "we confess that it comes from him from whom we beg its pardon". In English, "beg its pardon" is the idiom for apologizing to something. It makes no sense here and hides the point that we ask God to spare us. A reader would not follow the logic. ANF's "whose forgiveness we implore" is also loose, but at least it reads as English; the current wording does not. The proposed fix, "we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it", is faithful. It keeps "profitemur" as "confess", "accidere" as "comes", and gives "veniam eius deprecamur" as "pray to be spared it". "Beg to be excused from it" would also work.
verdict.better_correction: we confess that it comes from him from whom we pray to be spared it

kept.english_quote: the man whom Christ bought for the whole world, and indeed set free
kept.source_quote: ut furtivo, quem ceram [= coram] toto mundo Christus emit, immo et manumisit
kept.why: 'ceram' is an OCR slip for 'coram' (openly, before). The point is that you buy him back secretly, as if he were stolen goods, though Christ bought him openly before the whole world. 'For the whole world' loses that contrast.
kept.corrected_english: as if he were stolen goods, the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free

verdict.reason: The locked source in tofip_source.json §12 reads "sub tunica et sinu, quod aiunt, ut furtivo, quem ceram toto mundo Christus emit, immo et manumisit". "ceram" is not a word that fits here. It is plainly a copy-text slip for "coram" ("openly, in the presence of"), and the standard text of De fuga 12 reads "coram toto mundo". The contrast is the point of the sentence. You haggle for him secretly, under your tunic, as if he were stolen goods ("ut furtivo"), when Christ bought him openly before the whole world. The live English reads "as if by stealth—the man whom Christ bought for the whole world, and indeed set free". That turns "in the presence of the world" into "for the benefit of the world", so the sense is wrong and the contrast Tertullian builds is lost. This is a real but low-severity sense error, not a style preference. The proposed fix is faithful. To fit the existing sentence, splice it in as: "...under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if he were stolen goods—the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free." "as if by stealth" for "ut furtivo" could stand, but "as if he were stolen goods" is more exact and keeps the contrast with "openly".
verdict.better_correction: But you bargain for him with an informer or a soldier or some petty thief of a governor, under your tunic and in your pocket, as they say, as if he were stolen goods—the man whom Christ bought openly before the whole world, and indeed set free.

kept.english_quote: since he is selling nothing other than what he will provide for your reward
kept.source_quote: siquidem non aliud venditat, quam quod praestaturus est praemio tuo
kept.why: Here 'praemio tuo' means 'for your payment' (the bribe you give him), not a reward to you.
kept.corrected_english: since he is selling nothing other than what he will deliver in return for your payment

verdict.reason: I checked the source and English for section 12 in ~/SaneApps/clients/translations/books/tertullian-on-flight-in-persecution/translations/tofip_source.json and tofip_english.json. Both quotes match exactly. The Latin reads: "Da mihi pecuniam. Certe ne eum tradat, siquidem non aliud venditat, quam quod praestaturus est praemio tuo." The extortionist sells only what he will hand over, which is his silence, and he hands it over in return for the payment you give him. Here "praemio tuo" means your payment to him. The ablative marks the price he gets. Thelwall's ANF translation reads it the same way ("for the reward you give"). The live English, "what he will provide for your reward", most naturally means something given to you as your reward. That reverses who pays whom, so it is a real wrong-sense error, though a minor one. It is not a style preference. The proposed fix, "since he is selling nothing other than what he will deliver in return for your payment", is faithful. A slightly closer option that keeps the original verb is: "since he is selling nothing other than what he will provide in return for your payment".

kept.english_quote: Why then do you buy Christ back at the cost of a man, in the man in whom Christ is?
kept.source_quote: Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est?
kept.why: Here 'de homine' means 'from a man' (the extortioner you pay), not 'at the cost of a man'.
kept.corrected_english: Why then do you ransom Christ from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?

verdict.reason: The source is quoted correctly: tofip_source.json §12 reads "Ut quid ergo de homine Christum redimis in homine, in quo Christus est?". The surrounding lines use redimere/mercari with de or ab for the party something is bought away from: "hominem de terris, immo ab inferis mercatus" and "illum redemit ab angelis munditenentibus potestatibus...". Tertullian's point is a contrast. Christ bought man back from the cosmic powers, and now you buy Christ back from a mere man: the informer, soldier or governor named just before ("pacisceris cum delatore vel milite vel furunculo aliquo praeside"). "At the cost of a man" would need a price ablative or "pretio hominis", not "de homine", and it loses the contrast with the next line about Simon and the bribe. This is a real error of sense, not a style choice, though a minor one. The proposed fix "Why then do you ransom Christ from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?" is faithful. "Buy Christ back from a man" would match the section's existing buy-back wording equally well.
verdict.better_correction: Why then do you buy Christ back from a man, in the man in whom Christ is?

kept.english_quote: so that its outcome can be established more easily
kept.source_quote: quo facilius de obitu eius constare possit
kept.why: Here 'obitus' (from obire, to go to meet) means how we should meet or face persecution, which is the question of the whole treatise. It does not mean its outcome.
kept.corrected_english: so that it may more easily be settled how we ought to meet it

verdict.reason: The quote checks out. The source (tofip_source.json §1) reads "utrum a deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu eius constare possit", and the English gives "so that its outcome can be established more easily". Here obitus is the noun from obire, "to go to meet" or "to face". The question is how the Christian should meet persecution, which is the subject of the whole treatise: "quomodo eas excipere fides debeat", flee or not. Thelwall's ANF translation reads it the same way: "as to our duty in respect of meeting it." "Outcome" would be exitus, and Tertullian uses that word a few lines later ("what is the outcome of persecution"). So the current English blurs two separate points: how to face persecution, and what persecution produces. That is wrong sense, not a style choice, though it is minor. The proposed fix keeps the right sense and the meaning of constare: "so that it may more easily be settled how we ought to meet it". "How we ought to face it" would also work.

kept.english_quote: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:31)
kept.source_quote: Et vidit deus quia bonum est
kept.why: Genesis 1:31 reads 'very good' (valde bona). The refrain quoted is Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25.
kept.corrected_english: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:10)

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in tofip_source.json §4 reads only "Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est, Et vidit deus quia bonum est". It gives no verse number, so "(Genesis 1:31)" was added by the translator. That added reference points to the wrong verse. Genesis 1:31 says "very good" ("valde bona"), about everything God made. Tertullian quotes the shorter refrain "it was good" ("bonum est"), which appears at Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21 and 25. A careful editor would fix this, though it changes no meaning, so "low" severity is right. The fix "(Genesis 1:10)" is accurate. Writing "(Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25)" would show that Tertullian is quoting a repeated phrase rather than one verse, and dropping the reference would also be faithful, since the Latin names no verse.
verdict.better_correction: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:10, 12, 18, 21, 25)

kept.english_quote: This was not to evade danger under the name of persecution.
kept.source_quote: non propter eludendum periculum proprio nomine persecutionis
kept.why: Here 'proprio nomine' means 'for its own sake / on its own account'. The sense is that flight was not commanded to dodge the danger of persecution for its own sake. 'Under the name of' misreads the idiom.
kept.corrected_english: This was not to escape the danger of persecution for its own sake.

verdict.reason: The quotes match. Source §6: "ideo illis fugere tunc ad tempus praecepti, non propter eludendum periculum proprio nomine persecutionis (atquin persecutiones eos passuros praedicabat...), sed propter profectum annuntiationis". English: "This was not to evade danger under the name of persecution." Here "proprio nomine" means "on its own account" or "as such", the sense it has in legal Latin. It sets up a contrast with "sed propter profectum annuntiationis": flight was not commanded so they could escape persecution's danger for its own sake. It was commanded so the preaching could advance. "Under the name of persecution" is a word-for-word rendering that does not give that sense. A reader will most likely take it as "using persecution as a pretext", which is wrong and also unclear. So the claim stands as a low-severity wrong-sense error. The proposed fix, "to escape the danger of persecution for its own sake", has the right idea but is ambiguous. "For its own sake" can be read as attaching to "persecution" ("persecution's own sake") instead of to the act of escaping. Placing the phrase so it modifies the purpose makes the contrast with "the progress of the announcement" clear.
verdict.better_correction: This was not so that they might escape the danger of persecution on their own account.

kept.english_quote: in the registers of beneficiaries and informers
kept.source_quote: in matricibus beneficiariorum et curiosorum
kept.why: Beneficiarii are soldiers on special police duty, not 'beneficiaries'. As English, 'beneficiaries' gives the reverse picture.
kept.corrected_english: in the registers of the police-soldiers and informers

verdict.reason: The claim matches the files. tofip_source.json §13 reads "cum in matricibus beneficiariorum et curiosorum inter tabernarios et (??)ianeos et fures balnearum et aleones et lenones Christiani quoque vectigales continentur", and tofip_english.json §13 has "Christians are listed as taxpayers in the registers of beneficiaries and informers". Here beneficiarii is a technical term. It means soldiers detached for special duty under a governor, who did police and extortion work at stations and checkpoints. They sit alongside the curiosi, the informers or secret police. To a modern reader, English "beneficiaries" means people who receive a benefit. That is a false friend: it hides the point that Christians were paying protection money to soldiers (compare "a militibus ... redimendam" at the end of the same section). A careful translator would fix it, so the claim is not a style preference. Severity low is right. The proposed fix "police-soldiers" is faithful. "Military police" reads a little more naturally, but either is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: in the registers of the military police and informers

kept.english_quote: And if you consult the Spirit, what does that saying of the Spirit prove more than anything?
kept.source_quote: Spiritum vero si consulas, quid magis sermone illo spiritus probat?
kept.why: Here 'probat' means 'approves', and the question is what the Spirit approves more than that saying (quoted next). The English makes no sense.
kept.corrected_english: And if you consult the Spirit, what does the Spirit approve more than that saying?

verdict.reason: The quote in tofip_source.json §9 is exact: "Spiritum vero si consulas, quid magis sermone illo spiritus probat?" Here "sermone illo" is an ablative of comparison, "spiritus" is the subject (it could also be read as a genitive), and "probat" means "approves". So the sense is "what does the Spirit approve more than that saying?" "That saying" points ahead to the oracle quoted next ("Publicaris... bonum tibi est"). The live English, "what does that saying of the Spirit prove more than anything?", makes the saying the subject, renders "probat" as "prove", and adds "than anything", which is not in the Latin. The result is garbled and loses the point of the comparison. This is a real error, not a style preference. The proposed fix is faithful. Thelwall's ANF reading is close ("what does He approve more than that utterance of the Spirit?"), but I recalled it from memory and did not check it against a copy. Reading "spiritus" as a genitive gives an equally good fix: "what does He approve more than that saying of the Spirit?"
verdict.better_correction: And if you consult the Spirit, what does He approve more than that saying of the Spirit?

kept.english_quote: Another magus, who opposed the apostles along with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his eyes.
kept.source_quote: alter magus, qui cum Sergio Paulo, quoniam isdem aduersabatur apostolis, luminum amissione multatus est
kept.why: 'cum Sergio Paulo' means the magus (Elymas) was with Sergius Paulus, the proconsul who believed (Acts 13:7-12). The English makes Sergius Paulus an opponent of the apostles.
kept.corrected_english: Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight because he opposed those same apostles.

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute it. The claim quotes the source (toi_source.json §9) exactly: "alter magus, qui cum Sergio Paulo, quoniam isdem aduersabatur apostolis, luminum amissione multatus est." The "quoniam" clause is a parenthesis. That leaves "qui cum Sergio Paulo [erat]", which places the magus in Sergius Paulus's company, as in Acts 13:7. ANF reads it the same way: "who dwelt with Sergius Paulus (since he was opposing himself to the same apostles)". The subject of "aduersabatur" is the magus alone, and "isdem" points back to the apostles who cursed Simon. The live English says "who opposed the apostles along with Sergius Paulus". That makes Sergius Paulus a co-opponent of the apostles, but in Acts 13:12 the proconsul believes. This is a real wrong-person error that changes the meaning. The proposed correction, "Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight because he opposed those same apostles," keeps "cum", "isdem" and "quoniam" (as "because"). "Loss of his sight" for "luminum amissione" is fine.
verdict.better_correction: Another magus, who was with Sergius Paulus, was punished with the loss of his sight, since he opposed those same apostles.

kept.english_quote: he does not commit the act himself, but he supplies what another does.
kept.source_quote: nec per se non faciet quod faciendum alio subministrat
kept.why: Double negative: he will not fail to do himself what he supplies to another to do, so he too is guilty. The English says the opposite, that he does not commit it himself.
kept.corrected_english: for he himself is not innocent of doing what he supplies another to do.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json, Idolatry §11, reads: "sic et homicidii interdictio ostendit mihi lanistam quoque ab ecclesia arceri: nec per se non faciet quod faciendum alio subministrat." The "nec ... non" is a litotes meaning "nor will he fail to do himself what he supplies another to do." Tertullian's point is that the gladiator-trainer is guilty of the killing himself. The English in toi_english.json says "he does not commit the act himself, but he supplies what another does." That concedes the trainer's innocence and drops the second negative, which reverses the sense; ANF gives "he will not fail to do himself what he subministers to another to do." The proposed fix, "for he himself is not innocent of doing what he supplies another to do," gets the meaning right. Its "not innocent of" is a little loose for "non faciet" (he does it), so the alternative below is closer to the Latin.
verdict.better_correction: he too does himself what he supplies another to do.

kept.english_quote: it is still blotted out under the crime of idolatry.
kept.source_quote: in idololatriae tamen crimine expungitur
kept.why: 'expungitur' here is an accounting term: each sin is entered/settled under the account of idolatry. 'Blotted out' suggests the sin is erased or forgiven, the opposite of the argument that idolatry contains all sins.
kept.corrected_english: it is still charged to the account of the crime of idolatry.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The source and English match the quotes exactly. In toi_source.json §1 the Latin reads "nam etsi suam speciem tenet unumquodque delictum, etsi suo quodque nomine iudicio destinatur, in idololatriae tamen crimine expungitur." In toi_english.json §1 the English reads "it is still blotted out under the crime of idolatry."

Tertullian often uses expungere in its late, bookkeeping sense: to check off, settle or reckon an account. Here it means each sin is entered and settled under the heading of idolatry. ANF (Thelwall) renders it "it is marked off under the general account of idolatry."

"Blotted out" uses the classical "strike out, erase" sense. An English reader takes it to mean the sin is wiped away or cancelled. That is the reverse of the argument, which is that idolatry contains and answers for every sin, as the next sentences show: "the idolater is also a murderer," and so on.

So this is a real sense error, not a style preference. The proposed "it is still charged to the account of the crime of idolatry" is faithful. "Yet it is reckoned to the account of the crime of idolatry" would be a slightly closer alternative.
verdict.better_correction: yet it is reckoned to the account of the crime of idolatry.

kept.english_quote: If he does anything for the ambition of praise, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.
kept.source_quote: si quid ad elogii ambitionem facit, non extraneum nec inimicum, sed ipsum se.
kept.why: 'elogium' is the written charge (indictment). The clause means 'if it adds to the grandeur of the charge': he has killed not a stranger but himself. 'He does anything for the ambition of praise' invents a motive and garbles the logic.
kept.corrected_english: If it adds anything to the weight of the charge, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.

verdict.reason: The source (toi_source.json §1) reads exactly as quoted: "quaeris quem occiderit? si quid ad elogii ambitionem facit, non extraneum nec inimicum, sed ipsum se." Here "elogium" is the legal term for the written charge, so "ad elogii ambitionem" means "to the grandeur (aggravation) of the charge". The verb "facit" is impersonal: "if it adds anything". The standard rendering agrees; ANF/Thelwall has "If it contributes aught to the aggravation of the charge, no stranger nor personal foe, but his own self." The live English, "If he does anything for the ambition of praise", turns this into a motive the idolater has, which is not in the source. It also breaks the logic: the point is that killing himself makes the charge worse. That is a real error of sense, not a style choice. The proposed fix, "If it adds anything to the weight of the charge, it is not a stranger or an enemy, but himself", is faithful. A tighter version could be "If it adds anything to the gravity of the charge: not a stranger or an enemy, but himself." That drops "it is", which the Latin does not need, and still answers "Whom has he killed?" Either wording works.
verdict.better_correction: If it adds anything to the gravity of the charge: not a stranger or an enemy, but himself.

kept.english_quote: If anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God.
kept.source_quote: artificum, quos numquam in domum dei admitti oportet si quis eam disciplinam norit
kept.why: The relative 'quos' refers to the idol-making craftsmen; they are the ones not to be admitted, as anyone who knows the discipline understands. The English makes the person who knows the discipline the one excluded.
kept.corrected_english: Anyone who knows that discipline knows that such craftsmen should never be admitted into the house of God.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json §5 reads "excusationes huiusmodi artificum, quos numquam in domum dei admitti oportet si quis eam disciplinam norit". "quos" (masculine plural accusative) can only refer back to "artificum", the craftsmen. So the people who must never be admitted are the craftsmen, and "si quis ... norit" is a side condition: anyone who knows the discipline would see that. The live English in toi_english.json §5 splits this off as its own sentence: "If anyone knows that discipline, they should never be admitted into the house of God." The singular "they" most naturally points back to "anyone", so it says the person who knows the discipline is barred. That reverses the sense; it is not a style choice. The proposed fix is faithful. A smoother version keeps it in one sentence: "I will answer far more vigorously the excuses of such craftsmen, who, as anyone who knows that discipline is aware, should never be admitted into the house of God."
verdict.better_correction: I will answer far more vigorously the excuses of such craftsmen, who, as anyone who knows that discipline is aware, should never be admitted into the house of God.

kept.english_quote: But, someone says, that knowledge was permitted until the gospel, so that once Christ was born no one from then on would interpret anyone's birth from the heavens.
kept.source_quote: at enim scientia ista usque ad euangelium fuit concessa, ut Christo edito nemo exinde natiuitatem alicuius de caelo interpretetur.
kept.why: This is Tertullian's own answer to the magi argument, not an opponent's objection. 'Someone says' is added and assigns his thesis to the other side.
kept.corrected_english: But that knowledge was permitted only until the gospel, so that once Christ was born no one from then on should interpret anyone's birth from the heavens.

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source in toi_source.json §9 matches the quote exactly: "at enim scientia ista usque ad euangelium fuit concessa, ut Christo edito nemo exinde natiuitatem alicuius de caelo interpretetur." The English in toi_english.json §9 paragraph 4 begins "But, someone says, that knowledge was permitted until the gospel...". No word in the Latin means "someone says". "At enim" can open an objection, but here the context shows it is Tertullian's own answer, for three reasons. (1) The opponent's argument is the magi defence ("sed magi ab oriente uenerunt"), which Tertullian has just mocked ("de Christo scilicet est mathesis hodie"). (2) The sentence itself says astrology ended with Christ, which is Tertullian's thesis. An astrologer defending his trade would never argue it. (3) The next sentence, "nam et tus illud et myrram et aurum ... quasi clausulam sacrificationis et gloriae saecularis, quam Christus erat adempturus", is plainly Tertullian supporting that point, and paragraph 5 builds on it ("ut exinde aliter incederent"). So "someone says" adds words that are not in the source and gives Tertullian's own view to the opponent. That is a real wrong-speaker error. The proposed correction is faithful. It drops the invented attribution, and "only until" is a fair reading of "usque ad" together with the purpose clause ("so that from then on no one..."). "Should interpret" fits the purpose subjunctive "interpretetur".

kept.english_quote: I maintain that it still offends against idolatry, because it pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols and fattens every demon.
kept.source_quote: in crimen offendere idololatriae eam opinor, quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet, quae omne daemonium saginat.
kept.why: 'in crimen offendere idololatriae' means to fall into the charge of idolatry; 'offends against idolatry' says it opposes idolatry. Also 'eam ... quae' restricts the charge to the trade that serves the idols' soul (incense), not to all just profit.
kept.corrected_english: I think that trade still falls into the charge of idolatry which deals in the very soul and spirit of idols and fattens every demon.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. I checked §11 in toi_source.json and the Latin matches the quote: "sit nunc aliqua iustitia quaestus secura de cupiditatis et mendacii obseruatione, in crimen offendere idololatriae eam opinor, quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet, quae omne daemonium saginat."

There are two errors:

1. Wrong sense. "in crimen offendere idololatriae" means to run into, or fall under, the charge of idolatry. In English, "offends against idolatry" means breaking or opposing idolatry, which turns the meaning around. The Latin "crimen" (charge) is also left out.

2. Wrong scope. "eam ... quae" is restrictive: it means "that trade which serves the soul of idols", and the next sentences name it as incense ("tura dico"). The English "because it pertains" makes the clause a reason, so it condemns all just profit. Tertullian condemns only the trade that serves idols.

Standard renderings agree. Thelwall (ANF) has "that trade which pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols, which pampers every demon, falls into the crime of idolatry", and Waszink has the same sense.

The proposed fix is faithful. Its only problem is word order: the relative clause sits apart from "trade" ("that trade still falls ... which deals"), so the cleaner version below keeps them together.
verdict.better_correction: But suppose there is some just profit, free from the charge of desire and lying. I still think that the trade which concerns the very soul and spirit of idols, which fattens every demon, falls into the charge of idolatry.

kept.english_quote: So let them light their lamps daily—lamps that have no light. Let them fasten laurels to their doorposts, laurels that will soon burn, with fires hanging over them.
kept.source_quote: accendant igitur quotidie lucernas, quibus lux nulla est, affigant postibus lauros postmodum arsuras, quibus ignes imminent; illis competunt et testimonia tenebrarum et auspicia poenarum.
kept.why: Both 'quibus' clauses refer to the pagans (picked up by 'illis'): those who have no light, over whom fires of judgment hang. The English attaches them to the lamps and laurels and loses the point.
kept.corrected_english: So let those who have no light light lamps daily; let those over whom fires hang fasten to their doorposts laurels that will later burn. To them belong both the testimonies of darkness and the omens of punishment.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. The Latin in toi_source.json matches the quote: "accendant igitur quotidie lucernas, quibus lux nulla est, affigant postibus lauros postmodum arsuras, quibus ignes imminent; illis competunt et testimonia tenebrarum et auspicia poenarum. Tu lumen es mundi et arbor uirens semper."

Each "quibus" clause belongs to the unstated subject of the verbs accendant and affigant, meaning the pagans: "those who have no light" and "those over whom fires hang." "illis" ("to them belong...") then refers back to those same people, not to the lamps. The next sentence, "Tu lumen es mundi et arbor uirens semper" ("You are the light of the world and a tree always green"), sets the Christian against those people. That contrast only works if they are the ones with no light and with fire over them: Christians have light and stay green, while pagans have no light and will burn. Thelwall's translation (ANF) reads it the same way: "Let, therefore, them who have no light, light their lamps daily; let them over whom the fires of hell are imminent, affix to their posts laurels doomed presently to burn."

The current English, "lamps that have no light", makes the lamps the ones without light. That is close to nonsense, since lit lamps give light. "With fires hanging over them" makes the threat fall on the laurels, so the reader loses Tertullian's warning that judgment hangs over the people. This is a wrong-sense error, not a style choice.

The proposed correction is faithful: "So let those who have no light light lamps daily; let those over whom fires hang fasten to their doorposts laurels that will later burn. To them belong both the testimonies of darkness and the omens of punishment." "Later" for postmodum is accurate. One small point outside this claim: the live English cites Matthew 5:14 after "a tree always green", but only "light of the world" comes from that verse.

kept.english_quote: When we borrow money from pagans, bound by pledges, we give security in writing under oath and deny ourselves. The pagans, of course, want to know the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.
kept.source_quote: pecuniam de ethnicis mutuantes sub pignoribus fiduciati iurati cauent et se negant; se scire uolunt scilicet tempus persecutionis et locus tribunalis et persona praesidis.
kept.why: The subject is 'those (Christians) who borrow', not 'we'. 'Se negant' means they deny that they are Christians, but English 'deny ourselves' reads as self-denial. 'Se scire uolunt' has the same borrowers as its subject (ironic: they want to pick the time and place of their own persecution); the English makes 'the pagans' the subject.
kept.corrected_english: Those who borrow money from pagans on pledges give written security under oath and so deny that they are Christians. They want, of course, to choose for themselves the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.

verdict.reason: The claim holds; I checked toi_source.json and toi_english.json, §23. "mutuantes ... cauent et se negant" is third person plural. Its subject is the Christians who borrow, so "we" is the wrong person. Tertullian is describing others, not himself. With "we", "deny ourselves" reads as self-denial in the ascetic sense (Matt 16:24), but "se negant" means they deny that they are Christians. That reverses the sense. In "se scire uolunt", the reflexive "se" and the verb "uolunt" go back to the same borrowers. The pagans appear only in the ablative "de ethnicis", so the English is wrong to make "The pagans" the subject. The proposed fix gets the person and the denial right. But "to choose for themselves" adds a gloss: the source says "scire" (to know), not "choose". This passage is textually hard, so the fix should stay close to the Latin and not settle the reading by interpretation.
verdict.better_correction: Those who borrow money from pagans on pledges give written security under oath, and so deny that they are Christians. They wish, of course, to know for themselves the time of persecution, the place of the tribunal, and the person of the governor.

kept.english_quote: For he does what belongs to the servants of idols.
kept.source_quote: id enim facit quod ad idolorum mancipes pertinet.
kept.why: 'mancipes' are the owners/proprietors of idols, i.e. the demons to whom idols are 'mancipantur' in the preceding sentence. 'Servants' reverses owner and slave.
kept.corrected_english: For he does what belongs to the owners of idols.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source quote is exact, from toi_source.json §1: "...non daemoniis et immundis spiritibus deputetur quibus idola mancipantur, sine dubio idololatrian admittit quicunque delinquit. id enim facit quod ad idolorum mancipes pertinet." A "manceps" is a purchaser, contractor or proprietor: the one who takes something in hand as property. The word never means a servant; the slave is "mancipium". Here the word picks up "quibus idola mancipantur" (the demons and unclean spirits to whom idols are made over as property). So "idolorum mancipes" means those demons, the owners of the idols. The argument runs: every sin is assigned to the demons, so a sinner does the demons' work, and that is idolatry. The English "For he does what belongs to the servants of idols" flips owner and slave. It also points the line at the wrong people, idol-worshippers instead of the demons, which breaks the argument's chain. The standard ANF rendering is "proprietors of idols". The proposed "For he does what belongs to the owners of idols" is faithful. "proprietors of idols" would also do.

kept.english_quote: any sophists or Chaldeans, by which I mean astrologers, or enchanters
kept.source_quote: aut sophistas aut Chaldaeos aut incantatores
kept.why: 'by which I mean astrologers' is an added gloss in Tertullian's voice; the Latin has only 'Chaldaeos'.
kept.corrected_english: any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters

verdict.reason: I couldn't refute this claim. The Latin of section 9 (toi_source.json) reads "post euangelium nusquam inuenias aut sophistas aut Chaldaeos aut incantatores aut coniectores aut magos, nisi plane punitos". It has no word or phrase meaning "by which I mean astrologers". The live English (toi_english.json, section 9, last paragraph) reads "any sophists or Chaldeans, by which I mean astrologers, or enchanters or diviners or magi". That inserts a first-person gloss in Tertullian's voice. "Chaldaei" did commonly mean astrologers, so the gloss is right about the meaning. But the text presents it as Tertullian's own words, so it is an addition and not a word choice. Low severity is right. The proposed fix "any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters" is faithful, and the rest of the sentence ("or diviners or magi, except plainly punished ones") should stay as it is. If a reader needs the sense, put it in a note, not in the text.
verdict.better_correction: After the gospel you will find nowhere any sophists or Chaldeans or enchanters or diviners or magi, except plainly punished ones.

kept.english_quote: lovers of women, and betrayers also of this curiosity
kept.source_quote: amatores feminarum, proditores etiam huius curiositatis
kept.why: 'proditores' here means those who disclosed (revealed) this curious art to humans (the Enoch tradition). 'Betrayers of this curiosity' does not make sense in English.
kept.corrected_english: lovers of women, and also the revealers of this curious art

verdict.reason: The quotes are accurate. toi_source.json §9 reads "angelos esse illos desertores dei, amatores feminarum, proditores etiam huius curiositatis, propterea quoque damnatos a deo", and toi_english.json §9 reads "those angels were deserters of God, lovers of women, and betrayers also of this curiosity". Here "proditor" comes from prodo, "to bring forth" or "disclose". It refers to the Enoch tradition that the fallen angels taught humans astrology and the other arts. This is Tertullian's point: the angels are condemned, so astrology is condemned with them. English "betray" can still mean "reveal a secret", but a modern reader of "betrayers of this curiosity" will take it as "disloyal to this curiosity", which reverses the sense. "Curiosity" on its own also hides that "curiositas" here means a forbidden curious art, namely astrology. The claim stands as low severity. ANF (Thelwall) renders the phrase as "discoverers of this curious art". The proposed "and also the revealers of this curious art" is faithful. "Disclosers" would work equally well.
verdict.better_correction: lovers of women, and also the revealers of this curious art

kept.english_quote: if even now the work of idolatry is nearly accomplished without an idol through the burning of fragrances
kept.source_quote: si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur
kept.why: 'fere' goes with 'sine idolo': idolatry is now mostly carried out without an idol. 'Nearly accomplished' says the work is almost but not fully done.
kept.corrected_english: if even now the work of idolatry is mostly carried out without an idol, by the burning of fragrances

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against the source and it holds. In toi_source.json §11 the Latin reads exactly "si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur", and toi_english.json §11, paragraph 6, renders it as "the work of idolatry is nearly accomplished without an idol through the burning of fragrances". Here "fere" means "for the most part" or "generally" and goes with "sine idolo", not with "perpetratur". The Latin says idolatry is usually performed without an idol. The English says the work is almost but not quite finished, which is a different meaning and loses the point. The next sentence confirms the reading: "nam facilius sine idolo idololatria, quam sine turarii merce" ("idolatry is easier without an idol than without the incense-dealer's goods"). This is the standard reading; Thelwall (ANF) translates it as "perpetrated, for the most part, without the idol". The proposed fix, "mostly carried out without an idol, by the burning of fragrances", is faithful. "Generally carried out" would also work.

kept.english_quote: He should easily obtain victory over the one he feeds daily.
kept.source_quote: facile debuit de eo impetrare, quem cotidie pascit.
kept.why: 'impetrare de eo' means to get what he asked from him. The point is that the demon obliges its daily feeder. 'Victory over' is not in the source and flips the point.
kept.corrected_english: He could easily get what he asked from the one he feeds every day.

verdict.reason: I checked the claim against toi_source.json and toi_english.json for section 11, and it holds. The Latin reads "ille quidem si excluserit daemonium, non sibi placeat de fide. neque enim inimicum exclusit. facile debuit de eo impetrare, quem cotidie pascit." Here "impetrare de eo" means to get what you ask from someone. It is a word for a granted request, not for conquest. The ANF translation agrees: "he ought to have found it easy to get his request from one whom he daily feeds." Tertullian's point is that the exorcism proves nothing about the dealer's faith. The demon is no enemy to him, so it simply grants a favor to the man who feeds it. The English "obtain victory over" adds the idea of conquest. That turns a demon granting a favor into a struggle the dealer wins, which runs against the sentence just before it ("He has not cast out an enemy"). The error is small and low severity, but real. The proposed fix, "He could easily get what he asked from the one he feeds every day.", is faithful. A version closer to "debuit" would be: "It was easy for him to get his request granted by the one he feeds every day."
verdict.better_correction: It was easy for him to get his request granted by the one he feeds every day.

kept.english_quote: Since the same apostle calls desire idolatry
kept.source_quote: cum bis et idololatria ab eodem apostolo dicta sit cupiditas
kept.why: 'bis' (twice: Colossians 3:5, Ephesians 5:5) is dropped.
kept.corrected_english: Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. In toi_source.json section 11 the Latin reads exactly "cum bis et idololatria ab eodem apostolo dicta sit cupiditas", and toi_english.json section 11, paragraph 1, reads "Since the same apostle calls desire idolatry". The English drops "bis" (twice). Tertullian is pointing to Colossians 3:5 and Ephesians 5:5, so the word carries meaning: it shows how strongly Paul stated the point. The severity is low, but this is a real omission and not a style choice. The proposed fix, "Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry", is faithful, and "covetousness" is closer to "cupiditas" in the Pauline sense. One caution: the earlier sentence renders the same word as "desire, the root of all evils", and the paragraph uses "desire" four more times. Switching to "covetousness" in only one place would break that consistency. The smallest fix is to add "twice" and keep the paragraph's current word. Switching to "covetousness" throughout is also faithful.
verdict.better_correction: Since the same apostle has twice called desire idolatry (or, if the whole paragraph is changed to match, "Since the same apostle has twice called covetousness idolatry")

kept.english_quote: sealed with signs no longer of accusers but of angels.
kept.source_quote: signatae signis non iam aduocatorum, sed angelorum
kept.why: 'aduocati' are the witnesses/advocates who sealed the contract, not accusers.
kept.corrected_english: sealed with the seals no longer of witnesses but of angels.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I checked §23 of toi_source.json and toi_english.json, and both quotes match the files exactly. In Latin, "aduocati" are people called in to support a party, such as advocates or the witnesses who seal a document. They are not accusers. The English says nearly the opposite. That also flattens Tertullian's contrast: on earth, the pledge was sealed by human supporters, but at the judgment the same letters come sealed by angels. Thelwall's ANF translation reads "sealed with the seals no longer of advocates, but of angels." The proposed "witnesses" is faithful, since in Roman practice the signatories who sealed a pledge were witnesses. "Seals" for "signis" is also fine. "Advocates" would be a little closer to the word itself, but either fixes the error. The severity is low, and the claim is valid.
verdict.better_correction: sealed with the seals no longer of advocates (the witnesses who signed), but of angels.

kept.english_quote: We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God’s will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things.
kept.source_quote: non quod aliquis obsistat, quo minus uoluntas dei fiat, et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus, sed in omnibus petimus fieri uoluntatem eius
kept.why: Both clauses sit under the 'non quod' negation. Tertullian denies that we pray for success for God's will, as if it needed help. The English breaks the clause off and states it as fact: 'and we pray for the success of his will.' That reverses his point.
kept.corrected_english: We do not say this as though someone were resisting God’s will being done and we were praying that his will succeed. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things.

verdict.reason: The source in top_source.json §4 reads exactly as quoted: "non quod aliquis obsistat, quo minus uoluntas dei fiat, et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus, sed in omnibus petimus...". Both "obsistat" and "oremus" are subjunctive and joined by "et", so both sit under "non quod". Tertullian is denying the idea that we pray for God to succeed in his will, as if someone could stop him. The live English says "We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God's will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will." In that sentence, "and we pray for the success of his will" reads most naturally as a positive statement of what we do. That reverses the point the "sed" contrast is making. A reader could take it as part of the "because" clause, but the plain-indicative wording invites the wrong reading, so this is a real faithfulness error and not a style choice. The proposed correction ("as though someone were resisting God's will being done and we were praying that his will succeed") keeps both clauses under the negation and is faithful. Optionally, "praying that he succeed in his will" keeps "ei" (for him) a little closer.

kept.english_quote: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and life is bread.
kept.source_quote: Christus enim panis noster est, quia uita Christus et uitae panis.
kept.why: 'uitae panis' is genitive: 'the bread of life', a phrase that sets up the John 6:35 quote that follows. 'life is bread' misreads the grammar and states a claim Tertullian does not make.
kept.corrected_english: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and the bread of life.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The locked source for section 6 (top_source.json) reads "Christus enim panis noster est, quia uita Christus et uitae panis." "uitae" is genitive (or at most dative), so the clause cannot be read as "life is bread". The natural reading is "Christ is life and [Christ is] the bread of life", which sets up the next line, "ego sum, inquit, panis uitae". The English "and life is bread" (top_english.json §6) matches the variant "et uita panis" found in other editions (ANF follows that variant with "bread is life"), not the text this book uses. Even that variant would not give "life is bread". So this is a real wrong-sense error against the locked source. The proposed fix is faithful, but the comma before "and" makes it read like a fragment. Dropping it ties "the bread of life" to Christ more clearly.
verdict.better_correction: For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life and the bread of life.

kept.english_quote: It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not receive from men what we hope for from God.
kept.source_quote: interest nostra, quod dei gratia exerceatur, solius dei conscientiae commendare, ne, quod a deo speramus, ab homine compensemus.
kept.why: 'quod dei gratia exerceatur' is the object of 'commendare': what is practiced by God's grace should be left to God's knowledge alone. The English makes 'that God's grace be exercised' the thing that matters, which changes the claim and leaves the sentence muddled.
kept.corrected_english: It is right for us to entrust what is practiced by God's grace to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not take our reward from men for what we hope for from God.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The source in top_source.json §22 reads: "interest nostra, quod dei gratia exerceatur, solius dei conscientiae commendare, ne, quod a deo speramus, ab homine compensemus." "quod ... exerceatur" is a relative clause, and that clause is the object of "commendare". The subject of "interest nostra" is the infinitive "commendare", so the sense is "it is in our interest to entrust what is practiced by God's grace to God's knowledge alone." The live English, "It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone", reads "quod" as "that". This makes "God's grace being exercised" the thing that matters, which misparses the sentence and blurs Tertullian's point: do the virtue in secret and leave it to God. Severity is low because "entrust it to God alone" still survives. The proposed correction fixes the structure but has two faults. "It is right for us" changes "interest nostra" ("it is to our advantage" or "it concerns us") into a moral claim. "take our reward from men" is fine for "ab homine compensemus" but drops the singular "man", which is minor. A closer rendering is below.
verdict.better_correction: It is in our interest to entrust what is done by God's grace to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not take from man the reward for what we hope for from God.

kept.english_quote: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, as in the story of Daniel's companions, or shut the mouths of lions
kept.source_quote: non roris angelum in mediis ignibus sistit nec ora leonibus obstruit
kept.why: The Latin has no 'as in the story of Daniel's companions'. It is a translator's gloss placed in the running text as if Tertullian wrote it. The identification is correct (Daniel 3), but it should be a reference in parentheses or a note.
kept.corrected_english: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames (Daniel 3), or shut the mouths of lions

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim. The source quote is exact: top_source.json §29 reads "non roris angelum in mediis ignibus sistit nec ora leonibus obstruit nec esurientibus rusticorum prandium transfert". Nothing in it matches "as in the story of Daniel's companions". The English adds a gloss in the running text as if Tertullian had written it. The identification is right (the three youths of Daniel 3, with the dew-bringing angel of LXX Dan 3:49-50), so this is a low-severity addition, not a change of sense. The gloss is also lopsided: it names the source for the first allusion but not for the next two, the lions (Daniel 6) and the meal carried to the hungry (Habakkuk bringing food to Daniel, Bel and the Dragon 33-39). The proposed fix, "(Daniel 3)" inline, is better than the gloss, but it still puts an editor's reference in Tertullian's sentence and keeps the same lopsidedness. The section has no notes field, so the cleanest fix is to cut the gloss and leave the allusions as unglossed as the Latin does. If references are wanted, give all three in a note or footnote, not in the text.
verdict.better_correction: It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace. (If references are wanted, put them in a note covering all three: Dan 3:49-50 LXX; Dan 6:22; Bel and the Dragon 33-39.)

kept.english_quote: sitting down after the appointed prayer
kept.source_quote: quod adsignata oratione assidendi mos est quibusdam
kept.why: 'adsignata oratione' (ablative absolute) means 'when prayer has been sealed' or 'concluded'. The custom under attack is sitting down once prayer is finished. 'Appointed' misreads 'adsignare' and hides that point. The next sentences ('after finishing prayer') confirm the intended sense.
kept.corrected_english: sitting down once prayer has been concluded

verdict.reason: The source matches the quote (top_source.json §16: "Item quod adsignata oratione assidendi mos est quibusdam"). "adsignata oratione" is an ablative absolute: "when the prayer has been signed off or sealed", that is, finished. ANF gives "when prayer is ended" and Evans "when prayer has been sealed". "Appointed" reads adsignare in its "assign or allot" sense. That sense does not fit here. It also adds the idea of a set or scheduled prayer, which is not in the text. Tertullian's point is about sitting down at the close of any prayer, and "transacta oratione" ("after finishing prayer") in the next sentence confirms this. The error is minor because the English already says "after", but it is a real wrong sense a careful translator would fix. The proposed "sitting down once prayer has been concluded" is faithful. "Once prayer has been sealed" is a more literal option.
verdict.better_correction: I do not see the reason why some people have a custom of sitting down once prayer has been concluded (literally "sealed")

kept.english_quote: So also on the day of Easter, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance
kept.source_quote: sic et die paschae, quo communis et quasi publica ieiunii religio est
kept.why: For Tertullian, 'dies paschae' is the paschal fast day before the resurrection feast. Rendering it 'Easter' tells a modern reader that the whole church fasted on Easter Sunday, which is wrong and makes the passage confusing.
kept.corrected_english: So also on the day of the Pascha, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance

verdict.reason: The claim holds, at low severity. The quotes match the files. In top_source.json §18 the Latin reads "sic et die paschae., quo communis et quasi publica ieiunii religio est, merito deponimus osculum", and top_english.json §18 has "So also on the day of Easter, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance". "Easter" is the only place this book renders pascha. In Tertullian, "dies paschae" means the paschal fast day before the resurrection feast (Good Friday or Holy Saturday). It does not mean Easter Sunday: he says elsewhere (De corona 3) that fasting on the Lord's day is forbidden. The sentence itself names the day as one of public fasting, so "Easter" gives a modern reader the wrong day and contradicts Tertullian. This is a real error of sense, not a matter of style. Standard English versions avoid "Easter" here. Thelwall (ANF) uses "the day of the passover", and others use "Pascha" or "Good Friday". I checked this from memory, not against those texts in this session. The proposed "So also on the day of the Pascha" is faithful. It could be made clearer as "So also on the day of the Pascha (the paschal fast)", but the correction as given is acceptable.
verdict.better_correction: So also on the day of the Pascha, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance

kept.english_quote: this is the one you redeemed from the Jews
kept.source_quote: hic est quem a Iuda redemistis
kept.why: 'a Iuda' is Judas (singular), not 'the Jews', and 'redemistis' here means 'you bought', the price paid to Judas. 'Redeemed' also reads as the theological word for salvation, which reverses the irony.
kept.corrected_english: this is the one you bought from Judas

verdict.reason: I checked translations/tots_source.json for section 30. The Latin reads exactly "hic est quem a Iuda redemistis". "Iuda" is the ablative of Iudas, meaning Judas. The word for "the Jews" would be "Iudaeis", which is the form Tertullian uses elsewhere in this work ("Iudaeorum"). Here "redimo" means "to buy or purchase", and the line points to the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas. The ANF translation reads "This is He whom you purchased from Judas." The live English, "this is the one you redeemed from the Jews", gets the source person wrong and gives the verb its theological sense. It also makes no sense in context, because the people being addressed are the persecutors, that is, the Jews, so they cannot have redeemed him from themselves. This is a real error. The proposed fix, "this is the one you bought from Judas", is faithful and fits the parallel "this is the one..." clauses around it.

kept.english_quote: all the kinds of evils which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted consist of the works of God
kept.source_quote: omnes species malorum, quae etiam ethnici ut indubitata et prohibent et defendunt, ex operibus dei constant
kept.why: 'defendunt' here has its legal sense, to punish or guard against. 'Defend' makes the pagans uphold the evils, the opposite of the point.
kept.corrected_english: all the kinds of evils which even the pagans, treating them as undoubted, both forbid and punish, consist of the works of God

verdict.reason: The quotes match. The Latin in tots_source.json reads "ceterum omnes species malorum, quae etiam ethnici ut indubitata et prohibent et defendunt, ex operibus dei constant", and the English in tots_english.json, section 2, paragraph 6, reads "which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted". In Tertullian and other late Latin, "defendere" often means to ward off, avenge or punish (as in "defendere iniuriam"). It is paired here with "prohibent", and both verbs act on "malorum" (evils). Standard translations agree: Thelwall (ANF) has "prohibit and guard against", and Glover (Loeb) has "forbid and punish". In English, "defend" an evil means to uphold or justify it. That reverses Tertullian's point that even pagans treat these evils as wrongs. The error is real and changes the meaning; it is not a matter of style. The proposed fix, "both forbid and punish", is faithful. Its phrase "treating them as undoubted" correctly makes "ut indubitata" ("as undoubted evils") describe the evils, not the verbs. Minor polish is optional, for example "which even the pagans forbid and punish as undoubted evils".
verdict.better_correction: Besides, all the kinds of evils which even the pagans forbid and punish as undoubted evils consist of the works of God.

kept.english_quote: whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns
kept.source_quote: quaecumque condidit non in exitum operum constat condidisse quae damnat
kept.why: 'in exitum operum quae damnat' means 'to issue in (result in) the works he condemns'. The English says God did not create things to destroy evil works, which reverses the argument.
kept.corrected_english: whatever he created he certainly did not create to issue in the works he condemns

verdict.reason: I could not refute the claim, so it stands. In tots_source.json, section 2 reads: "indubitate quaecumque condidit non in exitum operum constat condidisse quae damnat[at]". (The source has a typo here, "damnatat" for "damnat".) The phrase "in exitum operum quae damnat" means "to issue in / result in the works he condemns", with "exitus" meaning outcome. Thelwall's standard rendering agrees: "whatever He has made He has not made to issue in deeds which He condemns". The live English says "whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns". That makes "exitum" mean "destruction" and says God did not create things to destroy evil works. This wrecks Tertullian's argument. His point is that creation was not meant to lead to sin, even though sin is carried out through created things. The next clause, "licet eadem opera per ea quae condidit administrentur", only makes sense with that reading. The proposed fix is faithful. Its "certainly" stands for "constat", but in the full sentence it repeats "undoubtedly" (indubitate). Dropping it reads more cleanly, as in the version below.
verdict.better_correction: then undoubtedly whatever he created he did not create to issue in the works he condemns, even though those same works are carried out through the things he created

kept.english_quote: have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants
